chapters.title: Chapter 1: States of Matter and Phase Changes

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1(i) Matter is present in neon signs in the state of:

(a) Supercritical fluid (b) Plasma (c) Gas (d) Liquid crystal
Correct answer: Plasma

Q: 1(ii) Hazardous effects of shopping bags are studied in:

(a) Geochemistry (b) Inorganic Chemistry (c) Analytical Chemistry (d) Environmental Chemistry
Correct answer: Environmental Chemistry

Q: 1(iii) The man-made polymer is:

(a) Starch (b) Polystyrene (c) Protein (d) Cellulose
Correct answer: Polystyrene

Q: 1(iv) The crystals of which substance has rhombic shape?

(a) Brass (b) Sulphur (c) Graphite (d) Bronze
Correct answer: Sulphur

Q: 1(v) Which liquid among the following is a colloidal solution?

(a) Milk (b) Slaked lime used for white wash (c) Vinegar solution (d) Mixture of AgCl in water
Correct answer: Milk

Q: 1(vi) Which of the following is a heterogeneous mixture?

(a) A solution of calcium hydroxide in water (b) A solution of potassium nitrate in water (c) Hot chocolate (d) Concrete mixture
Correct answer: Concrete mixture

Q: 1(vii) A state of matter whose properties are between those of liquids and crystalline solids:

(a) Liquid crystal (b) Supercritical fluid (c) Plasma (d) Dark matter
Correct answer: Liquid crystal

Q: 1(viii) When the tiny visible particles of a substance are dispersed through a medium, the mixture is named as:

(a) True solution (b) Colloid (c) Suspension (d) Saturated solution
Correct answer: Suspension

Q: 1(ix) A solution of KClO3 has a solubility of about 13.2 g per 100 cm3 at 40 degrees C. How its solubility will be affected, if you decrease the temperature?

(a) The solubility will increase (b) The solubility will decrease (c) The solubility will remain the same (d) The solubility will first increase with temperature and then it will decrease
Correct answer: The solubility will decrease

Q: 1(x) You are studying the rate of hydrolysis of starch under different conditions of temperature. In which branch of chemistry this topic will fall?

(a) Organic Chemistry (b) Analytical Chemistry (c) Biochemistry (d) Physical Chemistry
Correct answer: Physical Chemistry

mcqs.q: 1(i) Matter is present in neon signs in the state of:
mcqs.why: In a neon sign the electric discharge ionises the gas into free electrons and positive ions. This ionised state of matter is plasma, the fourth state of matter, also found in the Sun and in fluorescent tubes.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) Hazardous effects of shopping bags are studied in:
mcqs.why: Used shopping bags are plastic waste that pollutes soil and water. Studying the harmful effects of chemical substances on air, water and soil is the work of environmental chemistry.

mcqs.q: 1(iii) The man-made polymer is:
mcqs.why: Starch, protein and cellulose are natural polymers produced by living organisms. Polystyrene is prepared artificially by polymerising styrene, so it is a man-made (synthetic) polymer.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) The crystals of which substance has rhombic shape?
mcqs.why: Sulphur exists in allotropic forms. Its form that is stable at room temperature is rhombic sulphur, which forms rhombic yellow crystals. Brass and bronze are alloys, not crystals of a single element, and graphite has hexagonal layers.

mcqs.q: 1(v) Which liquid among the following is a colloidal solution?
options: Slaked lime used for white wash
mcqs.why: Milk is an emulsion: tiny droplets of fat are dispersed in water and the particle size lies in the colloidal range, so milk is a colloidal solution. Vinegar is a true solution, while AgCl in water forms a suspension.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) Which of the following is a heterogeneous mixture?
options: A solution of calcium hydroxide in water
A solution of potassium nitrate in water
mcqs.why: Concrete is a mixture of cement, sand and gravel whose composition is not uniform throughout, so it is a heterogeneous mixture. The calcium hydroxide and potassium nitrate solutions are uniform (homogeneous) throughout.

mcqs.q: 1(vii) A state of matter whose properties are between those of liquids and crystalline solids:
mcqs.why: Liquid crystals flow like liquids yet keep an ordered arrangement of particles like crystalline solids, so their properties lie between those of liquids and crystalline solids.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) When the tiny visible particles of a substance are dispersed through a medium, the mixture is named as:
mcqs.why: When the dispersed particles are big enough to be seen (larger than colloidal particles) and they settle on standing, the mixture is called a suspension. Still smaller invisible particles give a colloid, and particles dissolved at molecular level give a true solution.

mcqs.q: 1(ix) A solution of KClO3 has a solubility of about 13.2 g per 100 cm3 at 40 degrees C. How its solubility will be affected, if you decrease the temperature?
options: The solubility will remain the same
The solubility will first increase with temperature and then it will decrease
mcqs.why: KClO3 is a solid solute whose solubility increases with rise in temperature. Decreasing the temperature reverses this: less KClO3 can remain dissolved, so its solubility decreases from about 13.2 g per 100 cm3 at 40 degrees C.

mcqs.q: 1(x) You are studying the rate of hydrolysis of starch under different conditions of temperature. In which branch of chemistry this topic will fall?
mcqs.why: The rate of hydrolysis means how fast the reaction proceeds and how conditions such as temperature affect its speed. Rates and the principles behind chemical changes are studied in physical chemistry.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) Why is there a need to divide Chemistry into many branches? Give three reasons.

Chemistry is a vast and complex subject covering a huge variety of substances and changes. (1) Dividing it into branches (physical, inorganic, organic, analytical, bio-, environmental and others) makes its study organised and manageable. (2) Each branch has its own methods and problems, so specialists can go deeper. (3) Different kinds of matter and reactions need different approaches, e.g. compounds of carbon are studied separately in organic chemistry.

Q: 2(ii) Reactions may take place due to electrons present outside the nucleus or they may take place inside the nucleus. Which branches of Chemistry cover these two types of reactions?

Reactions that take place through the electrons present outside the nucleus (ordinary chemical reactions: combination, decomposition, displacement and so on) are covered by the main branches such as physical, inorganic and organic chemistry. Reactions that take place inside the nucleus (radioactivity, fission and fusion) are covered by nuclear chemistry.

Q: 2(iii) What types of problems are solved in analytical chemistry?

Analytical chemistry solves problems of identification and measurement: which substances are present in a sample (qualitative analysis) and how much of each is present (quantitative analysis). It is used to test the purity of substances, the composition of ores, food, medicines, water and industrial products.

Q: 2(iv) Both graphite and graphene have hexagonal layered structures. What is the difference?

Graphite is made of many hexagonal layers of carbon atoms stacked over one another, held together by weak forces, so the layers can slide. Graphene is a single one-atom-thick layer of the same hexagonal carbon network, separated from graphite; it is the basic sheet from which graphite is built up.

Q: 2(v) Why are supercritical fluids important?

A supercritical fluid has properties of both a gas and a liquid: it can flow and spread like a gas yet dissolve substances like a liquid. Because of this it is important as a solvent in industry, e.g. for extracting caffeine from coffee and for dry cleaning and chemical processing, replacing harmful ordinary solvents.

Q: 2(vi) In which state does matter exist in the Sun?

Matter exists in the Sun in the plasma state: at its extremely high temperature the gases are ionised into a mixture of electrons and positive ions, which is plasma, the fourth state of matter.

Q: 2(vii) What is the importance of graphene?

Graphene is extremely strong, very light, flexible and an excellent conductor of heat and electricity, and it is almost transparent. These properties make it important for future electronics, touch screens, batteries, sensors and strong composite materials, which is why it is called a material of the future.

Q: 2(viii) Which form of matter do most of the material things in this world belong to?

Most material things in this world are mixtures: very few things around us are pure elements or pure compounds. Air, water from taps, soil, food, wood, petrol and our own bodies are all mixtures of many substances.

mcqs.q: Why is chemistry divided into many branches?
options: To increase the number of textbooks
So that students can avoid difficult topics
To make its vast study organised and manageable
Because every element needs a separate science
mcqs.why: Chemistry covers a huge variety of substances and changes. Dividing it into branches such as physical, inorganic, organic and analytical chemistry makes the study organised and manageable, and each branch can use its own methods and go deeper.

mcqs.q: Reactions that take place inside the nucleus, such as radioactivity, fission and fusion, are covered by:
mcqs.why: Ordinary chemical reactions take place through the electrons outside the nucleus. Reactions inside the nucleus itself - radioactivity, fission and fusion - are the subject of nuclear chemistry.

mcqs.q: Reactions that take place through the electrons outside the nucleus, such as combination and decomposition, are covered by:
mcqs.why: Combination, decomposition and displacement reactions all involve the outer electrons of atoms. These ordinary reactions are covered by the main branches: physical, inorganic and organic chemistry.

mcqs.q: Analytical chemistry solves problems of:
options: Which substances are present in a sample and how much of each
The structure of the atomic nucleus
mcqs.why: Analytical chemistry is about identification and measurement: qualitative analysis finds which substances are present in a sample and quantitative analysis finds how much of each is present, e.g. in testing the purity of food, water, ores and medicines.

mcqs.q: The difference between graphite and graphene is that graphene is:
options: A stack of many hexagonal layers
Made of carbon atoms bonded tetrahedrally
A single one-atom-thick hexagonal layer of carbon
An impure amorphous form of carbon
mcqs.why: Graphite is built of many hexagonal layers of carbon atoms stacked over one another and held by weak forces. Graphene is just one such layer, a single one-atom-thick hexagonal sheet separated from graphite.

mcqs.q: Graphite feels slippery because its layers:
options: Are joined by strong ionic bonds
Are charged and repel each other
Are held together by weak forces and slide over one another
mcqs.why: Within each layer of graphite the carbon atoms are strongly bonded in hexagons, but the layers are held to each other only by weak forces, so they slide easily - which is why graphite is slippery and works as a lubricant.

mcqs.q: Supercritical fluids are important as industrial solvents because they:
options: Flow and spread like a gas yet dissolve substances like a liquid
Are cheaper than all other solvents
React with every substance they touch
Are always found at room temperature
mcqs.why: A supercritical fluid has properties of both a gas and a liquid: it flows and spreads like a gas but dissolves substances like a liquid. It is therefore used to extract caffeine from coffee and in dry cleaning, replacing harmful ordinary solvents.

mcqs.q: Matter in the Sun exists in the state of:
mcqs.why: At the extremely high temperature of the Sun, gases are ionised into a mixture of free electrons and positive ions. This ionised mixture is plasma, the fourth state of matter.

mcqs.q: Graphene is called a material of the future because it is:
options: Extremely strong, very light, flexible and an excellent conductor
Found as thick blocks in nature
mcqs.why: Graphene combines extreme strength with lightness, flexibility, near-transparency and excellent conduction of heat and electricity, making it important for future electronics, touch screens, batteries and sensors.

mcqs.q: Most material things in this world belong to the category of:
mcqs.why: Very few things around us are pure elements or pure compounds. Air, tap water, soil, food, wood, petrol and even our own bodies are mixtures of many substances.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) How does a supercritical state look like?

A supercritical fluid looks like a single uniform fluid that is neither a proper liquid nor a gas: above the critical temperature and pressure the boundary (meniscus) between the liquid and its vapour disappears, and the whole substance becomes one dense fluid phase that fills its container like a gas but has the density and dissolving power of a liquid.

Q: 3(ii) In what way is plasma created in a fluorescent tube?

In a fluorescent tube a low-pressure gas (mercury vapour mixed with an inert gas) is present. When electricity is passed, the fast-moving electrons collide with the gas atoms and ionise them, producing a mixture of ions and free electrons, that is, plasma. The excited mercury atoms emit ultraviolet light, which makes the fluorescent coating inside the tube glow with visible light.

Q: 3(iii) Most of the molecules we study in biochemistry are organic in nature. Where does the difference exist in organic and biochemistry branches of Chemistry?

Organic chemistry studies the compounds of carbon in general, whether they occur in living or non-living matter, and concentrates on their preparation, structure and reactions. Biochemistry studies the chemical substances and processes occurring inside living organisms: although the molecules studied (proteins, carbohydrates, fats, enzymes) are organic, the emphasis is on their role in life processes such as digestion, respiration and growth.

Q: 3(iv) Give the reason of brilliance shown by diamond. Can you improve it?

Diamond is brilliant because of its very high refractive index and strong dispersion: light entering a cut diamond undergoes total internal reflection several times at its facets and is split into colours before leaving, producing the sparkle and fire. The brilliance can be improved by cutting the diamond into more and better-angled facets (an ideal cut), and by keeping it clean, so that maximum light is reflected back to the eye.

Q: 3(v) Explain the dissolution of sodium chloride in water.

Sodium chloride is an ionic compound of Na+ and Cl- ions held in a crystal lattice. Water is a polar solvent: its molecules attract the ions, the oxygen (negative) ends pulling Na+ ions and the hydrogen (positive) ends pulling Cl- ions out of the lattice. The freed ions become surrounded (hydrated) by water molecules and spread uniformly through the water, so the salt dissolves.

Q: 3(vi) Why do different compounds have different solubilities in water at a particular temperature?

Different compounds have different strengths of attraction between their own particles and different attractions for water particles. A solute dissolves well when its particles are attracted strongly by water and its own lattice is easily broken up; it dissolves poorly when its internal attractions are much stronger. The energy changes on dissolving also differ from compound to compound, so at a given temperature each has its own solubility.

Q: 3(vii) Why NaCl can not be crystallized from water just like KNO3?

The solubility of potassium nitrate rises steeply with temperature, so a hot saturated solution deposits beautiful crystals on cooling, and crystallisation purifies it. The solubility of sodium chloride, however, changes very little with temperature, so cooling its solution gives almost no crystals. NaCl is therefore obtained by evaporating the water, not by cooling crystallisation like KNO3.

Q: 3(viii) Why graphite is slippery to touch? Which property of graphite enables it to be used as lubricant?

Graphite has a layered structure: within each layer the carbon atoms are strongly bonded in hexagons, but the layers are held to each other only by weak forces, so they slide easily over one another. That is why graphite feels slippery and soft. This layer-sliding property makes it a good dry lubricant for machine parts where oil cannot be used.

mcqs.q: Above the critical temperature and pressure, a supercritical fluid looks like:
options: Two clearly separated layers of liquid and gas
A solid suspended in a gas
A liquid with a sharp meniscus in a half-filled container
A single dense fluid phase with no liquid-vapour boundary
mcqs.why: Above the critical temperature and pressure the boundary (meniscus) between the liquid and its vapour disappears. The substance becomes one dense fluid phase that fills its container like a gas but has the density and dissolving power of a liquid.

mcqs.q: Plasma is created inside a fluorescent tube when:
options: Fast-moving electrons collide with gas atoms and ionise them
The tube is heated to a very high temperature
The gas is compressed to a high pressure
Sunlight passes through the glass tube
mcqs.why: A fluorescent tube contains a low-pressure gas. When electricity passes, fast-moving electrons collide with the gas atoms and ionise them, producing a mixture of ions and free electrons - that is, plasma.

mcqs.q: The visible glow of a fluorescent tube is produced when:
options: Ultraviolet light from mercury atoms strikes the fluorescent coating
The glass of the tube becomes red hot
Room light is reflected by the coating
mcqs.why: The excited mercury atoms in the plasma emit ultraviolet light. This ultraviolet light makes the fluorescent coating inside the tube glow with visible light.

mcqs.q: Biochemistry differs from organic chemistry because biochemistry studies:
options: Carbon compounds obtained only from rocks
Chemical substances and processes inside living organisms
Reactions taking place inside the nucleus
mcqs.why: Both branches study organic molecules, but biochemistry concentrates on the substances and processes occurring inside living organisms - digestion, respiration and growth - while organic chemistry studies carbon compounds in general, living or non-living.

mcqs.q: The brilliance (sparkle) of a cut diamond is mainly due to:
options: A yellow colour inside the diamond
The metal setting holding the diamond
Its high refractive index and total internal reflection at its facets
mcqs.why: Diamond has a very high refractive index and strong dispersion. Light entering a cut diamond undergoes total internal reflection several times at its facets and is split into colours before leaving, producing the sparkle and fire; a better cut improves the brilliance.

mcqs.q: Sodium chloride dissolves in water because water molecules:
options: Pull Na+ and Cl- ions out of the crystal lattice and surround (hydrate) them
React chemically with the salt to form a new compound
Break the Na+ and Cl- ions into atoms
mcqs.why: Water is a polar solvent. Its oxygen (negative) ends attract Na+ ions and its hydrogen (positive) ends attract Cl- ions, pulling them out of the lattice. The freed ions become surrounded (hydrated) by water molecules and spread uniformly through the water.

mcqs.q: When NaCl dissolves, the oxygen end of a water molecule attracts:
mcqs.why: The oxygen end of a water molecule carries the negative side of the polar molecule, so it attracts the positive sodium ions, Na+. The hydrogen (positive) ends attract the chloride ions, Cl-.

mcqs.q: Different compounds have different solubilities in water at the same temperature because of differences in:
options: The sizes of the crystals in the bottle
The attractions between their own particles and their attractions for water
The names given to the compounds
mcqs.why: A solute dissolves well when water attracts its particles strongly and its own lattice is easily broken up. Because the internal attractions and the energy changes on dissolving differ from compound to compound, each compound has its own solubility at a given temperature.

mcqs.q: NaCl cannot be crystallised from its solution by cooling, like KNO3, because the solubility of NaCl:
mcqs.why: The solubility of KNO3 rises steeply with temperature, so cooling a hot saturated solution deposits crystals. The solubility of NaCl changes very little with temperature, so cooling gives almost no crystals; NaCl is obtained by evaporating the water instead.

mcqs.q: KNO3 can be purified by crystallisation because, on cooling its hot saturated solution:
options: Its solubility falls sharply and pure crystals separate out
It reacts with water to form a new salt
All impurities also crystallise with it
mcqs.why: Since the solubility of KNO3 falls sharply on cooling, pure KNO3 separates as crystals from the cooling solution while the soluble impurities stay behind in the mother liquor, so crystallisation purifies it.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study each of the following topics: (a) Rate of a reaction (b) Digestion of food in human body (c) Properties of plasma (d) Ecosystem (e) Reactions taking place during fireworks (f) Measurement of the absorption of wavelength with the help of ultraviolet spectrometer.

(a) Rate of a reaction: Physical Chemistry. (b) Digestion of food in human body: Biochemistry. (c) Properties of plasma: Physical Chemistry (plasma physics/chemistry). (d) Ecosystem: Environmental Chemistry. (e) Reactions taking place during fireworks: Inorganic Chemistry (the coloured metal salts used are inorganic compounds). (f) Measurement of the absorption of wavelength with the help of ultraviolet spectrometer: Analytical Chemistry (spectroscopic analysis).

Q: 4(ii) What are allotropic forms? Explain the allotropic forms of carbon and sulphur. How does coal differ from diamond?

Allotropic forms (allotropes) are the different physical forms of the same element, having different arrangements of atoms and therefore different properties. Carbon: diamond (each atom bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network; hardest natural substance, non-conductor), graphite (hexagonal layers; soft, slippery, conductor) and fullerenes/graphene. Sulphur: rhombic sulphur (yellow crystals, stable at room temperature) and monoclinic sulphur (needle-shaped crystals, formed above about 96 degrees C), besides plastic sulphur. Coal differs from diamond because coal is an impure, amorphous form of carbon mixed with other substances, formed from decayed vegetation; it has no regular crystal structure, is soft and black, and is used as a fuel, whereas diamond is pure crystalline carbon, extremely hard and transparent.

Q: 4(iii) What are supercritical fluids. How are they different from ordinary liquids?

A supercritical fluid is the state of a substance above its critical temperature and critical pressure, where the liquid and gas phases merge into a single phase. It differs from an ordinary liquid because it has no surface tension or meniscus, expands to fill its container like a gas, and its density and solvent power can be adjusted by changing pressure; yet like a liquid it can dissolve substances. Carbon dioxide above 31 degrees C and high pressure is a common example.

Q: 4(iv) Define solubility of a solute. How does the solubility of solutes change with the increase in temperature?

The solubility of a solute is the amount of solute (in grams) which can dissolve in 100 g of a solvent at a particular temperature to form a saturated solution. Effect of temperature: for most solid solutes solubility increases with rise in temperature (e.g. KNO3, KClO3), for a few it decreases, and for some like NaCl it changes very little. For gases, solubility in liquids decreases as temperature increases, which is why soda water is kept refrigerated.

Q: 4(v) What types of movements are present in gaseous and liquid molecules?

In gases, the molecules are far apart and move freely and randomly in all directions at high speeds: they have translational motion (and rotation). In liquids, the molecules are close together but can slide past one another, so they have translational and rotational movement within the liquid, and also vibrate about their positions. In both states the motion increases with temperature.

Q: 4(vi) Differentiate between the areas which are studied under inorganic and organic chemistry.

Organic chemistry studies the compounds of carbon, especially hydrocarbons and their derivatives (compounds of carbon with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, halogens and so on), which include fuels, plastics, medicines, food substances and the chemicals of living bodies. Inorganic chemistry studies all other compounds: the elements themselves, minerals, metals, salts, acids, bases and gases obtained mostly from non-living sources. Carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, carbonates and carbides are conventionally included in inorganic chemistry.

mcqs.q: The rate of a chemical reaction is studied in the branch called:
mcqs.why: Physical chemistry deals with the principles and measurements behind chemical changes, including how fast a reaction proceeds - its rate - and how conditions affect that rate.

mcqs.q: Digestion of food in the human body is studied in:
mcqs.why: Digestion is a chemical process occurring inside a living organism, and the chemistry of life processes - the substances and reactions in living bodies - is the field of biochemistry.

mcqs.q: Reactions taking place during fireworks are studied in inorganic chemistry because fireworks use:
mcqs.why: The brilliant colours of fireworks come from metal salts such as those of sodium, strontium and copper. Metal salts are inorganic compounds, so these reactions fall under inorganic chemistry.

mcqs.q: The study of an ecosystem, including pollution effects, belongs to:
mcqs.why: An ecosystem involves the chemical substances in air, water and soil and their effects on living things. Studying chemicals in the environment is the work of environmental chemistry.

mcqs.q: Measuring the absorption of wavelengths with an ultraviolet spectrometer is a topic of:
mcqs.why: Using instruments such as an ultraviolet spectrometer to identify substances and measure how much is present is spectroscopic analysis, which is part of analytical chemistry.

mcqs.q: Allotropic forms (allotropes) of an element are:
options: Compounds of an element with oxygen
Different physical forms of the same element with different arrangements of atoms
Mixtures of an element with other elements
mcqs.why: Allotropes are the different physical forms of the same element. Their atoms are arranged differently, so their properties differ - for example diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.

mcqs.q: Which pair consists of two allotropes of the same element?
mcqs.why: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon: in diamond each atom is bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network, while graphite has hexagonal layers. Coal is an impure, amorphous form of carbon mixed with other substances, not an allotrope.

mcqs.q: Rhombic sulphur changes into needle-shaped monoclinic sulphur at about:
mcqs.why: Rhombic sulphur, with yellow crystals, is the form stable at room temperature. Above about 96 degrees C it changes into monoclinic sulphur, which forms needle-shaped crystals - the two are allotropes of sulphur.

mcqs.q: The solubility of a solute is the amount of solute that can dissolve in:
options: 100 g of a solvent at a particular temperature to form a saturated solution
1 g of solvent at any temperature
100 g of solution at room temperature only
mcqs.why: Solubility is defined as the amount of solute (in grams) which can dissolve in 100 g of a solvent at a particular temperature to form a saturated solution.

mcqs.q: When the temperature of a liquid increases, the solubility of a gas in it:
mcqs.why: For gases dissolved in liquids, solubility decreases as temperature increases - the gas escapes more easily from the warm liquid. This is why soda water is kept refrigerated to keep the carbon dioxide dissolved.

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) Preparation of solutions leads to an important process in chemistry which enables us to purify a compound through crystallization. Describe a process in which potassium nitrate is purified by crystallizing it in water.

Dissolve the impure potassium nitrate in the minimum quantity of hot water to get a saturated solution. Filter it while hot to remove insoluble impurities. Allow the clear filtrate to cool slowly: since the solubility of KNO3 falls sharply on cooling, pure KNO3 separates out as crystals, while the soluble impurities stay in the mother liquor. Filter off the crystals, wash them with a little cold water and dry them. The crystals obtained are much purer than the starting salt.

Q: 5(ii) Graphene is called a miracle material and it is the material of the future. Which of its many properties makes it very useful in electronics?

Graphene is an excellent conductor of electricity (its electrons move through the single hexagonal sheet very fast) while being almost transparent, extremely thin, flexible and very strong. The combination of high electrical conductivity with transparency and flexibility makes it ideal for touch screens, flexible displays, fast transistors and other future electronic devices.

mcqs.q: To purify KNO3 by crystallisation, the impure salt is first dissolved in:
options: A large quantity of cold water
The minimum quantity of hot water
mcqs.why: The impure potassium nitrate is dissolved in the minimum quantity of hot water to obtain a saturated solution; using the minimum hot water ensures maximum crystals separate on cooling.

mcqs.q: Insoluble impurities are removed from the hot KNO3 solution by:
mcqs.why: The hot saturated solution is filtered while hot to remove insoluble impurities. Filtering must be done hot so that KNO3 does not crystallise out in the filter paper itself.

mcqs.q: When the clear hot filtrate of KNO3 is allowed to cool slowly:
options: The water evaporates completely at once
KNO3 changes into a different compound
Pure KNO3 crystals separate out because its solubility falls sharply
mcqs.why: The solubility of KNO3 falls sharply on cooling, so pure KNO3 separates out as crystals from the cooling solution, while the soluble impurities remain dissolved in the mother liquor.

mcqs.q: The liquid left behind after the KNO3 crystals are filtered off is called:
mcqs.why: The liquid remaining after crystallisation, which holds the soluble impurities, is called the mother liquor. The crystals are filtered off from it, washed with a little cold water and dried.

mcqs.q: The separated KNO3 crystals are washed with a little cold water rather than hot water so that:
options: The crystals do not redissolve during washing
The impurities dissolve into the crystals
mcqs.why: KNO3 is much more soluble in hot water, so washing with hot water would dissolve and lose the purified crystals. A little cold water removes the mother liquor from their surface with minimum loss.

mcqs.q: During crystallisation of KNO3, the soluble impurities:
options: Stay dissolved in the mother liquor
Settle as a solid layer at the bottom
mcqs.why: Soluble impurities remain dissolved in the liquid (mother liquor) when the pure KNO3 crystallises out, because only a small amount of solution is present and it stays saturated with the impurities - this is what makes crystallisation a purification process.

mcqs.q: The property of graphene that makes it most useful in electronics is its:
mcqs.why: Electrons move very fast through the single hexagonal sheet of graphene, giving it excellent electrical conductivity. Combined with its thinness and flexibility, this makes it ideal for fast transistors and other electronic devices.

mcqs.q: Graphene is ideal for touch screens because it combines:
options: Electrical conductivity with transparency and flexibility
mcqs.why: A touch screen material must conduct electricity, let light through and bend without breaking. Graphene is an excellent conductor, almost transparent and flexible, so it suits touch screens and flexible displays.

mcqs.q: In graphene, the electrons move:
options: Only when the sheet is heated strongly
Very fast through the single hexagonal sheet
Not at all, because it is an insulator
mcqs.why: Graphene is a single one-atom-thick hexagonal sheet of carbon. Its electrons move through this sheet very fast, which is the reason for its outstanding electrical conductivity.

mcqs.q: Which of the following devices can benefit most from graphene's properties?
mcqs.why: Flexible displays and fast transistors need a material that is thin, flexible, transparent and highly conductive. Graphene has exactly this combination of properties, so it is called a material of the future for electronics.

lessons.title: In-text Exercise & Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: In-text Exercise: Calculate the relative atomic mass of Lead (Pb). Isotopic abundances of isotopes Pb-204, Pb-206, Pb-207 and Pb-208 are 2.0, 24.0, 22.0, 52.0 respectively.

Given data: isotopes and abundances: Pb-204 = 2.0%, Pb-206 = 24.0%, Pb-207 = 22.0%, Pb-208 = 52.0%. Step 1 - Formula: relative atomic mass = (mass of isotope 1 x its % abundance + mass of isotope 2 x its % abundance + ...) / 100. Step 2 - Substitute the values: = (204 x 2.0 + 206 x 24.0 + 207 x 22.0 + 208 x 52.0) / 100. Step 3 - Multiply each term: = (408 + 4944 + 4554 + 10816) / 100. Step 4 - Add: = 20722 / 100. Step 5 - Final answer: relative atomic mass of lead = 207.22.

Q: 1(i) How many electrons can be accommodated at the most in the third shell of the elements?

(a) 8 (b) 18 (c) 10 (d) 32
Correct answer: 18

Q: 1(ii) What information was obtained from discharge tube experiments?

(a) Structure of atom was discovered. (b) Neutrons and protons were discovered. (c) Electrons and protons were discovered. (d) Presence of nucleus in an atom was discovered.
Correct answer: Electrons and protons were discovered.

Q: 1(iii) Why have isotopes not been shown in the periodic table?

(a) Periodic table cannot accommodate a large number of isotopes of different elements. (b) Some of the isotopes are unstable and they give rise to different elements (c) All the isotopes have same atomic number; so there is no need to give them separate places. (d) Isotopes do not show periodic behavior.
Correct answer: All the isotopes have same atomic number; so there is no need to give them separate places.

Q: 1(iv) Which particle is present in different number in the isotopes?

(a) Electron (b) Neutron (c) Proton (d) Both neutron and electron
Correct answer: Neutron

Q: 1(v) In which isotope of oxygen there are the equal number of protons, electrons and neutrons?

(a) O-17 (b) O-16 (c) O-18 (d) Non of these
Correct answer: O-16

Q: 1(vi) What will be the relative atomic mass of nitrogen given the abundances of its two isotopes, N-14 and N-15 are 99.64 and 0.35 respectively.

(a) 14.0210 (b) 14.0021 (c) 14.2100 (d) 14.1200
Correct answer: 14.0021

Q: 1(vii) How is radiocarbon dating useful for archeologists?

(a) It helps determine the age of organic matter. (b) It helps determine the composition of matter. (c) It helps determine the usefulness of matter. (d) It helps determine whether the matter is radioactive or not.
Correct answer: It helps determine the age of organic matter.

Q: 1(viii) What does keep the particles present in the nucleus intact?

(a) Particles are held together by strong nuclear force. (b) Particles are held together by weak nuclear force. (c) Particles are held together by electrostatic force. (d) Particles are held together by dipolar force.
Correct answer: Particles are held together by strong nuclear force.

Q: 1(ix) How do electrons keep themselves away from the oppositely charged nucleus?

(a) By keeping themselves stationary (b) By revolving around the nucleus (c) Due to their wave-like nature (d) A magnetic field around the nucleus keeps them away
Correct answer: By revolving around the nucleus

Q: 1(x) Rubidium consists of two isotopes Rb-85 and Rb-87. The percent abundance of the light isotope is 72.2%. What is the percent abundance of the heavier isotope? Its atomic mass is 85.47

(a) 15% (b) 27.8% (c) 37% (d) 72%
Correct answer: 27.8%

mcqs.q: 1(i) How many electrons can be accommodated at the most in the third shell of the elements?
mcqs.why: The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by 2n^2, where n is the shell number. For the third shell n = 3, so the capacity is 2 x (3)^2 = 2 x 9 = 18 electrons.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) What information was obtained from discharge tube experiments?
options: Presence of nucleus in an atom was discovered.
mcqs.why: In the discharge tube, cathode rays were found to consist of negatively charged particles - electrons - and the positive (canal) rays led to the discovery of the proton. So the discharge tube experiments discovered electrons and protons; the nucleus was discovered later by Rutherford's scattering experiment.

mcqs.q: 1(iii) Why have isotopes not been shown in the periodic table?
options: Periodic table cannot accommodate a large number of isotopes of different elements.
Some of the isotopes are unstable and they give rise to different elements
All the isotopes have same atomic number; so there is no need to give them separate places.
Isotopes do not show periodic behavior.
mcqs.why: Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number (same number of protons) and differ only in neutrons. Since an element's place in the periodic table is decided by its atomic number, all isotopes of an element share the same single place - there is no need to show them separately.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) Which particle is present in different number in the isotopes?
mcqs.why: Isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons but different mass numbers. The particle whose number changes from one isotope to another is the neutron.

mcqs.q: 1(v) In which isotope of oxygen there are the equal number of protons, electrons and neutrons?
mcqs.why: Oxygen has atomic number 8, so every oxygen atom has 8 protons and 8 electrons. In O-16 the number of neutrons is 16 - 8 = 8. Hence protons, electrons and neutrons are all 8 in number and equal.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) What will be the relative atomic mass of nitrogen given the abundances of its two isotopes, N-14 and N-15 are 99.64 and 0.35 respectively.
mcqs.why: Working: relative atomic mass = (14 x 99.64 + 15 x 0.35) / 100 = (1394.96 + 5.25) / 100 = 1400.21 / 100 = 14.0021. Because N-14 is overwhelmingly abundant (99.64%), the value lies very close to 14.

mcqs.q: 1(vii) How is radiocarbon dating useful for archeologists?
options: It helps determine the age of organic matter.
It helps determine the composition of matter.
It helps determine the usefulness of matter.
It helps determine whether the matter is radioactive or not.
mcqs.why: Radiocarbon dating uses the radioactive isotope carbon-14. Living things keep a fixed proportion of C-14, which decays after death at a known rate; measuring the C-14 left in old wood, bones or cloth tells archaeologists the age of the organic matter.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) What does keep the particles present in the nucleus intact?
options: Particles are held together by strong nuclear force.
Particles are held together by weak nuclear force.
Particles are held together by electrostatic force.
Particles are held together by dipolar force.
mcqs.why: The protons in a nucleus repel each other electrically, yet the nucleus does not fly apart because the protons and neutrons are bound by the very strong attractive nuclear force acting between the nucleons at short range.

mcqs.q: 1(ix) How do electrons keep themselves away from the oppositely charged nucleus?
options: A magnetic field around the nucleus keeps them away
mcqs.why: According to the atomic model used in this chapter, electrons do not fall into the oppositely charged nucleus because they keep revolving around it in their shells, like planets around the Sun; their motion keeps them in orbit.

mcqs.q: 1(x) Rubidium consists of two isotopes Rb-85 and Rb-87. The percent abundance of the light isotope is 72.2%. What is the percent abundance of the heavier isotope? Its atomic mass is 85.47
mcqs.why: The two abundances must add up to 100%. Percent abundance of the heavier isotope Rb-87 = 100 - 72.2 = 27.8%. (This agrees with the given atomic mass 85.47, which lies closer to 85 because the light isotope is more abundant.)

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) Why is it said that almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus?

The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, which are heavy particles, while the electrons revolving around it have negligible mass (an electron is about 1/1836 of a proton). So practically the whole mass of the atom is the mass of its nucleus, even though the nucleus is very small in size.

Q: 2(ii) Why are elements different from one another?

Elements differ from one another because their atoms contain different numbers of protons (different atomic numbers), and hence different numbers of electrons arranged in shells. It is the number and arrangement of electrons that gives each element its own chemical behaviour.

Q: 2(iii) How many neutrons are present in Bi-210 (atomic number 83)?

Step 1 - Formula: number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number. Step 2 - Substitute: neutrons = 210 - 83. Step 3 - Final answer: 127 neutrons are present in Bi-210.

Q: 2(iv) Why is tritium (H-3) a radioactive element?

Tritium (H-3) has one proton and two neutrons in its tiny nucleus. This proton-neutron combination is unstable for hydrogen, so the nucleus throws out radiation (a beta particle) and changes into helium-3; therefore tritium is a radioactive isotope.

Q: 2(v) How can an atom absorb and envolve energy?

An atom absorbs energy when an electron jumps from a lower shell to a higher shell, for example when the atom is heated or struck by light. It evolves (emits) energy when the electron falls back from the higher shell to a lower shell, giving out the absorbed energy as light of a definite colour.

mcqs.q: Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus because:
options: The nucleus is the largest part of the atom
The nucleus contains most of the electrons
The nucleus contains the heavy protons and neutrons, while electrons have negligible mass
mcqs.why: Protons and neutrons are heavy particles and both sit in the nucleus. An electron has only about 1/1836 of the mass of a proton, so the revolving electrons contribute almost nothing; practically the whole mass of the atom is the mass of its nucleus.

mcqs.q: The mass of an electron is about:
options: 1/1836 of the mass of a proton
Equal to the mass of a proton
1/100 of the mass of a proton
Twice the mass of a neutron
mcqs.why: An electron is an extremely light particle: its mass is about 1/1836 of the mass of a proton. That is why the mass of an atom is taken as the combined mass of its protons and neutrons.

mcqs.q: Elements are different from one another because their atoms have different:
mcqs.why: Each element has its own number of protons - its atomic number - and hence its own number and arrangement of electrons in shells. It is the number and arrangement of electrons that gives each element its own chemical behaviour.

mcqs.q: How many neutrons are present in Bi-210 (atomic number 83)?
mcqs.why: Working: number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 210 - 83 = 127. So Bi-210 contains 127 neutrons (and 83 protons).

mcqs.q: Tritium (H-3) is radioactive because:
options: Its nucleus of one proton and two neutrons is unstable and emits a beta particle
mcqs.why: Tritium has one proton and two neutrons in its tiny nucleus. This proton-neutron combination is unstable for hydrogen, so the nucleus throws out a beta particle and changes into helium-3; that is why tritium is a radioactive isotope.

mcqs.q: When tritium decays by beta emission, it changes into:
mcqs.why: Tritium (H-3) has 1 proton and 2 neutrons. On emitting a beta particle one neutron changes into a proton, giving a nucleus of 2 protons and 1 neutron - helium-3.

mcqs.q: An atom absorbs energy when an electron:
options: Falls from a higher shell to a lower shell
Jumps from a lower shell to a higher shell
mcqs.why: When an atom is heated or struck by light, an electron absorbs energy and jumps from a lower (inner) shell to a higher (outer) shell. The atom is then in an excited state.

mcqs.q: An atom evolves (emits) energy in the form of light when an electron:
options: Falls back from a higher shell to a lower shell
mcqs.why: The excited electron falls back from the higher shell to a lower shell and gives out the absorbed energy as light of a definite colour. Absorption is jump outward; emission is fall inward.

mcqs.q: Using the in-text data (Pb-204 = 2.0%, Pb-206 = 24.0%, Pb-207 = 22.0%, Pb-208 = 52.0%), the relative atomic mass of lead is:
Which particles contribute almost nothing to the mass of an atom?
mcqs.why: Electrons have negligible mass (about 1/1836 of a proton). Protons and neutrons, which make up the nucleus, account for practically the entire mass of the atom.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) Why does the energy of electron increase as we move from first shell to second shell?

According to Bohr's model, each shell has a fixed energy and the energy of a shell increases with its distance from the nucleus, because an electron farther from the nucleus is less strongly attracted by it. So an electron in the second shell has more energy than one in the first shell, and so on.

Q: 3(ii) Why is it needed to lower the pressure of the gas inside the discharge tube?

At ordinary pressure the gas molecules are too close together: the electrons and ions produced would collide too frequently and recombine, and the discharge could not pass through the gas easily. Lowering the pressure increases the distance between molecules so that particles can travel and gain enough energy between collisions to ionise the gas and produce cathode rays and canal rays.

Q: 3(iii) What is the classical concept of an electron? How has this concept changed with time?

Classically the electron was imagined as a tiny solid particle of definite mass and charge revolving around the nucleus in a definite orbit, like a planet around the Sun. With time this concept changed: experiments showed the electron also behaves like a wave (wave-particle duality), and in the modern quantum model the electron is described by probability clouds (orbitals) rather than fixed paths.

Q: 3(iv) Why the nuclei of the radioactive elements are unstable?

The protons in a nucleus repel one another electrically because they carry the same charge. The nucleus stays together only while the strong nuclear force of attraction between the nucleons overcomes this repulsion. In radioactive elements the nuclei are too large or have an unsuitable proton-neutron ratio, so the balance fails, the nucleus is unstable and it throws out radiation to become more stable.

Q: 3(v) During discharge tube experiments, how did the scientists conclude that the same type of electrons and protons are present in all the elements?

In the discharge tube, whichever gas was taken, the cathode rays produced always consisted of particles having the same charge-to-mass ratio, identified as electrons; and the positive (canal) rays from hydrogen gave the lightest positive particle, the proton, found with the same charge in all gases. Since the same electrons and protons appear from every element, scientists concluded that all atoms are built of these same fundamental particles.

mcqs.q: According to Bohr's model, the energy of an electron increases as we move from the first shell to the second shell because:
options: Shell energy increases with distance from the nucleus, as the electron is less strongly attracted
The second shell contains more protons
Electrons in the second shell are heavier
The nucleus attracts outer electrons more strongly
mcqs.why: In Bohr's model each shell has a fixed energy, and the energy of a shell increases with its distance from the nucleus because an electron farther away is less strongly attracted by it. So an electron in the second shell has more energy than one in the first shell.

mcqs.q: The pressure of the gas inside a discharge tube is lowered so that:
options: Particles can travel and gain enough energy between collisions to ionise the gas
More gas can be filled in the tube
mcqs.why: At ordinary pressure the gas molecules are too close together: electrons and ions collide too frequently, recombine, and the discharge cannot pass easily. Lowering the pressure increases the distance between molecules so particles gain enough energy between collisions to ionise the gas and produce cathode rays and canal rays.

mcqs.q: At ordinary pressure, a discharge cannot pass properly through a gas because:
options: The gas has no electrons at all
The molecules are too close, so particles collide too frequently and recombine
The gas turns into plasma permanently
mcqs.why: At ordinary pressure the molecules are crowded together. The electrons and ions produced collide again and again and recombine before they can travel far, so cathode rays and canal rays cannot be produced properly; the pressure must be lowered.

mcqs.q: In the classical concept, an electron was imagined as:
options: A wave spread over the whole atom
A probability cloud with no path
A tiny solid particle revolving in a definite orbit like a planet around the Sun
mcqs.why: Classically the electron was pictured as a tiny solid particle of definite mass and charge revolving around the nucleus in a definite orbit, just as a planet revolves around the Sun.

mcqs.q: In the modern quantum model, the electron is described by:
options: Probability clouds (orbitals) rather than fixed paths
A solid shell around the nucleus
mcqs.why: Experiments showed the electron also behaves like a wave (wave-particle duality). In the modern quantum model the electron is therefore described by probability clouds called orbitals, not by fixed planetary paths.

mcqs.q: The nuclei of radioactive elements are unstable because:
options: The repulsion between protons overcomes the balancing strong nuclear force in their large or unbalanced nuclei
They contain no neutrons at all
mcqs.why: Protons in a nucleus repel one another because they carry the same charge. The nucleus holds together only while the strong nuclear force overcomes this repulsion. In radioactive elements the nuclei are too large or have an unsuitable proton-neutron ratio, so the balance fails and the nucleus throws out radiation to become more stable.

mcqs.q: Scientists concluded that the same electrons are present in all elements because cathode rays from every gas:
options: Had different colours for each gas
Were heavier than the gas atoms
Always consisted of particles with the same charge-to-mass ratio
mcqs.why: Whichever gas was taken in the discharge tube, the cathode rays always consisted of particles having the same charge-to-mass ratio, identified as electrons. The same electrons appearing from every element showed that all atoms are built of the same fundamental particles.

mcqs.q: The proton was identified from the positive (canal) rays obtained from:
options: Hydrogen, which gave the lightest positive particle
mcqs.why: The positive (canal) rays from hydrogen gave the lightest positive particle, the proton, and the same charged particle was found in the rays from all other gases - showing protons are present in all elements.

mcqs.q: In Bohr's model, each shell of an atom has:
options: A fixed energy, increasing with distance from the nucleus
The same energy as every other shell
Energy decreasing with distance from the nucleus
mcqs.why: Bohr proposed that electrons revolve in shells of fixed energy. The farther a shell is from the nucleus, the higher its energy, because the electron there is less strongly attracted by the nucleus.

mcqs.q: The strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together by:
options: Repelling the electrons from the nucleus
Attracting protons and neutrons to one another at short range
mcqs.why: The nucleons (protons and neutrons) attract one another through the strong nuclear force, which acts at very short range. While this attraction overcomes the electrical repulsion between protons, the nucleus stays intact.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) Explain the structure of a hydrogen atom.

The hydrogen atom is the simplest atom. It has one proton in its nucleus and one electron revolving around the nucleus in the first shell (K shell). It has no neutron. Being electrically neutral, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so its atomic number is 1 and mass number is 1. (Its heavier isotopes, deuterium and tritium, contain one and two neutrons respectively.)

Q: 4(ii) How does the theory of atomic structure explain the ionization of atoms by a radioactive isotope?

Radioactive isotopes throw out fast particles and rays (alpha, beta and gamma). When these radiations pass through a gas, their energy knocks electrons out of the atoms of the gas, leaving positive ions and free electrons behind; this is ionisation. Atomic theory explains it: the atom consists of electrons around a nucleus, and radiation with enough energy can remove an electron, converting a neutral atom into an ion.

Q: 4(iii) What is radioactivity? Explain any three applications of radioactive isotopes.

Radioactivity is the spontaneous throwing out of radiation (alpha, beta or gamma rays) by the unstable nuclei of heavy elements, in which the nucleus changes into a new, more stable nucleus. Applications of radioactive isotopes: (1) In medicine, to diagnose and treat diseases, e.g. cobalt-60 for treating cancer and iodine-131 for thyroid disorders. (2) In agriculture and research, as tracers to follow the uptake of fertilisers by plants. (3) In industry and archaeology, e.g. checking welds and thickness of sheets, and carbon-14 dating to find the age of old organic remains.

Q: 4(iv) Find out the relative atomic mass of mercury from the following data: Hg-196 = 0.0146%, Hg-198 = 10.02%, Hg-201 = 13.22%, Hg-204 = 6.85%, Hg-199 = 16.34%, Hg-200 = 23.13%, Hg-202 = 29.80%.

Given data: Hg-196 = 0.0146%, Hg-198 = 10.02%, Hg-199 = 16.34%, Hg-200 = 23.13%, Hg-201 = 13.22%, Hg-202 = 29.80%, Hg-204 = 6.85%. Step 1 - Formula: relative atomic mass = (sum over isotopes of isotopic mass x % abundance) / 100. Step 2 - Substitute: = (196 x 0.0146 + 198 x 10.02 + 199 x 16.34 + 200 x 23.13 + 201 x 13.22 + 202 x 29.80 + 204 x 6.85) / 100. Step 3 - Multiply each term: = (2.86 + 1983.96 + 3251.66 + 4626.00 + 2657.22 + 6019.60 + 1397.40) / 100. Step 4 - Add the terms: = 19938.70 / 100. Step 5 - Final answer: relative atomic mass of mercury = 199.39 (about 199.4) from the data as printed.

mcqs.q: The hydrogen atom consists of:
options: One proton, one neutron and one electron
One proton in the nucleus and one electron in the first shell, with no neutron
One neutron and one electron only
mcqs.why: Hydrogen is the simplest atom: one proton in its nucleus and one electron revolving in the first (K) shell. It has no neutron, so its atomic number and mass number are both 1. Its heavier isotopes deuterium and tritium contain one and two neutrons respectively.

mcqs.q: Deuterium (H-2) differs from ordinary hydrogen (H-1) in having:
mcqs.why: Deuterium is an isotope of hydrogen: it has the same one proton and one electron as H-1, but its nucleus also contains one neutron, making its mass number 2.

mcqs.q: Radioactive radiations ionise a gas because they:
options: Heat the gas until it melts
Add protons to the gas atoms
Convert the gas into a liquid
Knock electrons out of the gas atoms, leaving positive ions and free electrons
mcqs.why: Alpha, beta and gamma radiations carry energy. When they pass through a gas, this energy knocks electrons out of the atoms, leaving positive ions and free electrons behind - this is ionisation, explained by the atom's structure of electrons around a nucleus.

mcqs.q: Radioactivity is:
options: The spontaneous throwing out of radiation by unstable nuclei, changing them into more stable nuclei
The emission of light by hot metals
The splitting of molecules by heat
mcqs.why: Radioactivity is the spontaneous throwing out of radiation (alpha, beta or gamma rays) by the unstable nuclei of heavy elements. In the process the nucleus changes into a new, more stable nucleus.

mcqs.q: Cobalt-60 is used in medicine for:
options: Checking the thickness of steel sheets
mcqs.why: The gamma rays from cobalt-60 can destroy cancerous cells, so Co-60 is used in the treatment of cancer. Iodine-131 is used for thyroid disorders and carbon-14 for dating old organic remains.

mcqs.q: Iodine-131 is used in medicine for disorders of the:
mcqs.why: Iodine is taken up by the thyroid gland, so the radioactive isotope iodine-131 is used to diagnose and treat thyroid disorders - it collects in the gland and its radiation can be detected or used in treatment.

mcqs.q: Carbon-14 dating is used to find:
options: The age of old organic remains
mcqs.why: Living organisms contain a fixed proportion of carbon-14, which decays at a known rate after death. Measuring the C-14 remaining in old wood, bones or cloth gives the age of the organic remains.

mcqs.q: Radioactive tracers are used in agriculture to:
options: Follow the uptake of fertilisers by plants
Measure the age of the soil
mcqs.why: A radioactive isotope mixed with a fertiliser can be traced as the plant absorbs it, because its radiation is detectable. Tracers thus show how fertilisers are taken up and used by plants.

mcqs.q: From the printed data for mercury isotopes, the relative atomic mass of mercury comes out to be:
mcqs.why: Working: (196 x 0.0146 + 198 x 10.02 + 199 x 16.34 + 200 x 23.13 + 201 x 13.22 + 202 x 29.80 + 204 x 6.85) / 100 = 19938.70 / 100 = 199.39. Note: the printed abundances add up to only 99.37%, so the result is computed from the data exactly as printed.

mcqs.q: The atomic number and mass number of ordinary hydrogen are both:
mcqs.why: Ordinary hydrogen has one proton (atomic number 1) and no neutron, so its mass number (protons + neutrons) is also 1. It is the only atom with no neutron.

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) How can scientists synthesize elements in the laboaratory?

Scientists synthesise new elements by nuclear reactions: they bombard the nuclei of a target element with fast-moving particles (protons, neutrons or the nuclei of light elements) in particle accelerators. The bombarding particle joins the nucleus, producing a new, heavier element that does not occur in nature, e.g. the transuranium elements made in laboratories.

Q: 5(ii) A system just like our solar system exists in an atom. Comment on this statement.

The statement refers to Rutherford's/Bohr's model of the atom: just as the planets revolve around the Sun in the solar system, electrons revolve around the central nucleus in definite orbits or shells. The comparison is useful but not perfect: the planets are held by gravity while electrons are held by electrostatic attraction, and electrons, unlike planets, can jump between orbits by absorbing or emitting energy.

mcqs.q: Scientists synthesise new elements in the laboratory by:
options: Mixing two elements and heating them strongly
Cooling gases to very low temperatures
Bombarding target nuclei with fast-moving particles in particle accelerators
mcqs.why: New elements are made by nuclear reactions: the nuclei of a target element are bombarded with fast-moving protons, neutrons or light nuclei in particle accelerators. The bombarding particle joins the nucleus, producing a new, heavier element.

mcqs.q: The particles used to bombard target nuclei include:
options: Protons, neutrons and the nuclei of light elements
mcqs.why: In particle accelerators, target nuclei are bombarded with fast-moving particles such as protons, neutrons or the nuclei of light elements. When such a particle joins the target nucleus, a new heavier element is produced.

mcqs.q: The transuranium elements are:
options: Elements heavier than uranium made artificially in laboratories
Elements found deep in the earth
mcqs.why: The transuranium elements do not occur in nature; they have been synthesised in laboratories by bombarding uranium and other heavy nuclei with fast particles in accelerators.

mcqs.q: The statement 'a system just like our solar system exists in an atom' refers to:
options: Rutherford's/Bohr's model, in which electrons revolve around the nucleus like planets around the Sun
The wave model of the electron only
mcqs.why: In the Rutherford-Bohr model the massive central nucleus is like the Sun and the electrons revolve around it in definite orbits or shells, just as planets revolve around the Sun in the solar system.

mcqs.q: In the solar-system model of the atom, electrons are held in their orbits by:
mcqs.why: Planets are held by gravity, but electrons are held by the electrostatic (electrical) attraction between their negative charge and the positive nucleus - one way in which the solar-system comparison is not exact.

mcqs.q: Unlike planets, electrons in an atom can:
options: Change into other particles at will
Jump between orbits by absorbing or emitting energy
mcqs.why: Planets stay in their orbits, but an electron can absorb energy and jump to a higher orbit, or emit energy and fall back to a lower one. This jumping is a key difference between the atom and the solar system.

mcqs.q: In the solar-system comparison, the nucleus of the atom corresponds to:
mcqs.why: The nucleus is the massive centre of the atom around which the electrons revolve, just as the Sun is the massive centre of the solar system around which the planets revolve.

mcqs.q: A new, heavier element is produced in an accelerator when:
options: A bombarding particle joins the target nucleus
mcqs.why: When a fast-moving proton, neutron or light nucleus strikes a target nucleus and joins it, the total number of protons/neutrons increases and a new, heavier element - often one not found in nature - is produced.

mcqs.q: Particle accelerators are used in element synthesis to:
options: Speed up the particles used to bombard target nuclei
mcqs.why: A bombarding particle must move very fast to overcome the repulsion of the target nucleus and join it. Particle accelerators give protons, neutrons or light nuclei the very high speeds needed.

mcqs.q: The solar-system model of the atom is useful but not perfect because:
options: Atoms are much bigger than the solar system
The nucleus is smaller than the Sun
Electrons have no mass at all
Electrons are held by electrostatic force and can jump between orbits, unlike planets
mcqs.why: The comparison explains revolution around a centre, but planets are held by gravity while electrons are held by electrostatic attraction, and electrons - unlike planets - can jump between orbits by absorbing or emitting energy.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1(i) When molten copper and molten zinc are mixed together, they give rise to a new substance called brass. Predict what type of bond is formed between copper and zinc.

(a) Coordinate covalent bond (b) Ionic bond (c) Metallic bond (d) Covalent bond
Correct answer: Metallic bond

Q: 1(ii) Which element is capable of forming all the three types of bonds; covalent, coordinate covalent and ionic?

(a) Carbon (b) Oxygen (c) Magnesium (d) Silicon
Correct answer: Oxygen

Q: 1(iii) Why is H2O a liquid while H2S is a gas?

(a) Because in water, the atomic size of oxygen is smaller than that of sulphur (b) Because water is a polar compound and there exists strong forces of attraction between its molecules (c) Because H2O molecule is lighter than H2S (d) Because water can easily freeze into ice
Correct answer: Because water is a polar compound and there exists strong forces of attraction between its molecules

Q: 1(iv) Which of the following bonds is expected to be the weakest?

(a) C - C (b) Cl - Cl (c) O - O (d) F - F
Correct answer: O - O

Q: 1(v) Which form of carbon is used as a lubricant?

(a) Coal (b) Diamond (c) Graphite (d) Charcoal
Correct answer: Graphite

Q: 1(vi) Keeping in view the intermolecular forces of attraction, indicate which compound has the highest boiling point.

(a) H2O (b) H2S (c) HF (d) NH3
Correct answer: H2O

Q: 1(vii) Which metal has the lowest melting point?

(a) Li (b) Na (c) K (d) Rb
Correct answer: Rb

Q: 1(viii) Which ionic compound has the highest melting point?

(a) NaCl (b) KCl (c) LiCl (d) RbCl
Correct answer: NaCl

Q: 1(ix) Which compound contains both covalent and ionic bonds?

(a) MgCl2 (b) NH4Cl (c) CaO (d) PCl3
Correct answer: NH4Cl

Q: 1(x) Which among the following has a double covalent bond?

(a) Ethane (b) Methane (c) Ethylene (d) Acetylene
Correct answer: Ethylene

mcqs.q: 1(i) When molten copper and molten zinc are mixed together, they give rise to a new substance called brass. Predict what type of bond is formed between copper and zinc.
mcqs.why: Brass is an alloy of two metals, copper and zinc. Atoms of metals are held together by the metallic bond - the attraction between positive metal ions and the sea of free electrons around them - so the bond formed between copper and zinc is metallic.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) Which element is capable of forming all the three types of bonds; covalent, coordinate covalent and ionic?
mcqs.why: Oxygen forms a covalent bond in O2, a coordinate covalent bond (for example in ozone and in the oxonium ion, where oxygen donates a lone pair), and ionic bonds in metal oxides such as Na2O. So oxygen can form all three types of bonds.

mcqs.q: 1(iii) Why is H2O a liquid while H2S is a gas?
options: Because in water, the atomic size of oxygen is smaller than that of sulphur
Because water is a polar compound and there exists strong forces of attraction between its molecules
Because H2O molecule is lighter than H2S
Because water can easily freeze into ice
mcqs.why: Water molecules are polar and are held together by strong intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonding), so much energy is needed to separate them and water is a liquid. In H2S the forces between molecules are weak, so H2S is a gas.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) Which of the following bonds is expected to be the weakest?
mcqs.why: Among the given single bonds, the O-O bond is the weakest. The two small oxygen atoms carry lone pairs that repel each other strongly, weakening the bond between them; the C-C bond has no such lone-pair repulsion and is much stronger.

mcqs.q: 1(v) Which form of carbon is used as a lubricant?
mcqs.why: Graphite has a layered structure in which the layers slide easily over one another, so it is soft, slippery and used as a lubricant. Diamond is hard, and coal and charcoal are impure forms of carbon.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) Keeping in view the intermolecular forces of attraction, indicate which compound has the highest boiling point.
mcqs.why: Water has the strongest hydrogen bonding among the given compounds: each water molecule can form an extended network of hydrogen bonds, so the most energy is needed to separate its molecules and it has the highest boiling point.

mcqs.q: 1(vii) Which metal has the lowest melting point?
mcqs.why: Down the group of alkali metals the atoms get bigger, the attraction between the positive ions and the electron sea becomes weaker, and the melting point falls. Rubidium, being the lowest of the given metals in the group, has the lowest melting point.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) Which ionic compound has the highest melting point?
mcqs.why: The melting point of these ionic chlorides falls as the ions get larger and the lattice attraction weakens (KCl, RbCl), while LiCl has some covalent character because the very small Li+ ion polarises the Cl- ion, lowering its melting point. NaCl therefore has the highest melting point of the four.

mcqs.q: 1(ix) Which compound contains both covalent and ionic bonds?
mcqs.why: In NH4Cl the ammonium ion NH4+ and chloride ion Cl- are held by an ionic bond, while the four N-H bonds inside the ammonium ion are covalent (one of them formed as a coordinate bond). So NH4Cl contains both ionic and covalent bonds.

mcqs.q: 1(x) Which among the following has a double covalent bond?
mcqs.why: Ethylene (C2H4) has a double covalent bond between its two carbon atoms (C=C). Ethane and methane have only single bonds, while acetylene has a triple bond.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) What type of elements lose their outer electron easily and what type of elements gain electron easily?

Metals (electropositive elements, on the left of the periodic table) lose their outer electrons easily because their atoms have large sizes and low ionisation energies, forming positive ions. Non-metals (electronegative elements, on the right) gain electrons easily because their atoms are small and attract electrons strongly, forming negative ions.

Q: 2(ii) Why do lower molecular mass covalent compounds exist as gases or low boiling liquids.

Their molecules are held together only by weak intermolecular (van der Waals) forces, because there are no ions or strong bonds between molecules. Very little heat energy is needed to separate the molecules, so such compounds melt and boil at low temperatures and exist as gases or low-boiling liquids.

Q: 2(iii) Give one example of an element which exists as a crystalline solid and it has covalent bonds between its atoms.

Diamond (also silicon and silicon dioxide, sand): in diamond each carbon atom is joined to four other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds in a giant crystalline network, making it a hard crystalline solid.

Q: 2(iv) Which property of metals makes them malleable and ductile?

The non-directional nature of the metallic bond: the positive metal ions are held in a 'sea' of free electrons, and when a force is applied the layers of ions can slide over one another without the bond breaking, because the electron sea re-adjusts around them. Hence metals can be hammered into sheets (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile).

Q: 2(v) Is cordinate covalent bond a strong bond?

Yes. Once formed, a coordinate covalent bond is exactly like an ordinary covalent bond: the shared pair of electrons holds the atoms together with comparable strength, and it cannot be distinguished from a normal covalent bond in the finished molecule, e.g. the N-H bonds in the ammonium ion are all equally strong.

Q: 2(vi) Write down dot and cross formula of HNO3.

Dot and cross structure of HNO3 (draw with dots for one atom's electrons and crosses for the others): hydrogen is joined to an oxygen atom by a shared pair (single bond). This oxygen is joined to nitrogen by a single shared pair. Nitrogen is joined to the second oxygen by a double bond (two shared pairs), and to the third oxygen by a coordinate bond: nitrogen provides both electrons of the pair (shown as two dots from nitrogen). The third oxygen therefore carries a negative character and nitrogen a positive character in the structure HO-N(=O)-O.

mcqs.q: Metals lose their outer electrons easily because their atoms:
options: Are large and have low ionisation energies
Are small and attract electrons strongly
Are on the right of the periodic table
mcqs.why: Metals are electropositive elements on the left of the periodic table. Their atoms are large and their ionisation energies are low, so their outer electrons are easily removed and they form positive ions.

mcqs.q: Non-metals gain electrons easily because their atoms:
options: Are large with low ionisation energies
Are small and attract electrons strongly
Have a sea of free electrons
mcqs.why: Non-metals are electronegative elements on the right of the periodic table. Their atoms are small and attract electrons strongly, so they gain electrons easily and form negative ions.

mcqs.q: Covalent compounds of low molecular mass exist as gases or low-boiling liquids because:
options: Strong hydrogen bonds join all their molecules
Only weak van der Waals forces hold their molecules together
Their covalent bonds break on heating
mcqs.why: Between the molecules of a covalent compound there are no ions or strong bonds - only weak intermolecular (van der Waals) forces. Very little heat energy separates the molecules, so such compounds melt and boil at low temperatures.

mcqs.q: Diamond is a crystalline solid with covalent bonds because in diamond:
options: Carbon atoms are held by a sea of electrons
Weak forces hold separate molecules together
Each carbon atom is joined to four others in a giant covalent network
mcqs.why: In diamond each carbon atom is joined to four other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds in a giant crystalline network (silicon and silicon dioxide are similar). This giant structure makes diamond a hard crystalline solid.

mcqs.q: The property of the metallic bond that makes metals malleable and ductile is that it is:
options: Non-directional, so layers of ions can slide in the electron sea without breaking the bond
Present only at the surface of the metal
Broken whenever a force is applied
mcqs.why: In a metal the positive ions sit in a sea of free electrons and the bond is non-directional. When a force is applied, layers of ions slide over one another while the electron sea re-adjusts around them, so the metal can be hammered into sheets (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile) without breaking.

mcqs.q: Once formed, a coordinate covalent bond is:
options: Much weaker than a covalent bond
As strong as an ordinary covalent bond and indistinguishable from it
Broken as soon as the molecule forms
mcqs.why: Yes, a coordinate covalent bond is a strong bond. Once formed it is exactly like an ordinary covalent bond - the shared pair holds the atoms with comparable strength and cannot be distinguished from a normal covalent bond, e.g. all the N-H bonds in the ammonium ion are equally strong.

mcqs.q: In the ammonium ion NH4+, the four N-H bonds are:
options: Three strong and one very weak
All equally strong, including the one formed by coordinate bonding
Broken one by one in water
mcqs.why: One N-H bond in NH4+ is formed when nitrogen donates its lone pair to H+ (coordinate bond), but once formed all four N-H bonds are identical and equally strong - a coordinate bond cannot be distinguished from an ordinary covalent bond in the finished ion.

mcqs.q: In the dot-and-cross structure of HNO3, the coordinate bond is formed when:
options: Hydrogen donates both electrons to oxygen
The second oxygen donates a pair to hydrogen
Nitrogen gains a pair from hydrogen
Nitrogen provides both electrons of the shared pair to the third oxygen atom
mcqs.why: In HNO3, hydrogen is singly bonded to one oxygen, which is singly bonded to nitrogen; nitrogen is double-bonded to the second oxygen and joined to the third oxygen by a coordinate bond in which nitrogen provides both electrons of the pair, HO-N(=O)-O.

mcqs.q: Electropositive elements, which lose electrons easily, are found:
options: On the left side of the periodic table
On the right side of the periodic table
In the middle of the transition block only
mcqs.why: Electropositive elements are metals, placed on the left of the periodic table. Their large atoms with low ionisation energies lose outer electrons easily and form positive ions.

mcqs.q: Besides diamond, an element/compound that is a crystalline solid with covalent bonds is:
mcqs.why: Silicon and silicon dioxide (sand) have giant structures of strong covalent bonds like diamond. NaCl is ionic, copper is metallic, and iodine is a molecular covalent solid, not a giant covalent crystal.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) Why HF is a liquid while HCl is a gas?

Fluorine is the most electronegative element and very small, so HF molecules are strongly polar and are held together by strong hydrogen bonding; considerable energy is needed to separate them, so HF is a liquid at room temperature. In HCl the intermolecular forces are much weaker (only dipole-dipole and van der Waals forces, no effective hydrogen bonding), so its molecules escape easily and HCl is a gas.

Q: 3(ii) Why covalent compounds are generally not soluble in water?

Most covalent compounds consist of non-polar molecules. Water is a polar solvent and dissolves substances whose particles can interact with its charges, such as ions and polar molecules. Non-polar covalent molecules have no attraction for water molecules strong enough to break up their own intermolecular forces, so they remain undissolved. (Polar covalent compounds like HCl and sugar are exceptions and do dissolve.)

Q: 3(iii) How do metals conduct heat?

Metals contain free (mobile) electrons. When one end of a metal is heated, the electrons there gain kinetic energy and move rapidly towards the colder parts, carrying the energy with them; the vibrating positive ions also pass energy to their neighbours. This fast transfer by free electrons makes metals good conductors of heat.

Q: 3(iv) How many oxides does nitrogen form. Write down the formulae of oxides?

Nitrogen forms five well-known oxides: nitrous oxide N2O, nitric oxide NO, nitrogen trioxide N2O3, nitrogen dioxide NO2 (which exists in equilibrium with its dimer N2O4) and nitrogen pentoxide N2O5.

Q: 3(v) What will happen if NaBr is treated with AgNO3 in water?

Both compounds are soluble ionic salts, so a double decomposition (precipitation) reaction occurs: NaBr + AgNO3 -> AgBr + NaNO3. A pale yellow precipitate of silver bromide, AgBr, is formed, which is insoluble in water; sodium nitrate stays in solution.

Q: 3(vi) Why does iodine exist as a solid while Cl2 exist as a gas?

Iodine molecules (I2) are much larger and heavier than chlorine molecules (Cl2), so the van der Waals forces between I2 molecules are much stronger. At room temperature these forces are strong enough to hold iodine molecules in a solid lattice, whereas the weak forces between the small Cl2 molecules cannot do so and chlorine remains a gas.

mcqs.q: HF is a liquid at room temperature while HCl is a gas because:
options: HF molecules are heavier than HCl molecules
HF molecules are held together by strong hydrogen bonding
HCl molecules attract each other more strongly
mcqs.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and very small, so HF molecules are strongly polar and held together by strong hydrogen bonding; considerable energy is needed to separate them, so HF is a liquid. In HCl there is no effective hydrogen bonding, only weak dipole-dipole and van der Waals forces, so HCl is a gas.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen bonding in HF is strong mainly because fluorine:
options: Is present in the liquid state
Is the most electronegative element and very small
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding is strongest with small, highly electronegative atoms. Fluorine is the most electronegative element and its atom is very small, so the H-F bond is strongly polar and HF molecules attract one another strongly through hydrogen bonds.

mcqs.q: Most covalent compounds are not soluble in water because:
options: Their non-polar molecules have no attraction for water strong enough to break up their own forces
