Q: 1(vii) The following reaction is performed in a closed vessel. CaCO3(s) <==> CaO(s) + CO2(g). How the equilibrium will be affected if you increase the pressure?

(a) The forward reaction will be favoured (b) The backward reaction will be favoured (c) No effect on backward reaction (d) No effect on forward or backward reaction
Correct answer: The backward reaction will be favoured

Q: 1(viii) When a reaction will become a reversible one?

(a) If the activation energy of the forward reaction is comparable to that of backward reaction (b) If the activation energy of the forward reaction is higher than that of backward reaction (c) If the activation energy of the forward reaction is lower than that of backward reaction (d) If the enthalpy change of both the reactions is zero.
Correct answer: If the activation energy of the forward reaction is comparable to that of backward reaction

Q: 1(ix) Is reversible reaction useful for preparing compounds on large scale?

(a) No (b) Yes (c) They are useful only when equilibrium lies far to the right side (d) They are useful only when equilibrium lies far to the left side
Correct answer: They are useful only when equilibrium lies far to the right side

Q: 1(x) What will happen to the concentrations of the products if a reversible reaction at equilibrium is not disturbed?

(a) They will remain constant (b) They will keep on increasing (c) They will keep on decreasing (d) They will remain constant for some time and then start decreasing
Correct answer: They will remain constant

mcqs.q: 1(i) What will happen if the rates of forward and reverse reactions are very high?
options: The equilibrium point will reach very soon.
The equilibrium point will reach very late.
The reaction will not attain the state of dynamic equilibrium.
The reaction will be practically irreversible.
mcqs.why: Equilibrium is reached when the rates of the forward and reverse reactions become equal. If both rates are very high, they become equal very quickly, so the equilibrium point is reached very soon.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) Predict which components of the atmosphere react in the presence of lightning.
mcqs.why: Lightning provides the enormous activation energy needed for the very strong N triple bond to react. In lightning, nitrogen and oxygen of the atmosphere combine: N2 + O2 -> 2NO. The other pairs of gases do not react in this way.

mcqs.q: 1(iii) An inorganic chemist places one mole of PCl5 in a container A and one mole of each Cl2 and PCl3 in container B. Both the containers were sealed and heated to the same temperature to reach the state of equilibrium. Guess about the composition of mixtures in both the containers.
options: Both the containers will have the same composition of mixtures.
Container A will have more concentration of PCl3 than B.
Container A will have less concentration of PCl3 than B.
Both the containers will have zero concentration of its reactants.
mcqs.why: The equilibrium composition depends only on the temperature and the overall amounts of the elements present, not on which side you start from. Container A (PCl5 alone) and container B (PCl3 + Cl2) contain the same overall mixture for the equilibrium PCl5 <==> PCl3 + Cl2, so at the same temperature both reach exactly the same equilibrium composition.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) CaO or lime is used extensively in steel, glass and paper industries. It is produced in a reversible reaction by the decomposition of lime (CaCO3). Choose the conditions to produce maximum amount of lime.
options: Heating at high temperature in a closed vessel
Heating at high temperature in an open vessel
Cooling it in a closed vessel
Cooling it in an open vessel
mcqs.why: The decomposition CaCO3 <==> CaO + CO2 is endothermic (the book's wording in this question calls it 'exothermic', which is a misprint - the chosen answer is the same either way). Heating at high temperature favours the endothermic forward reaction, and in an open vessel the CO2 escapes as it forms, so the reaction keeps going forward and the maximum amount of lime (CaO) is produced.

mcqs.q: 1(v) What condition should be met for the reversible reaction to achieve the state of equilibrium?
options: All the reactants should be converted into the products.
50% of the reactants should be converted into products.
The concentrations of all the reactants and the products should become constant.
One of the products should be removed from the reaction mixture.
mcqs.why: A reversible reaction is at equilibrium when the forward and reverse rates are equal, which shows itself as the concentrations of all reactants and products becoming constant (not necessarily equal, and not requiring complete conversion).

mcqs.q: 1(vi) Why the gas starts coming out when you open a can of fizzy drink?
options: Because the solubility of the gas increases
Because the gas is insoluble in water
Because the gas is dissolved under pressure hence it comes out when pressure is decreased
Because the solubility of the gas decreases at high pressure
mcqs.why: In a fizzy drink, carbon dioxide is dissolved in the liquid under high pressure. When the can is opened, the pressure above the liquid falls, the solubility of the gas decreases, and the excess dissolved gas escapes as bubbles.

mcqs.q: 1(vii) The following reaction is performed in a closed vessel. CaCO3(s) <==> CaO(s) + CO2(g). How the equilibrium will be affected if you increase the pressure?
options: The forward reaction will be favoured
The backward reaction will be favoured
No effect on forward or backward reaction
mcqs.why: For CaCO3(s) <==> CaO(s) + CO2(g), increasing the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. The forward reaction produces a gas (CO2) while the backward reaction consumes it, so higher pressure favours the backward reaction and shifts the equilibrium to the left.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) When a reaction will become a reversible one?
options: If the activation energy of the forward reaction is comparable to that of backward reaction
If the activation energy of the forward reaction is higher than that of backward reaction
If the activation energy of the forward reaction is lower than that of backward reaction
If the enthalpy change of both the reactions is zero.
mcqs.why: A reaction becomes reversible when the products can react back to give the reactants under the same conditions. This happens when the activation energy of the forward reaction is comparable to that of the backward reaction, so both directions proceed at appreciable rates.

mcqs.q: 1(ix) Is reversible reaction useful for preparing compounds on large scale?
options: They are useful only when equilibrium lies far to the right side
They are useful only when equilibrium lies far to the left side
mcqs.why: A reversible reaction is useful for preparing a compound on a large scale only if its equilibrium lies far to the right, so that most of the reactants are converted into the product; if the equilibrium lies to the left, the yield is too poor to be useful.

mcqs.q: 1(x) What will happen to the concentrations of the products if a reversible reaction at equilibrium is not disturbed?
options: They will remain constant for some time and then start decreasing
mcqs.why: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so every product molecule formed is balanced by one being changed back. The concentrations of the products (and reactants) therefore remain constant as long as the equilibrium is not disturbed.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?

In dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions do not stop; both continue at equal rates, so there is constant microscopic change but no net change in concentrations. In static equilibrium (e.g. a book resting on a table, or two equal weights balanced) nothing is actually happening: the opposing effects balance with no ongoing process at the molecular level.

Q: 2(ii) How the following reversible reaction will be affected if its temperature is increased? 2H2O(l) <==> (Electricity) 2H2(g) + O2(g)

The forward reaction (splitting of water) is endothermic, because energy (electricity/heat) is absorbed to decompose water. Increasing the temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the equilibrium shifts to the right: more water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen, and the reverse (combination) reaction is suppressed.

Q: 2(iii) How can you get the maximum yield in a reversible reaction?

Maximum yield is obtained by shifting the equilibrium to the product side and keeping it there: choose the favourable temperature and pressure (by Le Chatelier's principle), use an excess of the cheaper reactant, and remove the product from the mixture as soon as it is formed so that the reaction keeps moving forward instead of settling at equilibrium.

Q: 2(iv) How can you decrease the time to attain the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction?

Equilibrium is reached sooner if both the forward and reverse reactions are made faster: use a catalyst (which lowers the activation energy of both directions equally), raise the temperature, increase the concentrations (or pressure for gases), and use finely divided reactants to give a larger surface area. None of these changes the position of equilibrium, only the time taken to reach it.

Q: 2(v) What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium? N2(g) + O2(g) <==> 2NO(g)

There is no effect. The reaction has two moles of gas on the left (1 N2 + 1 O2) and two moles of gas on the right (2 NO); since the number of gas molecules is the same on both sides, increasing the pressure does not favour either direction and the equilibrium position stays unchanged (only the rates increase).

mcqs.q: Dynamic equilibrium differs from static equilibrium because in dynamic equilibrium:
options: Concentrations keep changing at the molecular level and in bulk
Both opposing reactions continue at equal rates, with constant microscopic change but no net change
mcqs.why: In dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions do not stop; both continue at equal rates, so there is constant change at the molecular level but no net change in concentrations. In static equilibrium (e.g. a book resting on a table) nothing is actually happening - the opposing effects simply balance.

mcqs.q: When the temperature of the equilibrium 2H2O(l) <==> 2H2(g) + O2(g) is increased:
options: The equilibrium shifts to the right and more water decomposes
The equilibrium shifts to the left
Only the reverse reaction speeds up
mcqs.why: The forward reaction (splitting of water) is endothermic because energy is absorbed to decompose water. Increasing the temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the equilibrium shifts to the right: more hydrogen and oxygen form and the reverse reaction is suppressed.

mcqs.q: The maximum yield in a reversible reaction is obtained by:
options: Sealing the vessel and waiting indefinitely
Choosing favourable temperature and pressure, using excess reactant and removing the product as it forms
Cooling every reaction to 0 degrees C
mcqs.why: By Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium is shifted to the product side by the favourable temperature and pressure, by using an excess of the cheaper reactant, and by removing the product from the mixture as soon as it is formed so the reaction keeps moving forward.

mcqs.q: Removing a product from an equilibrium mixture increases the yield because:
options: The reverse reaction becomes impossible in principle
The equilibrium keeps shifting forward to replace the removed product
mcqs.why: When a product is withdrawn as soon as it forms, the reverse reaction has nothing to act on and the system responds by making more product. The equilibrium therefore keeps shifting to the right instead of settling, forcing the reaction towards completion.

mcqs.q: A catalyst decreases the time taken to reach equilibrium because it:
options: Shifts the equilibrium to the right
Lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction only
Lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions equally
mcqs.why: A catalyst provides a path of lower activation energy for both directions equally, so both reactions speed up and equilibrium is reached sooner. It does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield.

mcqs.q: Equilibrium is reached sooner if the reactants are finely divided because:
options: A larger surface area makes both reactions faster
More product is formed at equilibrium
mcqs.why: Finely divided reactants expose a larger surface area, so collisions are more frequent and both the forward and reverse reactions run faster. Together with a catalyst, higher temperature and higher concentrations, this shortens the time to reach equilibrium without changing its position.

mcqs.q: Increasing the pressure has NO effect on the equilibrium N2(g) + O2(g) <==> 2NO(g) because:
options: Nitrogen does not respond to pressure
The number of gas molecules is the same (2) on both sides of the equation
NO is a liquid at high pressure
mcqs.why: The left side has 1 + 1 = 2 moles of gas and the right side has 2 moles of gas. Since pressure changes favour the side with fewer gas molecules, and here both sides are equal, increasing the pressure favours neither direction; only the rates increase.

mcqs.q: In the preparation of ethyl acetate, using concentrated sulphuric acid improves the yield because it:
options: Reacts with the alcohol to form a new ester
Raises the boiling point of the mixture
Absorbs the water as soon as it is formed, shifting the equilibrium to the right
mcqs.why: Concentrated H2SO4 is a powerful dehydrating agent: it absorbs the water produced in C2H5OH + CH3COOH <==> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O. With water withdrawn, the reverse hydrolysis cannot proceed, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium keeps shifting right until nearly all the alcohol and acid are converted.

mcqs.q: Which of the following changes the POSITION of equilibrium (not just the time to reach it)?
options: Increasing the concentration temporarily then restoring it
Changing the temperature of the system
mcqs.why: Temperature changes the relative energies of reactants and products and so shifts the equilibrium position (towards the endothermic direction on heating). A catalyst and finer division only change how quickly equilibrium is reached, not where it lies.

mcqs.q: Using an excess of the cheaper reactant in a reversible reaction:
options: Shifts the equilibrium towards the products and increases the conversion of the other reactant
mcqs.why: Adding more of one reactant disturbs the equilibrium; the system responds by consuming the added reactant, shifting the equilibrium to the product side. Using an excess of the cheaper reactant is therefore a standard way to maximise the yield of product from the other reactant.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) Why are some reactions irreversible while others are reversible?

A reaction is reversible when the products can react, under the same conditions, to give back the reactants: this happens when the activation energies and energies of the forward and backward reactions are comparable, and neither side is overwhelmingly more stable. A reaction is irreversible when the products are far more stable than the reactants, or when a product escapes from the system (as a gas or a precipitate), so the backward reaction practically cannot occur.

Q: 3(ii) Why are combustion reactions generally irreversible?

Combustion is strongly exothermic and the products (CO2 and H2O) are very stable compounds of much lower energy than the fuel and oxygen. The activation energy needed for the reverse reaction is enormous and there is no practical way to make CO2 and water recombine into fuel and oxygen under ordinary conditions; the gases also escape into the air. Hence combustion is generally irreversible.

Q: 3(iii) Can you make an irreversible reaction reversible and vice versa?

Within limits, yes. An apparently irreversible reaction can be made to run backwards by changing the conditions drastically (for example, CaCO3 decomposes on heating, while CaO and CO2 recombine under high pressure of CO2 on cooling; electrolysis reverses the burning of hydrogen). Conversely, a reversible reaction can be made practically one-way (forced to completion) by removing a product as it forms, or by using a large excess of one reactant. What cannot be changed is the fundamental energetics: a reaction needing a huge energy input will not reverse spontaneously.

Q: 3(iv) How do you know if a reaction is reversible or irreversible?

A reaction is reversible if, under suitable conditions, its products react together to reform the original reactants, and the reaction in a closed vessel stops short of completion, reaching a state where reactants and products coexist with constant concentrations (equilibrium). It is irreversible if it goes to completion: one or all reactants are used up, the products do not react back under the same conditions, and no equilibrium mixture is obtained.

Q: 3(v) Do the phase changes in water (solid to liquid, liquid to vapour) reversible or irreversible?

They are reversible. Ice melts into water on warming and water freezes back into ice on cooling; water evaporates into vapour and vapour condenses back into liquid. At a given temperature and pressure the two phases can exist together in a (physical) equilibrium, e.g. ice and water at 0 degrees C.

mcqs.q: A reaction is reversible when:
options: Its products can react under the same conditions to give back the reactants
mcqs.why: A reaction is reversible when the activation energies and energies of the forward and backward reactions are comparable and neither side is overwhelmingly more stable, so the products can react, under the same conditions, to reform the reactants.

mcqs.q: A reaction is irreversible when:
options: It takes place in a closed vessel
The products are far more stable than the reactants, or a product escapes as a gas or precipitate
mcqs.why: If the products are far more stable than the reactants, or if a product leaves the system as a gas or a precipitate, the backward reaction practically cannot occur and the reaction is irreversible.

mcqs.q: Combustion reactions are generally irreversible because:
options: They need a match to start
They are strongly exothermic and their products (CO2 and H2O) are very stable compounds of much lower energy
They take place in open air only
mcqs.why: In combustion the products carbon dioxide and water are very stable and much lower in energy than the fuel and oxygen. The activation energy for the reverse reaction is enormous and the gases escape into the air, so there is no practical way to recombine them into fuel and oxygen.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide and water do not recombine into fuel and oxygen under ordinary conditions because:
options: Fuels cannot be formed from gases
The reverse reaction would need an enormous input of energy
mcqs.why: Reforming fuel and oxygen from CO2 and H2O means climbing back up the large energy drop of combustion. Without a huge energy supply (as in photosynthesis or electrolysis-type processes), the reverse reaction cannot occur.

mcqs.q: The decomposition of CaCO3 can be run backwards (CaO + CO2 -> CaCO3) by:
options: Cooling under a high pressure of CO2
Heating it more strongly in open air
Grinding the CaO to a powder only
mcqs.why: An apparently irreversible reaction can be reversed by changing the conditions drastically: CaCO3 decomposes on heating in an open vessel, but CaO and CO2 recombine on cooling under high CO2 pressure. Electrolysis likewise reverses the burning of hydrogen.

mcqs.q: A reversible reaction can be made practically one-way (forced to completion) by:
options: Sealing it in a stronger vessel
Removing a product as it forms, or using a large excess of one reactant
mcqs.why: Continuously removing a product leaves the reverse reaction nothing to act on, so the equilibrium keeps shifting forward. A large excess of one reactant similarly drives the reaction nearly to completion with respect to the other reactant.

mcqs.q: You can tell a reaction is reversible if, in a closed vessel, it:
options: Stops short of completion, with reactants and products coexisting at constant concentrations
Gives out a lot of heat
mcqs.why: A reversible reaction in a closed vessel reaches equilibrium: reactants and products coexist with constant concentrations and the reaction appears to stop before completion. An irreversible reaction goes to completion with no equilibrium mixture.

mcqs.q: The phase changes of water (melting, evaporation) are:
options: Reversible - ice melts and water freezes; water evaporates and vapour condenses
mcqs.why: Ice melts into water on warming and water freezes back on cooling; water evaporates and vapour condenses back. At a given temperature and pressure the two phases exist together in physical equilibrium, e.g. ice and water at 0 degrees C.

mcqs.q: What fundamentally CANNOT be changed when trying to reverse a reaction?
options: The basic energetics - a reaction needing a huge energy input will not reverse spontaneously
mcqs.why: Conditions such as temperature, pressure and product removal can be changed, and these can reverse some reactions. But the fundamental energetics cannot be altered: a reaction whose reverse needs a huge energy input will never run backwards spontaneously.

mcqs.q: Electrolysis of water is an example of:
options: Reversing an (apparently) irreversible reaction by supplying energy
mcqs.why: Burning hydrogen in oxygen goes one way, but passing electricity through water reverses it: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2. Supplying energy under changed conditions makes the backward reaction occur.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) How can you drive the reversible reaction at equilibrium? (a) in the forward direction (b) in the backward direction

(a) In the forward direction: add more reactant (or remove product) so the system reacts to consume the added reactant and make more product; also choose temperature and pressure that favour the products (raise temperature for an endothermic forward reaction, lower it for an exothermic one; increase pressure when the forward reaction reduces the number of gas molecules). (b) In the backward direction: add more product (or remove reactant), and choose the opposite temperature/pressure conditions, so the equilibrium shifts towards the reactants.

Q: 4(ii) Explain how the rates of forward and backward reactions change when the system approaches equilibrium.

At the start only reactants are present, so the forward rate is at its maximum while the reverse rate is zero. As the reaction proceeds the reactants are used up, so the forward rate falls steadily; meanwhile products accumulate and the reverse rate rises from zero. When the two rates become equal, the system reaches equilibrium: both reactions continue at the same rate, so the concentrations no longer change.

Q: 4(iii) Describe the effect of a catalyst on the reversible reaction.

A catalyst speeds up both the forward and the reverse reaction equally, by providing a path of lower activation energy. It therefore does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield; it only makes the equilibrium state reach sooner. This is why catalysts are used industrially to save time without altering the product composition.

Q: 4(iv) How can a reversible reaction be forced to go to completion?

A reversible reaction is forced to completion by continuously withdrawing one or all of the products from the reaction mixture as soon as they are formed, so that the reverse reaction has nothing to act on and the equilibrium keeps shifting forward. Examples: in the decomposition of CaCO3 in a lime kiln the CO2 is swept away by the air current; in esterification the water is absorbed by concentrated sulphuric acid. Using a large excess of one reactant also drives the reaction nearly to completion with respect to the other reactant.

Q: 4(v) How does change in temperature affect the reaction at equilibrium?

Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction (the direction that absorbs heat), and lowering the temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction. So for an exothermic forward reaction (e.g. the Haber process) heating shifts the equilibrium backwards and decreases the yield, while cooling favours the products but makes the reaction slow; for an endothermic forward reaction heating increases the yield of products.

mcqs.q: To drive an equilibrium in the forward direction, you should:
options: Add more reactant or remove product as it forms
mcqs.why: Adding reactant (or removing product) disturbs the equilibrium; the system reacts to consume the added reactant and make more product, shifting the equilibrium forward. Suitable temperature and pressure for the products are chosen as well.

mcqs.q: For an endothermic forward reaction, the temperature should be ______ to favour the products:
mcqs.why: Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction. So for an endothermic forward reaction heating favours the products, while for an exothermic forward reaction cooling favours them (but slows the reaction).

mcqs.q: Increasing the pressure favours the forward reaction when the forward reaction:
options: Increases the number of gas molecules
Produces a liquid from a liquid
Reduces the number of gas molecules
mcqs.why: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, because that reduces the crowding. So pressure drives an equilibrium forward when the forward reaction reduces the number of gas molecules, e.g. N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 (4 molecules to 2).

mcqs.q: To drive an equilibrium in the backward direction, you should:
options: Add more product or remove reactant, with the opposite temperature/pressure conditions
Use an excess of the cheaper reactant
mcqs.why: Adding product (or removing reactant) makes the system convert product back into reactants, and choosing the opposite temperature and pressure conditions to those favouring the forward reaction shifts the equilibrium towards the reactants.

mcqs.q: At the very start of a reversible reaction, the rate of the forward reaction is:
options: Zero, while the reverse rate is maximum
At its maximum, while the reverse rate is zero
mcqs.why: At the start only reactants are present, so the forward rate is at its maximum and there are no products to react back - the reverse rate is zero. The rates then change until they become equal at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: As a reversible reaction approaches equilibrium:
options: The forward rate rises and the reverse rate falls
The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they become equal
mcqs.why: Reactants are used up, so the forward rate falls steadily; products accumulate, so the reverse rate rises from zero. When the two rates become equal, equilibrium is reached and concentrations stop changing.

mcqs.q: At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions:
options: Run only in the forward direction
Continue at the same rate, so concentrations no longer change
mcqs.why: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions keep running at equal rates. Every molecule of product formed is balanced by one changed back, so the concentrations of all substances remain constant.

mcqs.q: The effect of a catalyst on a reversible reaction at equilibrium is that it:
options: Speeds up both directions equally and does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield
Shifts the equilibrium to the right
mcqs.why: A catalyst provides a lower-activation-energy path for both the forward and reverse reactions, speeding both equally. It only makes equilibrium reach sooner - industrially valuable for saving time - without altering the product composition.

mcqs.q: A reversible reaction is forced to completion by:
options: Continuously withdrawing a product from the mixture as soon as it is formed
Heating it once and sealing the vessel
Waiting for a very long time
mcqs.why: If a product is continuously withdrawn, the reverse reaction has nothing to act on and the equilibrium keeps shifting forward. Examples: CO2 is swept away by the air current in a lime kiln, and in esterification the water is absorbed by concentrated sulphuric acid.

mcqs.q: Raising the temperature of an equilibrium system always shifts the equilibrium:
options: Towards the side with more gas molecules
In the endothermic direction (the direction that absorbs heat)
Towards the products in every reaction
mcqs.why: Heating favours the reaction that absorbs heat - the endothermic direction - because the system opposes the rise in temperature by absorbing the added heat. Lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the exothermic direction.

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) Study the effect of heat on hydrated copper sulphate. Why does this salt look coloured and why does it lose colour upon heating?

Hydrated copper sulphate, CuSO4.5H2O, is blue because the water molecules coordinated around the Cu2+ ions produce the blue colour of the hydrated ion. On heating, the salt loses its water of crystallisation and becomes anhydrous copper sulphate, CuSO4, which is white/off-white, so the colour disappears. The change is reversible: adding water to the white powder restores the blue colour (this is the chemical test for water).

Q: 5(ii) Synthesis of ammonia gas is very important industrially because it is used in the preparation of urea fertilizer. Explain the conditions you will use to get the maximum yield of ammonia.

For N2 + 3H2 <==> 2NH3, which is exothermic and reduces the number of gas molecules from 4 to 2, Le Chatelier's principle gives: (1) High pressure (about 200 atmospheres) to shift the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules, i.e. towards ammonia. (2) A moderately low temperature (about 450 degrees C): low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction, but the temperature is kept moderately high as a compromise so that the rate is acceptable. (3) An iron catalyst to reach equilibrium quickly (it does not change the yield). (4) Removing the ammonia as it forms (by cooling and liquefying it) and recycling the unreacted N2 and H2 back into the reactor, which forces the reaction towards completion.

mcqs.q: Hydrated copper sulphate, CuSO4.5H2O, is blue because:
options: Copper metal is dissolved in it
Water molecules are coordinated around the Cu2+ ions, giving the hydrated ion its blue colour
mcqs.why: The blue colour of hydrated copper sulphate comes from the water molecules coordinated around the Cu2+ ions. The hydrated copper ion is blue, so the crystals are blue.

mcqs.q: On heating, blue hydrated copper sulphate loses its colour because it:
options: Reacts with air to form a white gas
Loses its water of crystallisation and becomes white anhydrous copper sulphate
mcqs.why: Heating drives off the water of crystallisation: CuSO4.5H2O -> CuSO4 + 5H2O. Anhydrous copper sulphate is white/off-white, so the blue colour disappears on heating.

mcqs.q: The change between hydrated and anhydrous copper sulphate is used as:
options: A chemical test for water, because adding water to the white powder restores the blue colour
A way to prepare copper metal
mcqs.why: The change is reversible: adding water to white anhydrous copper sulphate turns it blue again. This is the standard chemical test for the presence of water.

mcqs.q: In the Haber process, N2 + 3H2 <==> 2NH3 is:
options: Endothermic and increases gas molecules from 2 to 4
Exothermic and reduces the number of gas molecules from 4 to 2
Exothermic with equal gas molecules on both sides
mcqs.why: The synthesis of ammonia gives out heat (exothermic) and 1 + 3 = 4 moles of gas form only 2 moles of ammonia gas. Both facts decide the industrial conditions chosen, by Le Chatelier's principle.

mcqs.q: A high pressure of about 200 atmospheres is used in the Haber process because it:
options: Shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia, the side with fewer gas molecules
mcqs.why: Increasing the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Since 4 moles of reactant gases give 2 moles of NH3, high pressure (about 200 atm) shifts the equilibrium to the right and increases the yield of ammonia.

mcqs.q: The temperature used in the Haber process is about 450 degrees C because:
options: Ammonia decomposes completely below this temperature
The catalyst melts at this temperature
High temperature increases the yield of ammonia
It is a compromise - low temperature favours the yield of the exothermic reaction but would be too slow
mcqs.why: Because the forward reaction is exothermic, a low temperature would give the best yield but the reaction would be far too slow. About 450 degrees C is chosen as a compromise between a good yield and an acceptable rate.

mcqs.q: The iron catalyst in the Haber process is used to:
options: Make the equilibrium reach sooner without changing the yield
Shift the equilibrium to the right
Replace the need for high pressure
mcqs.why: The iron catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached quickly. It does not change the position of equilibrium or the percentage yield.

mcqs.q: Ammonia is removed from the Haber reactor mixture by:
options: Cooling and liquefying it as it forms
Dissolving it in acid inside the reactor
mcqs.why: The ammonia formed is cooled and liquefied and drawn off from the mixture. Removing the product keeps the equilibrium shifting forward, and the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back into the reactor.

mcqs.q: Unreacted N2 and H2 in the Haber process are:
mcqs.why: Only part of the gas mixture is converted in each pass. The unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are separated from the liquefied ammonia and recycled back into the reactor, forcing the overall conversion towards completion.

mcqs.q: Ammonia is industrially important because it is used to prepare:
mcqs.why: Ammonia is synthesised on a huge scale in the Haber process mainly because it is the raw material for nitrogenous fertilisers such as urea, which supply nitrogen to crops.

lessons.title: In-text Exercise & Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: In-text Exercise: Give two examples of Bronsted-Lowry bases which are not bases by Arrhenius definition.

Ammonia, NH3, and the carbonate ion, CO3 2-, are Bronsted-Lowry bases because they accept protons (NH3 + H+ -> NH4+; CO3 2- + H+ -> HCO3-). They are not Arrhenius bases because they do not contain or directly release hydroxide ions, OH-, in water; Arrhenius bases are substances like NaOH and KOH that give OH- ions in aqueous solution.

Q: 1(i) Which acid is not used as a food or mixed with food?

(a) Tartaric acid (b) Ascorbic acid (c) Citric acid (d) Formic acid
Correct answer: Formic acid

Q: 1(ii) While baking, which gas is responsible for raising the bread and making it soft?

(a) Oxygen (b) Carbon dioxide (c) Nitrogen (d) Carbon monoxide
Correct answer: Carbon dioxide

Q: 1(iii) Predict the main characteristics of the reactions of metals with acids.

(a) Metals are dissolved (b) Metals are converted into salts (c) Hydrogen gas is evolved (d) All the above mentioned characteristics are true
Correct answer: All the above mentioned characteristics are true

Q: 1(iv) How many hydroxide ions, calcium hydroxide will release in water?

(a) 1 (b) 2 (c) Zero (d) 3
Correct answer: 2

Q: 1(v) In a neutralization reaction between KOH and H3PO4, how many molecules of KOH will react with one molecule of H3PO4?

(a) 2 (b) 1 (c) 3 (d) 4
Correct answer: 3

Q: 1(vi) Which acid is used in the preparation of soap?

(a) Tartaric acid (b) Citric acid (c) Stearic acid (d) Oxalic acid
Correct answer: Stearic acid

Q: 1(vii) Which compound is formed when SO2 is dissolved in water?

(a) SO3 (b) H2SO3 (c) H2SO4 (d) H2S2O7
Correct answer: H2SO3

Q: 1(viii) Which of the following contains oxalic acid?

(a) Tomato (b) Orange (c) Tamarind (d) Sour milk
Correct answer: Tomato

Q: 1(ix) Which compound in the following reaction is behaving as a conjugate base? CH3COOH(aq) + H2O(l) -> CH3COO-(aq) + H3O+(aq)

(a) CH3COOH (b) H2O (c) CH3COO- (d) H3O+
Correct answer: CH3COO-

Q: 1(x) When a chemical reaction is carried out with a substance Z; a gas is produced which turns red litmus paper blue. What is the reaction?

(a) Reaction of an acid with a metal carbonate (b) Reaction of an acid with metal hydrogen carbonate (c) Reaction of an alkali with an acid (d) Reaction of an alkali with ammonium salt
Correct answer: Reaction of an alkali with ammonium salt

mcqs.q: 1(i) Which acid is not used as a food or mixed with food?
mcqs.why: Tartaric acid (in tamarind and grapes), ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and citric acid (in citrus fruits) are all used in foods. Formic acid - the acid of ant stings - is not used as a food or mixed with food.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) While baking, which gas is responsible for raising the bread and making it soft?
mcqs.why: Baking powder contains sodium hydrogen carbonate and a weak acid. When heated in the dough they react and release carbon dioxide gas; the bubbles of CO2 raise the bread and make it soft and spongy.

mcqs.q: 1(iii) Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the reactions of metals with acids?
mcqs.why: When a metal reacts with an acid, the metal dissolves, it is converted into its salt, and hydrogen gas is evolved - all three of the book's statements are true. Carbon dioxide is NOT evolved in metal-acid reactions (CO2 comes from acids reacting with carbonates). Note: the book phrases this item with an 'all of the above' option; it is rebuilt here as a NOT question with the same content.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) How many hydroxide ions, calcium hydroxide will release in water?
mcqs.why: Calcium hydroxide has the formula Ca(OH)2: each formula unit contains two hydroxide groups, so in water it releases 2 hydroxide ions: Ca(OH)2 -> Ca2+ + 2OH-.

mcqs.q: 1(v) In a neutralization reaction between KOH and H3PO4, how many molecules of KOH will react with one molecule of H3PO4?
mcqs.why: Phosphoric acid H3PO4 is tribasic - it has three replaceable hydrogen ions. Each KOH molecule provides one OH- ion, so 3 molecules of KOH are needed to neutralise one molecule of H3PO4: H3PO4 + 3KOH -> K3PO4 + 3H2O.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) Which acid is used in the preparation of soap?
mcqs.why: Soap is the sodium (or potassium) salt of a long-chain fatty acid. Stearic acid is the fatty acid whose sodium salt, sodium stearate, is a common soap, so stearic acid is the acid used in soap preparation.

mcqs.q: 1(vii) Which compound is formed when SO2 is dissolved in water?
mcqs.why: Sulphur dioxide is an acidic oxide: it dissolves in water to form sulphurous acid, SO2 + H2O -> H2SO3. (H2SO4 is formed from SO3, not directly from SO2.)

mcqs.q: 1(viii) Which of the following contains oxalic acid?
mcqs.why: Tomatoes contain oxalic acid. (Oranges contain citric acid, tamarind contains tartaric acid, and sour milk contains lactic acid.)

mcqs.q: 1(ix) Which compound in the following reaction is behaving as a conjugate base? CH3COOH(aq) + H2O(l) -> CH3COO-(aq) + H3O+(aq)
mcqs.why: In CH3COOH + H2O -> CH3COO- + H3O+, the acid CH3COOH donates a proton and becomes CH3COO-. The species formed from an acid after it loses a proton is its conjugate base, so CH3COO- is the conjugate base (H3O+ is the conjugate acid of H2O).

mcqs.q: 1(x) When a chemical reaction is carried out with a substance Z; a gas is produced which turns red litmus paper blue. What is the reaction?
options: Reaction of an acid with a metal carbonate
Reaction of an acid with metal hydrogen carbonate
Reaction of an alkali with an acid
Reaction of an alkali with ammonium salt
mcqs.why: A gas that turns red litmus paper blue must be alkaline - ammonia. Ammonia is released when an alkali is warmed with an ammonium salt: e.g. NH4Cl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O + NH3. Acids with carbonates give CO2, which is acidic and would turn blue litmus red.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) Choose Arrhenius Acids among the following compounds. HF, NH4+, H2SO3, SO3, H2S, H2O

Arrhenius acids are substances that give H+ (protons/hydroxonium ions) when dissolved in water. From the list: HF, H2SO3 and H2S are Arrhenius acids. NH4+ is a Bronsted-Lowry acid (proton donor) but not an Arrhenius acid; SO3 is an acidic oxide that forms an acid with water; H2O is amphoteric.

Q: 2(ii) How does calcium metal react with dilute H2SO4?

Calcium reacts vigorously with dilute sulphuric acid to form calcium sulphate and hydrogen gas: Ca + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + H2. The reaction soon slows down because the calcium sulphate formed is only slightly soluble and coats the metal, separating it from the acid.

Q: 2(iii) Which salt is formed when HCl reacts with BaCO3?

Barium chloride, BaCl2, is formed (along with water and carbon dioxide): BaCO3 + 2HCl -> BaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

Q: 2(iv) How will you justify that HSO4- is a Bronsted - Lowry acid?

HSO4- can donate a proton to a base, for example to water: HSO4- + H2O -> SO4 2- + H3O+. A Bronsted-Lowry acid is defined as a proton donor; since HSO4- donates a proton, it is a Bronsted-Lowry acid (it is the conjugate acid of SO4 2-).

Q: 2(v) Why is HCl not edible although it is present in the stomach and responsible for digestion of food?

The hydrochloric acid of the stomach (gastric juice) is very dilute (about 0.5%) and is present in a controlled amount, just enough to help digestion and kill germs. The HCl available as a laboratory or commercial acid is far more concentrated and is strongly corrosive; swallowing it would burn and destroy the tissues of the mouth, throat and stomach. So the presence of dilute HCl in the stomach does not make 'HCl' edible.

mcqs.q: Which of the following are Arrhenius acids (giving H+ in water)?
mcqs.why: Arrhenius acids give H+ (hydroxonium) ions when dissolved in water: HF, H2SO3 and H2S do this. NH4+ is a Bronsted-Lowry acid (proton donor) but not an Arrhenius acid; SO3 is an acidic oxide that forms an acid with water; H2O is amphoteric.

mcqs.q: The ammonium ion NH4+ is best described as:
options: A Bronsted-Lowry acid but not an Arrhenius acid
mcqs.why: NH4+ can donate a proton, so it is a Bronsted-Lowry acid. It is not an Arrhenius acid because it is not a substance that simply dissolves in water to give H+ as its only positive ion in the Arrhenius sense.

mcqs.q: Sulphur trioxide, SO3, is classified as:
options: An acidic oxide that forms an acid with water
mcqs.why: SO3 itself does not contain hydrogen and is not an Arrhenius acid. It is an acidic oxide (acid anhydride): SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4, forming sulphuric acid.

mcqs.q: Water, in acid-base behaviour, is:
options: Neither an acid nor a base in any reaction
Amphoteric - it can act as both an acid and a base
mcqs.why: Water can donate a proton (acting as an acid) and can accept a proton to form H3O+ (acting as a base). A substance that behaves both ways is called amphoteric.

mcqs.q: Calcium metal reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form:
mcqs.why: Ca + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + H2. Calcium reacts vigorously at first, forming calcium sulphate and hydrogen, like other reactive metals with dilute acids.

mcqs.q: The reaction of calcium with dilute H2SO4 soon slows down because:
options: The slightly soluble calcium sulphate coats the metal and separates it from the acid
Calcium turns into a noble metal
mcqs.why: Calcium sulphate is only slightly soluble in water. It forms a protective coating on the surface of the calcium, separating the metal from the acid, so the reaction slows down and almost stops.

mcqs.q: When HCl reacts with BaCO3, the salt formed is:
mcqs.why: BaCO3 + 2HCl -> BaCl2 + H2O + CO2. The salt takes its negative part (chloride) from the acid, so the salt formed is barium chloride; water and carbon dioxide are the other products.

mcqs.q: HSO4- is a Bronsted-Lowry acid because it:
options: Can donate a proton, e.g. HSO4- + H2O -> SO4 2- + H3O+
mcqs.why: A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor. HSO4- donates a proton to water, forming SO4 2- and H3O+, so it is a Bronsted-Lowry acid - it is the conjugate acid of SO4 2-.

mcqs.q: The hydrochloric acid present in the human stomach is:
options: Very dilute (about 0.5%) and present in a controlled amount
mcqs.why: Gastric juice contains only about 0.5% HCl, just enough to help digestion and kill germs. Laboratory or commercial HCl is far more concentrated and strongly corrosive, so it would burn the mouth, throat and stomach - the dilute stomach acid does not make 'HCl' edible.

mcqs.q: Besides BaCl2, the reaction BaCO3 + 2HCl also produces:
mcqs.why: Acids react with metal carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide: BaCO3 + 2HCl -> BaCl2 + H2O + CO2. The CO2 is the gas that turns lime water milky in the test for carbonates.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) What chemical name will you give to soap as a compound?

Soap is a sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, e.g. sodium stearate, C17H35COONa, formed when a fat or oil (such as stearic acid compounds) reacts with sodium hydroxide. Chemically, soap is therefore the sodium salt of stearic acid (a carboxylate salt).

Q: 3(ii) In the presence of a drop of an acid, water is known to ionize as follows: H2O(l) <==> H+(aq) + OH-(aq). In your opinion, which name will be suitable for water: an acid, a base or both?

Water is both: it is an amphoteric substance. In the ionisation shown, water gives out an H+ ion (acting as an acid) and the OH- it leaves can accept a proton (acting as a base). With an acid, water behaves as a base (accepts H+ to form H3O+); with a base, it behaves as an acid (donates H+). So water is neither only an acid nor only a base; it is amphoteric.

Q: 3(iii) Why does Na2CO3 behave like a base in water?

Sodium carbonate is the salt of a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (H2CO3). In water its carbonate ions accept protons from water: CO3 2- + H2O <==> HCO3- + OH-. The hydroxide ions produced make the solution alkaline, so Na2CO3 behaves like a base in water (it turns red litmus blue).

Q: 3(iv) Is NaHCO3 a base or an acid? Justify your answer.

NaHCO3 is mainly basic in water, though it is amphoteric. Its HCO3- ion can accept a proton (base behaviour) and can also donate one (acid behaviour), but in water it accepts protons from water more effectively, producing OH- ions: HCO3- + H2O <==> H2CO3 + OH-, so its solution is mildly alkaline and it is commonly used as a mild base (baking soda, antacid).

Q: 3(v) What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?

'Strong' describes how completely an acid ionises in water: a strong acid (e.g. HCl) ionises almost completely, a weak acid only slightly. 'Concentrated' describes how much acid is dissolved in a given volume of solution. The two are independent: a concentrated solution of a weak acid (e.g. concentrated acetic acid) and a dilute solution of a strong acid are both possible.

mcqs.q: Chemically, soap is:
options: A sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid
A mixture of an acid and an alkali
A sodium salt of sulphuric acid
mcqs.why: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, e.g. sodium stearate, C17H35COONa, formed when a fat or oil reacts with sodium hydroxide. Chemically, soap is therefore a carboxylate salt.

mcqs.q: The formula of sodium stearate, a common soap, is:
mcqs.why: Sodium stearate is the sodium salt of stearic acid (C17H35COOH): replacing the acidic hydrogen by sodium gives C17H35COONa. C17H35COOH is the free acid, not the soap.

mcqs.q: Water is called amphoteric because it:
options: Is a liquid at room temperature
Has a neutral pH in all mixtures
Can both donate a proton (as an acid) and accept a proton (as a base)
mcqs.why: In its ionisation H2O <==> H+ + OH-, water gives out H+ (acid behaviour), and with an acid it accepts H+ to form H3O+ (base behaviour). A substance showing both acid and base behaviour is amphoteric.

mcqs.q: When water is mixed with an acid, water behaves as:
options: A base, accepting a proton to form H3O+
mcqs.why: With an acid, water accepts the proton: H2O + H+ -> H3O+. Accepting a proton is base behaviour in the Bronsted-Lowry sense, showing that water is amphoteric.

mcqs.q: Sodium carbonate behaves like a base in water because:
options: It is the salt of a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (H2CO3), and its carbonate ions produce OH- from water
It dissolves to give Na+ only
mcqs.why: Na2CO3 is formed from strong base NaOH and weak acid H2CO3. In water the carbonate ions accept protons: CO3 2- + H2O <==> HCO3- + OH-. The hydroxide ions produced make the solution alkaline, so it turns red litmus blue.

mcqs.q: An aqueous solution of sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO3, is:
options: Mildly alkaline (mainly basic, though the ion is amphoteric)
mcqs.why: The HCO3- ion can accept a proton (base) and can also donate one (acid), so it is amphoteric; but in water it accepts protons from water more effectively, producing OH- (HCO3- + H2O <==> H2CO3 + OH-). The solution is therefore mildly alkaline, and NaHCO3 is used as a mild base (baking soda, antacid).

mcqs.q: NaHCO3 (baking soda) is commonly used as:
options: A mild base, e.g. as an antacid
mcqs.why: Because its solution is mildly alkaline, sodium hydrogen carbonate is used as a mild base - as an antacid to neutralise excess stomach acid and in baking, where it releases CO2 with acids to raise dough.

mcqs.q: A 'strong' acid is one that:
options: Is present in a large amount in the bottle
Has a very high boiling point
mcqs.why: 'Strong' describes how completely an acid ionises in water: a strong acid such as HCl ionises almost completely, while a weak acid ionises only slightly. It says nothing about how much acid is dissolved.

mcqs.q: A 'concentrated' acid is one that:
options: Has a large amount of acid dissolved in a given volume of solution
mcqs.why: 'Concentrated' describes the amount of acid dissolved in a given volume. It is independent of strength: a concentrated solution of a weak acid (concentrated acetic acid) and a dilute solution of a strong acid are both possible.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct?
options: A concentrated solution of a weak acid, and a dilute solution of a strong acid, are both possible
mcqs.why: Strength (degree of ionisation) and concentration (amount per volume) are independent ideas. Concentrated acetic acid is a concentrated weak acid, and a few drops of HCl in a bucket of water give a dilute strong acid.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) Explain Arrhenius concept of acids and bases.

According to Arrhenius, an acid is a substance that, when dissolved in water, gives hydrogen ions (H+, present as hydroxonium ions H3O+) as the only positive ions, e.g. HCl -> H+ + Cl-. A base is a substance that gives hydroxide ions (OH-) in aqueous solution, e.g. NaOH -> Na+ + OH-. Neutralisation is the combination H+ + OH- -> H2O. The concept applies only to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basic behaviour of substances like NH3 that contain no OH-.

Q: 4(ii) Compare Arrhenius and Bronsted - Lowry concepts of acids and bases.

Arrhenius: an acid gives H+ ions in water and a base gives OH- ions in water; the definitions are limited to aqueous solutions and to substances containing H or OH. Bronsted-Lowry: an acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor, in any solvent or even without a solvent. The Bronsted-Lowry concept is wider: it explains NH3 and CO3 2- as bases, introduces conjugate acid-base pairs, and shows that water is amphoteric. Every Arrhenius acid/base is also a Bronsted-Lowry acid/base, but not vice versa.

Q: 4(iii) How does sulphuric acid react with the following compounds? NH4Cl, NH4NO3, MgO, MgCO3

Being a typical acid, sulphuric acid reacts as follows. With ammonium salts (on heating/warming) it behaves as an acid towards the base ammonia held in the salt, forming ammonium sulphate: 2NH4Cl + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4 + 2HCl (with concentrated acid, hydrogen chloride gas is expelled); similarly 2NH4NO3 + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4 + 2HNO3. With the basic oxide MgO it forms salt and water: MgO + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2O. With the carbonate MgCO3 it forms salt, water and carbon dioxide: MgCO3 + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2O + CO2.

Q: 4(iv) What happens when a base reacts with a non-metallic oxide. What do you infer about the nature of non-metallic oxide?

A base reacts with a non-metallic oxide to form a salt and water, e.g. Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O and 2NaOH + CO2 -> Na2CO3 + H2O. This is exactly how an acid reacts with a base (neutralisation). We infer that non-metallic oxides are acidic in nature (acidic oxides or acid anhydrides).

Q: 4(v) State the reason of showing acidic character by both dry HCl gas and HCl solution in water.

Strictly, dry HCl gas does NOT show acidic character: it does not change dry litmus and does not behave as an acid, because in the dry gas there are only HCl molecules and no hydrogen ions. The aqueous solution shows acidic character because water ionises the HCl molecules: HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-, and it is the hydroxonium ions that give all the acidic properties. (If the question intends the moist gas, it is the moisture that first ionises it.)

Q: 4(vi) Differentiate between an acid and its conjugate base.

An acid and its conjugate base form a pair differing by exactly one proton (H+). The acid is the proton donor with one more H+; when it donates that proton it becomes its conjugate base, which has one H+ less and one unit more negative charge. Examples: CH3COOH (acid) and CH3COO- (conjugate base); NH4+ (acid) and NH3 (conjugate base). The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.

mcqs.q: According to Arrhenius, an acid is a substance that in water gives:
options: Hydrogen ions, H+ (present as hydroxonium ions, H3O+), as the only positive ions
mcqs.why: Arrhenius defined an acid as a substance that, dissolved in water, gives hydrogen ions (present as hydroxonium ions H3O+) as the only positive ions, e.g. HCl -> H+ + Cl-.

mcqs.q: According to Arrhenius, a base is a substance that in water gives:
mcqs.why: An Arrhenius base gives hydroxide ions in aqueous solution, e.g. NaOH -> Na+ + OH-. Neutralisation is then the combination H+ + OH- -> H2O.

mcqs.q: A limitation of the Arrhenius concept is that it:
options: Applies only to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basic behaviour of NH3, which contains no OH-
mcqs.why: The Arrhenius definitions are limited to water as solvent and to substances containing H or OH. They cannot explain why ammonia, NH3, which has no hydroxide group, behaves as a base - the Bronsted-Lowry concept can.

mcqs.q: In the Bronsted-Lowry concept, a base is:
mcqs.why: Bronsted-Lowry: an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor, in any solvent or even without a solvent. This explains NH3 and CO3 2- as bases, since both accept protons.

mcqs.q: The relation between the two concepts is:
options: Every Bronsted-Lowry acid is an Arrhenius acid
The two concepts contradict each other completely
Every Arrhenius acid/base is also a Bronsted-Lowry acid/base, but not vice versa
They apply to completely different substances
mcqs.why: The Bronsted-Lowry concept is wider: it covers all Arrhenius cases and also substances like NH3 and CO3 2- as bases, introduces conjugate acid-base pairs and shows water is amphoteric. So every Arrhenius acid/base is a Bronsted-Lowry one, but not the reverse.

mcqs.q: When sulphuric acid reacts with magnesium oxide, the products are:
mcqs.why: MgO is a basic oxide, so it neutralises the acid: MgO + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2O - a salt and water, the typical products of an acid with a basic oxide.

mcqs.q: When sulphuric acid reacts with magnesium carbonate, the products are:
mcqs.why: Acids react with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide: MgCO3 + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2O + CO2. The CO2 effervescence is the test for a carbonate.

mcqs.q: Since bases react with non-metallic oxides to form salt and water (like neutralisation), we infer that non-metallic oxides are:
options: Acidic in nature (acidic oxides or acid anhydrides)
mcqs.why: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O and 2NaOH + CO2 -> Na2CO3 + H2O are neutralisation-type reactions. Since a base neutralises an acid, the non-metallic oxide CO2 must be acidic - non-metallic oxides are acidic oxides.

mcqs.q: Dry HCl gas does NOT show acidic character because:
options: HCl gas is not really an acid
In the dry gas there are only HCl molecules and no hydrogen ions
mcqs.why: Strictly, dry HCl gas shows no acidic behaviour: it does not change dry litmus because there are no H+ ions, only HCl molecules. In water the molecules ionise, HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-, and it is the hydroxonium ions that give the acidic properties. (This corrects the wording of the book's question, which implies dry gas shows acidic character.)

mcqs.q: An acid and its conjugate base differ by:
options: One electron only, with no change in hydrogen
Exactly one proton (H+); the acid has one more H+ than its conjugate base
mcqs.why: When an acid donates its proton it becomes its conjugate base: CH3COOH/CH3COO- and NH4+/NH3 are such pairs, differing by exactly one H+ and one unit of charge. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) Acids play significant roles within human body. Comment on this statement.

The statement is true. Hydrochloric acid in the stomach helps digestion and kills germs in food. Amino acids are the building blocks of the proteins of our body. Fatty acids are part of our stored energy (fats). Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is essential for health, folic acid for blood formation, and the nucleic acids DNA and RNA carry our hereditary information. Even the energy carrier system of the cells works through acids such as lactic acid formed in muscles. So acids are indispensable within the human body.

Q: 5(ii) What is observed when CO2 is passed through lime water (i) for a short duration (ii) for a long duration?

(i) For a short duration: the lime water turns milky (cloudy white) because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O. (ii) For a long duration: the milkiness disappears and the solution becomes clear again, because the excess carbon dioxide converts the insoluble carbonate into soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 -> Ca(HCO3)2.

mcqs.q: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach helps the body by:
options: Helping digestion and killing germs in food
mcqs.why: The dilute HCl of the gastric juice creates the acidic medium needed for digestion and kills germs entering with food. It is one of several essential acids in the human body.

mcqs.q: Amino acids are important in the body because they are:
options: Responsible for the colour of blood
mcqs.why: Proteins - the body's structural and functional molecules - are built by joining amino acids. Amino acids are therefore the building blocks of the proteins of our body.

mcqs.q: Ascorbic acid is better known as:
mcqs.why: Ascorbic acid is vitamin C, an acid essential for health. Folic acid is needed for blood formation, and fatty acids form part of our stored energy.

mcqs.q: Folic acid is essential in the body for:
mcqs.why: Folic acid is required for the formation of blood (red blood cells). Its deficiency causes a type of anaemia, which shows how important acids are within the human body.

mcqs.q: DNA and RNA, which carry our hereditary information, are:
mcqs.why: The hereditary information of the body is carried by the nucleic acids DNA and RNA - another example of acids playing a significant role within the human body, along with HCl in the stomach and amino acids in proteins.

mcqs.q: When CO2 is passed through lime water for a short duration, the lime water:
options: Turns milky because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed
mcqs.why: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O. The insoluble white calcium carbonate formed makes the lime water turn milky (cloudy white) - this is the standard test for carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: When CO2 is passed through lime water for a long duration, the milkiness:
options: Disappears, because excess CO2 converts CaCO3 into soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate
mcqs.why: With excess carbon dioxide the insoluble carbonate is converted into soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 -> Ca(HCO3)2. The solution therefore becomes clear again.

mcqs.q: Lime water is a solution of:
mcqs.why: Lime water is the clear solution of calcium hydroxide in water. It is used to test for CO2, which first turns it milky (CaCO3) and then, in excess, clears it (Ca(HCO3)2).

mcqs.q: The white milky substance first formed in lime water by CO2 is:
mcqs.why: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O. Calcium carbonate is insoluble in water, so it appears as a white suspension that makes the lime water look milky.

mcqs.q: The clear solution obtained after excess CO2 has passed through lime water contains:
mcqs.why: Excess CO2 reacts with the precipitated CaCO3 and water to form calcium hydrogen carbonate, Ca(HCO3)2, which is soluble - so the milkiness disappears and the solution becomes clear.

lessons.title: In-text Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Q: In-text Exercise (1): Barium (Ba) is present in 2nd group and 6th period. Answer the following questions about this element. (i) Is it a metal or a non-metal? (ii) Will it be electropositive or electronegative? (iii) What is the nature of its oxide? (iv) In which physical state you expect this element to exist?

(i) Barium is a metal: it is in Group 2 (alkaline earth metals), on the left side of the periodic table. (ii) It is electropositive: like other metals it loses its two outermost electrons easily to form Ba2+ ions. (iii) Its oxide, BaO, is basic in nature (metal oxides are basic). (iv) It exists as a solid at room temperature, like the other Group 2 metals.

Q: In-text Exercise (2): In which group and period you expect to find an element with the largest atomic radius?

Atomic size increases down a group and decreases across a period, so the largest atomic radius is found at the bottom left of the table: in Group 1 and the last (7th) period, i.e. the element francium (in practice caesium is the largest commonly considered).

Q: In-text Exercise (3): Can you predict the group number of the most electropositive and the most electronegative elements?

Electropositivity (metallic character) increases down Group 1 and decreases across a period, so the most electropositive elements are in Group 1, at the bottom of the group. Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, so the most electronegative elements are in Group 17 (the halogens), at the top of the group: fluorine is the most electronegative element.

Q: In-text Exercise (4): Choose among the following the element having the lowest ionization energy and the element with highest electron affinity. Also assign its group number and period number: Li, K, O, F, Cl.

Lowest ionization energy: potassium, K (Group 1, Period 4): ionization energy decreases down Group 1, so K < Li; the non-metals O, F and Cl have high values. Highest electron affinity: chlorine, Cl (Group 17, Period 3): electron affinity is greatest for the halogens, and Cl has a slightly higher value than F because fluorine's small size causes electron-electron repulsion. (Li: Group 1, Period 2; O: Group 16, Period 2; F: Group 17, Period 2.)

Q: In-text Exercise (5): Which two elements of the periodic table react to give (i) A basic oxide and (ii) An acidic oxide?

(i) A basic oxide is given by a metal reacting with oxygen, e.g. sodium and oxygen give sodium oxide, Na2O (or magnesium and oxygen give MgO). (ii) An acidic oxide is given by a non-metal reacting with oxygen, e.g. carbon and oxygen give carbon dioxide, CO2 (or sulphur and oxygen give SO2).

mcqs.q: Barium (Ba), in Group 2 and Period 6, is classified as:
mcqs.why: Barium is in Group 2 - the alkaline earth metals - on the left side of the periodic table. Elements on the left side are metals, so barium is a metal.

mcqs.q: Barium is electropositive because it:
options: Gains two electrons to form Ba2- ions
Loses its two outermost electrons easily to form Ba2+ ions
Shares electrons equally with all elements
mcqs.why: Like other metals, barium loses its two outermost electrons easily, forming Ba2+ ions. Losing electrons readily is electropositive (metallic) behaviour.

mcqs.q: The nature of barium oxide, BaO, is:
mcqs.why: Metal oxides are basic in nature. Barium is a metal, so its oxide BaO is a basic oxide, which reacts with acids to form salt and water.

mcqs.q: At room temperature, barium is expected to exist as a:
mcqs.why: Barium is a Group 2 metal, and all the alkaline earth metals are solids at room temperature, so barium exists as a solid.

mcqs.q: The element with the largest atomic radius is expected at the:
options: Bottom left of the table - Group 1, Period 7 (francium)
mcqs.why: Atomic size increases down a group and decreases across a period. Combining both trends, the largest atoms are at the bottom left: Group 1 in the last (7th) period, i.e. francium (in practice caesium is the largest commonly considered).

mcqs.q: The most electropositive elements are found in:
options: Group 1, towards the bottom of the group
mcqs.why: Electropositivity (metallic character) increases down Group 1 and decreases across a period, so the most electropositive elements are the Group 1 metals at the bottom of the group, such as caesium and francium.

mcqs.q: The most electronegative element is:
options: Caesium, at the bottom of Group 1
Fluorine, at the top of Group 17
mcqs.why: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, so it is greatest at the top right of the table: fluorine, at the top of Group 17 (the halogens), is the most electronegative element.

mcqs.q: Among Li, K, O, F and Cl, the element with the lowest ionization energy is:
mcqs.why: Ionization energy decreases down Group 1, so K (Period 4) has a lower value than Li (Period 2); the non-metals O, F and Cl hold their electrons strongly and have high ionization energies. Potassium therefore has the lowest ionization energy of the five.

mcqs.q: Among Li, K, O, F and Cl, the element with the highest electron affinity is:
mcqs.why: Electron affinity is greatest for the halogens (Group 17), which need only one electron to complete their octet. Chlorine's value is slightly higher than fluorine's because fluorine's very small atom causes strong electron-electron repulsion for the incoming electron.

mcqs.q: Which pair of elements reacts to give an ACIDIC oxide?
mcqs.why: Non-metals react with oxygen to give acidic oxides: carbon + oxygen -> CO2. Metals give basic oxides: sodium gives Na2O, magnesium gives MgO and barium gives BaO.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1(i) In which period and group will you place the element which is an important part of the solar cell?

(a) Third period and 14th group (b) Second period and 14th group (c) Third period and 15th group (d) Third period and 16th group
Correct answer: Third period and 14th group

Q: 1(ii) Identify the electronic configuration of the outermost shell of a transition metal.

(a) ns2 np4 (b) (n-1)d ns2 (printed as ndx ns2) (c) ns2 np6 (d) ns2 np5
Correct answer: (n-1)d ns2 (printed as ndx ns2)

Q: 1(iii) Which is the softest metal?

(a) Na (b) Ca (c) Al (d) Zn
Correct answer: Na

Q: 1(iv) A yellow solid element exists in allotropic forms which is also present in fossil fuels. Indicate the name.

(a) Carbon (b) Iodine (c) Aluminium (d) Sulphur
Correct answer: Sulphur

Q: 1(v) How many electrons can nitrogen accept in its outermost shell?

(a) 2 (b) 3 (c) 4 (d) 5
Correct answer: 3

Q: 1(vi) Which element is the most reactive element?

(a) Oxygen (b) Chlorine (c) Fluorine (d) Nitrogen
Correct answer: Fluorine

Q: 1(vii) Which element has the highest melting point?

(a) Na (b) K (c) Rb (d) Cs
Correct answer: Na

Q: 1(viii) In what order does the metallic character change in the second group?

(a) Mg > Ca > Ba > Sr (b) Sr > Ba > Ca > Mg (c) Mg > Sr > Ca > Ba (d) Ba > Sr > Ca > Mg
Correct answer: Ba > Sr > Ca > Mg

Q: 1(ix) Which of the following best describe the correct order of oxygen, fluorine, and nitrogen's atomic radii?

(a) O < F < N (b) N < F < O (c) F < O < N (d) O < N < F
Correct answer: F < O < N

Q: 1(x) The element having less value of ionization energy and less value of electron affinity is likely to belong to:

(a) Group 1 (b) Group 13 (c) Group 16 (d) Group 17
Correct answer: Group 1

mcqs.q: 1(i) In which period and group will you place the element which is an important part of the solar cell?
mcqs.why: Solar cells are made of silicon. Silicon has atomic number 14, with electronic configuration 2,8,4: it is in the third period (three shells) and Group 14 (four outer electrons).

mcqs.q: 1(ii) Identify the electronic configuration of the outermost shell of a transition metal.
mcqs.why: In transition metals the (n-1)d sub-shell is being filled while the outermost shell keeps the configuration ns2. The outermost-shell configuration of a transition metal is therefore (n-1)d ns2 (the book prints it in a compressed form).

mcqs.q: 1(iii) Which is the softest metal?
mcqs.why: Sodium is a soft alkali metal that can be cut with a knife; it is the softest of the given metals. Calcium, aluminium and zinc are all noticeably harder than sodium.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) A yellow solid element exists in allotropic forms which is also present in fossil fuels. Indicate the name.
mcqs.why: Sulphur is a yellow solid that exists in allotropic forms (rhombic and monoclinic) and is also present in fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum. Carbon is black, iodine is a dark violet solid, and aluminium is a metal.

mcqs.q: 1(v) How many electrons can nitrogen accept in its outermost shell?
mcqs.why: Nitrogen has five electrons in its outermost shell (2,5). To complete its octet it can accept 3 more electrons, forming the nitride ion N3-.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) Which element is the most reactive element?
mcqs.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the most reactive of all elements: it reacts with almost everything, even some noble gases. It is more reactive than chlorine and oxygen.

mcqs.q: 1(vii) Which element has the highest melting point?
mcqs.why: In Group 1 the melting point decreases down the group as the atoms get bigger and the metallic bonding weakens. Sodium, the highest of the given metals in the group, therefore has the highest melting point; caesium has the lowest.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) In what order does the metallic character change in the second group?
mcqs.why: Metallic character increases down Group 2 because the atoms get larger and lose electrons more easily. The order is therefore Ba > Sr > Ca > Mg, with barium the most metallic and magnesium the least.

mcqs.q: 1(ix) Which of the following best describe the correct order of oxygen, fluorine, and nitrogen's atomic radii?
mcqs.why: Atomic radius decreases across a period as nuclear charge increases. In Period 2, nitrogen (Z=7) is the largest of the three, then oxygen (Z=8), then fluorine (Z=9) the smallest, so the increasing order of radii is F < O < N.

mcqs.q: 1(x) The element having less value of ionization energy and less value of electron affinity is likely to belong to:
mcqs.why: Low ionization energy and low electron affinity mean the atom readily loses electrons and does not attract them - the behaviour of the electropositive metals of Group 1. Group 17 elements have high values of both.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) Why was atomic number chosen to arrange the elements in the periodic table?

Atomic number is the true identity of an element: it equals the number of protons, and hence the number of electrons, which decides the chemical properties. Arranging elements by increasing atomic number removed the defects of the atomic-mass arrangement (such as the misplaced pairs argon/potassium and cobalt/nickel) and made the periodic repetition of properties exact, because properties repeat when the outer electronic configuration repeats.

Q: 2(ii) What is the significance of the word periodic?

'Periodic' means repeating at regular intervals. The properties of elements repeat regularly after certain intervals of atomic number, because after an interval the same outer-shell electronic configuration occurs again. This repetition of properties is called periodicity, and it is the basis of the periodic table and the periodic law.

Q: 2(iii) Why does the size of a period increase as we move down the periodic table?

Moving down the table, each successive period corresponds to filling a shell of higher principal quantum number, and more sub-shells become available for filling: the first period fills only 1s (2 elements); the next two fill s and p sub-shells (8 each); the following periods also fill d sub-shells (adding 10 elements) and then f sub-shells (adding 14). Hence the periods get longer: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 elements.

Q: 2(iv) In a group, the elements have the same number of electrons in the outermost shell. Why is it so?

The group number is determined by the number of electrons in the outermost shell. Elements are placed in the same group precisely because their atoms have the same outermost electronic configuration: as we go down a group, complete inner shells are added but the outer configuration repeats. That is why group members show similar chemical properties.

Q: 2(v) Do you expect calcium to be more reactive than sodium? Give the reason of your answer.

No. Sodium (Group 1) has one outer electron and a lower ionization energy than calcium (Group 2), which has two outer electrons and a smaller atomic size with greater nuclear pull per electron. Sodium therefore loses its electron more easily and is more reactive than calcium (both react with water, but sodium far more violently).

Q: 2(vi) Which element has the maximum atomic radius and which element has the minimum atomic radius in third period?

In the third period (Na to Cl) atomic radius decreases from left to right. The maximum atomic radius is that of sodium, Na (the first element of the period), and the minimum is that of chlorine, Cl (the last element before the noble gas argon).

Q: 2(vii) Why are the most electronegative elements present in sixth and seventh groups?

The sixth and seventh groups (Groups 16 and 17) contain the non-metals of the right side of the table with small atomic sizes and high nuclear charge: their atoms need only two or one electrons to complete their octets, so they attract electrons very strongly. Electronegativity increases across a period and is highest at the top right, so the most electronegative elements (O, F, Cl) lie in these groups.

Q: 2(viii) The first ionization energy value of magnesium is less than the second one. Give reason.

The first ionization removes one of the two outer (3s) electrons of magnesium; after its removal the remaining outer electron is in a smaller, more positively charged ion (Mg+), so it is held much more tightly by the nucleus and needs considerably more energy to remove. Hence the second ionization energy is greater than the first.

Q: 2(ix) Is it possible for two metals or two non-metals to form an ionic bond?

No. An ionic bond needs transfer of electrons from an electropositive atom to an electronegative one. Two metals both tend to lose electrons, and two non-metals both tend to gain/share electrons, so neither pair can form the cation-anion combination needed. Two metals form a metallic bond/alloy; two non-metals form covalent bonds. (An ionic bond can, however, exist within a compound of non-metals such as NH4Cl, between NH4+ and Cl- ions.)

Q: 2(x) Which element has the least value of ionization energy and which element has the highest value of electronegativity?

Least ionization energy: caesium, Cs (bottom of Group 1; francium would be still lower but is rare and radioactive). Highest electronegativity: fluorine, F (top of Group 17), the most electronegative element of the table.

mcqs.q: Atomic number was chosen to arrange the elements because it:
options: Is always a whole multiple of the atomic mass
Is easier to measure than the electronic configuration
Equals the number of protons and electrons, which decides the chemical properties of the element
Increases by two at each step
mcqs.why: Atomic number is the true identity of an element: it equals the number of protons and hence the number of electrons, which decide chemical properties. Arranging by atomic number removed the defects of the mass arrangement and made the periodic repetition of properties exact.

mcqs.q: Arranging elements by atomic number removed the misplacement of which pairs?
mcqs.why: In the mass-based table, argon (mass about 40) had to be placed before potassium (about 39) and cobalt before nickel against mass order. With atomic number (Ar 18 < K 19; Co 27 < Ni 28) the order becomes natural and the defects disappear.

mcqs.q: The word 'periodic' in the periodic table means that the properties of elements:
options: Repeat regularly after certain intervals of atomic number
Change randomly from element to element
Depend only on the atomic mass
mcqs.why: 'Periodic' means repeating at regular intervals. Properties repeat regularly because, after an interval of atomic number, the same outer-shell electronic configuration occurs again. This repetition is called periodicity.

mcqs.q: The periods of the table get longer down the table (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32) because:
options: More sub-shells become available for filling - d sub-shells add 10 and f sub-shells add 14 elements
mcqs.why: The first period fills only 1s (2 elements); the next two fill s and p sub-shells (8 each); later periods also fill d sub-shells, adding 10 elements, and then f sub-shells, adding 14. Hence the periods contain 2, 8, 8, 18, 18 and 32 elements.

mcqs.q: Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same:
options: Number of electrons in the outermost shell
mcqs.why: The group number is determined by the number of outermost electrons. Going down a group, complete inner shells are added but the outer configuration repeats, so group members show similar chemical properties.

mcqs.q: Calcium is LESS reactive than sodium because:
options: Sodium has one outer electron and a lower ionization energy, so it loses its electron more easily
mcqs.why: Sodium (Group 1) has one outer electron and a lower ionization energy than calcium (Group 2), whose two outer electrons are held by a smaller atom with greater nuclear pull per electron. Sodium therefore loses its electron more easily and is more reactive - both react with water, but sodium far more violently.

mcqs.q: In the third period, the element with the maximum atomic radius is:
mcqs.why: Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period because the nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell. Sodium, the first element of Period 3, therefore has the maximum atomic radius of the period.

mcqs.q: In the third period, the element with the minimum atomic radius is:
mcqs.why: Radius decreases steadily across Period 3 from Na to Cl as the nuclear pull increases. Chlorine, the last element before the noble gas argon, has the minimum atomic radius of the period.

mcqs.q: The most electronegative elements lie in Groups 16 and 17 because these atoms:
options: Are large and lose electrons easily
