Are small, have high nuclear charge and need only one or two electrons to complete their octets
Are metals of the right side
mcqs.why: Groups 16 and 17 contain the non-metals of the right side of the table with small atomic sizes and high nuclear charge; their atoms need only two or one electrons to complete their octets, so they attract electrons very strongly. Electronegativity is highest at the top right (O, F, Cl).

mcqs.q: The second ionization energy of magnesium is greater than the first because:
options: Magnesium gains electrons after the first removal
The second electron is in a different element
The second electron is removed from a smaller, more positively charged Mg+ ion that holds it much more tightly
mcqs.why: The first ionization removes one of the two 3s electrons of magnesium. The remaining outer electron is then in the smaller Mg+ ion, which has a greater effective positive charge, so the electron is held much more tightly and considerably more energy is needed to remove it.

mcqs.q: Two metals cannot form an ionic bond with each other because:
options: Both tend to lose electrons, so no cation-anion pair can form
Metals never react with each other
mcqs.why: An ionic bond needs transfer of electrons from an electropositive atom to an electronegative one. Two metals both tend to lose electrons (and two non-metals both tend to gain/share), so neither pair gives the cation + anion combination. Two metals form a metallic bond/alloy instead.

mcqs.q: When two non-metal atoms combine, the bond formed is:
mcqs.why: Two non-metals both tend to gain electrons, so instead of transferring them they share pairs of electrons - a covalent bond. (An ionic bond can exist within a compound of non-metals such as NH4Cl, between the NH4+ and Cl- ions.)

mcqs.q: The element with the least value of ionization energy is:
options: Caesium, Cs, at the bottom of Group 1
mcqs.why: Ionization energy decreases down a group and increases across a period, so the least value is at the bottom left of the table: caesium, Cs. (Francium would be still lower but is rare and radioactive.)

mcqs.q: The element with the highest value of electronegativity is:
options: Fluorine, F, at the top of Group 17
mcqs.why: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, reaching its maximum at the top right of the table: fluorine, F, is the most electronegative element.

mcqs.q: An ionic bond between two ions both formed from non-metals exists in:
options: NH4Cl, between NH4+ and Cl- ions
mcqs.why: In ammonium chloride the cation NH4+ and the anion Cl- are both built from non-metal atoms (N, H, Cl), yet they are held by an ionic bond. NaCl, MgO and CaF2 all involve a metal.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) Suppose a new element is discovered. Where would you like to accommodate this element in the periodic table?

By its atomic number and electronic configuration: a newly discovered element is placed after the element with the next lower atomic number, in the group whose members have the same number of outermost electrons as the new element, and in the period corresponding to the number of shells being filled. Its properties can then be predicted from its group.

Q: 3(ii) What is the first element of the periodic table? Will it lose an electron or gain it?

The first element is hydrogen (atomic number 1, configuration 1s1). It usually loses its single electron to form H+ (like the alkali metals, e.g. in its reactions with non-metals in acids), but it can also gain one electron to form the hydride ion H- (like the halogens, e.g. in NaH). Because of its single electron it shows both behaviours; losing the electron is more common in its chemistry as an acid former.

Q: 3(iii) Atomic radii of boron and aluminum are 88 pm and 125 pm respectively. Which element is expected to lose electron or electrons easily?

Aluminium is expected to lose electrons more easily. Its atomic radius (125 pm) is larger than that of boron (88 pm), so its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and less strongly held; its ionization energy is therefore lower and it is more metallic than boron.

Q: 3(iv) How would you find the atomic radius of an atom?

A single atom cannot be isolated and measured directly, so atomic radius is found indirectly from the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the element. For a diatomic molecule or a metallic crystal, half of the internuclear distance (measured by X-ray diffraction of the crystal) is taken as the atomic radius: r = d/2, where d is the distance between the centres of two adjacent atoms.

Q: 3(v) Why is it not possible for oxygen atom to accept three electrons to form O3- ion like nitrogen which can accept electrons to form N3-?

Oxygen already has six electrons in its outer shell, so it needs only two electrons to complete its octet, forming O2-. A third electron would have to enter the next shell and would be strongly repelled by the eight electrons already present (the O2- ion has a complete octet and a double negative charge that repels further electrons). Nitrogen, with five outer electrons, needs three to complete its octet, so N3- completes the same octet without exceeding it; for oxygen the octet is complete at O2- itself.

mcqs.q: A newly discovered element is placed in the periodic table according to its:
options: Atomic number and electronic configuration - group by outermost electrons, period by number of shells
mcqs.why: The new element is placed after the element with the next lower atomic number, in the group whose members have the same number of outermost electrons, and in the period corresponding to the number of shells being filled. Its properties can then be predicted from its group.

mcqs.q: The first element of the periodic table is:
mcqs.why: Hydrogen has atomic number 1 and the configuration 1s1 - a single proton and a single electron. It is the first and lightest element of the periodic table.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen usually forms the ion H+ by:
options: Losing its single electron, like the alkali metals
mcqs.why: Hydrogen commonly loses its single electron to form H+, as in its chemistry as an acid former, resembling the alkali metals which also lose one electron.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen can also behave like a halogen by gaining one electron to form:
options: The hydride ion, H-, as in NaH
mcqs.why: With a very electropositive metal such as sodium, hydrogen gains one electron to complete its shell, forming the hydride ion H- in NaH - behaviour resembling the halogens, which also gain one electron.

mcqs.q: Aluminium (radius 125 pm) loses electrons more easily than boron (radius 88 pm) because:
options: It has more protons in its nucleus
Its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and less strongly held, so its ionization energy is lower
mcqs.why: Aluminium's atomic radius (125 pm) is larger than boron's (88 pm), so its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and less strongly held. Its ionization energy is therefore lower and it is more metallic, losing electrons more easily.

mcqs.q: The atomic radius of an atom is found indirectly as:
options: Half of the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the element
The diameter of a single isolated atom measured with a microscope
The size of its nucleus alone
Its atomic mass divided by two
mcqs.why: A single atom cannot be isolated and measured directly. The distance between the centres of two adjacent atoms (from X-ray diffraction of a crystal or a diatomic molecule) is measured, and half of it, r = d/2, is taken as the atomic radius.

mcqs.q: If the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms is d, the atomic radius r is:
mcqs.why: The internuclear distance d covers two atomic radii (one from each atom), so the radius of one atom is r = d/2 - the standard way atomic radii are obtained from X-ray diffraction data.

mcqs.q: An oxygen atom cannot accept three electrons to form O3- because:
options: Oxygen has no empty shell at all
Nitrogen and oxygen have the same number of outer electrons
Its octet is already complete at O2-; a third electron would enter the next shell and be strongly repelled
O3- exists but is very common
mcqs.why: Oxygen has six outer electrons and needs only two to complete its octet, forming O2-. A third electron would have to go into the next shell and would be strongly repelled by the eight electrons and double negative charge already present. Nitrogen, with five outer electrons, needs exactly three, so N3- completes the same octet without exceeding it.

mcqs.q: Nitrogen can form the ion N3- because it needs exactly:
options: One electron to complete its octet
Five electrons to complete its octet
No electrons - its octet is complete
Three electrons to complete its octet
mcqs.why: Nitrogen has five electrons in its outer shell. Accepting three more gives eight - a complete octet - so the nitride ion N3- is stable, whereas oxygen completes its octet with only two extra electrons.

mcqs.q: The properties of a newly discovered element can be predicted from:
options: Its position (group) in the periodic table
The laboratory where it was made
mcqs.why: Elements in the same group have the same outer electronic configuration and similar properties. Once a new element is placed in its group by atomic number and configuration, its properties and the formulae of its compounds can be predicted from the group.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) Which information is needed to locate the elements in the periodic table if you do not know its atomic number? Is atomic mass helpful for this purpose?

The electronic configuration of the element is needed: the number of electrons in the outermost shell fixes the group, and the number of occupied shells fixes the period. If the atomic number is unknown, the configuration can be worked out from the element's valency and the formulae of its compounds (e.g. its oxide and chloride). Atomic mass alone is not helpful: the modern table is based on atomic number, and mass order has exceptions (Ar/K, Co/Ni), so mass cannot locate an element reliably.

Q: 4(ii) How many blocks of elements are present in the periodic table? Are these blocks helpful in studying the properties of elements?

There are four blocks: s-block (Groups 1 and 2 plus helium), p-block (Groups 13 to 18), d-block (the transition elements) and f-block (lanthanides and actinides). Yes, the blocks are helpful: the block tells which sub-shell is being filled and groups together elements of similar character, e.g. s-block elements are reactive metals, p-block contains metals, metalloids and non-metals, and d-block elements are transition metals with variable valency and coloured compounds.

Q: 4(iii) Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons. (a) Atomic radius (b) Ionization energy

(a) Atomic radius decreases across a period: from left to right the nuclear charge increases by one at each step while the electrons are added to the same shell, so the increased pull of the nucleus draws the shell closer and the atoms get smaller. (b) Ionization energy increases across a period: the atoms become smaller and the nuclear charge increases, so the outer electrons are held more and more strongly and more energy is needed to remove one. (Small irregularities occur at half-filled and completely filled sub-shells.)

Q: 4(iv) Which physical properties of elements may lead us to know what type of bond it will form?

Melting and boiling points, electrical and thermal conductivity, hardness, density and lustre give a clue to the type of bonding. Very high melting points with conductivity only in the molten state suggest ionic bonding; conductivity in the solid state suggests metallic bonding; low melting and boiling points with no conductivity suggest simple covalent molecules; a very high melting point with no conductivity (or conductivity in the case of graphite) suggests a giant covalent structure.

Q: 4(v) Write down the names of four non-metals which exist in solid state at normal temperature.

Four solid non-metals at normal temperature: carbon (C), sulphur (S), phosphorus (P) and iodine (I). (Silicon and boron are also solids.)

Q: 4(vi) Why do second and third periods have equal number of elements while all other periods contain different number of elements?

The second and third periods both fill only the s and p sub-shells of their shells (2s2p and 3s3p): 2 + 6 = 8 elements each, because the 3d sub-shell is not filled in the third period (it belongs energetically with the fourth shell). Other periods differ because different sets of sub-shells are filled: the first fills only 1s (2 elements), the fourth and fifth also fill d sub-shells (18 each), and the sixth and seventh also fill f sub-shells (32 each).

mcqs.q: To locate an element in the table without knowing its atomic number, the information needed is:
options: Its electronic configuration - outermost electrons fix the group, occupied shells fix the period
mcqs.why: The number of electrons in the outermost shell fixes the group and the number of occupied shells fixes the period. The configuration can be worked out from the element's valency and the formulae of its compounds (e.g. its oxide and chloride).

mcqs.q: Atomic mass alone is NOT helpful for locating an element because:
options: The modern table is based on atomic number and mass order has exceptions such as Ar/K and Co/Ni
mcqs.why: In mass order, argon would come after potassium and cobalt after nickel, which puts them in the wrong groups. Since the modern table is based on atomic number, mass alone cannot locate an element reliably.

mcqs.q: The periodic table is divided into how many blocks?
options: Four - s, p, d and f blocks
mcqs.why: There are four blocks: s-block (Groups 1 and 2 plus helium), p-block (Groups 13 to 18), d-block (transition elements) and f-block (lanthanides and actinides). The block tells which sub-shell is being filled.

mcqs.q: The d-block elements are characterised by:
options: Variable valency and coloured compounds (they are transition metals)
mcqs.why: The d-block contains the transition metals, known for variable valency, coloured compounds and catalytic behaviour. The s-block, by contrast, contains reactive metals, and the p-block contains metals, metalloids and non-metals.

mcqs.q: Across a period, the atomic radius decreases because:
options: The nuclear charge increases at each step while electrons are added to the same shell, so the shell is pulled closer
Electrons are added to a new shell at each step
mcqs.why: From left to right across a period, each element has one more proton, increasing the nuclear pull, while the added electrons go into the same shell. The increased attraction draws the shell closer to the nucleus and the atoms get smaller.

mcqs.q: Across a period, the ionization energy increases because:
options: The atoms become smaller and the nuclear charge increases, so outer electrons are held more strongly
Electrons are added to the nucleus
mcqs.why: Across a period the atoms shrink and the nuclear charge rises, so the outer electrons are held more and more strongly and more energy is needed to remove one - ionization energy increases. (Small irregularities occur at half-filled and completely filled sub-shells.)

mcqs.q: Which set of physical properties gives a clue to the type of bonding in an element?
options: Its position in the table only
Melting and boiling points, electrical and thermal conductivity, hardness, density and lustre
mcqs.why: Very high melting points with conductivity only when molten suggest ionic bonding; conductivity in the solid state suggests metallic bonding; low melting/boiling points with no conductivity suggest simple covalent molecules; a very high melting point with no conductivity (except graphite) suggests a giant covalent structure.

mcqs.q: An element that conducts electricity in the solid state most likely has:
mcqs.why: Free electrons in the solid are the carriers of metallic bonding. Ionic solids cannot conduct (their ions are locked in the lattice), and simple covalent molecules have no charge carriers at all.

mcqs.q: Which set contains four non-metals that are solids at normal temperature?
mcqs.why: Carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine are solid non-metals at normal temperature. Bromine is a liquid non-metal, chlorine is a gas, and mercury is a liquid metal.

mcqs.q: The second and third periods each contain exactly 8 elements because:
options: Both fill only the s and p sub-shells of their shells (2 + 6 = 8); the 3d sub-shell is not filled in the third period
The d sub-shell holds only 8 electrons
Eight groups existed in Mendeleev's table
mcqs.why: Period 2 fills 2s and 2p, and Period 3 fills 3s and 3p: 2 + 6 = 8 elements each, because the 3d sub-shell belongs energetically with the fourth shell and is filled only in Period 4. Other periods differ: Period 1 fills only 1s (2), Periods 4-5 also fill d (18), Periods 6-7 also fill f (32).

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) Arrangement of the elements in the form of a periodic table is a remarkable achievement of chemists. Comment on this statement citing the benefits of this table.

The periodic table organises all the elements into one systematic arrangement in which position predicts properties. Its benefits: the study of more than 100 elements is reduced to the study of a few groups and periods; properties of an element and the formulae of its compounds can be predicted from its position; errors in atomic masses were corrected and gaps led to the prediction and discovery of new elements (e.g. gallium and germanium); and trends such as metallic character, atomic size and valency become clear at a glance.

Q: 5(ii) Both lithium and beryllium show behaviour different from rest of the alkali and alkaline earth metals respectively. Can you think of the possible reasons for this difference?

Lithium and beryllium are the first members of their groups and have very small atoms with only two shells. Their high charge density makes them behave partly like the elements diagonally below-right: lithium resembles magnesium and beryllium resembles aluminium (the diagonal relationship). They form more covalent compounds, their hydroxides are weaker (Be(OH)2 is amphoteric), and their salts are less ionic than those of the heavier group members. The small size and high ionization energies of these first elements are the reason for the difference.

Q: 5(iii) Modern periodic table is the amended form of the earlier table developed by Mandeleev. Elaborate how these two tables are different from each other.

Mendeleev's table arranged the elements in increasing order of atomic mass, in 8 groups, and was based on the formulae of oxides and hydrides; it left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties, but it had defects: hydrogen had no proper place, isotopes could not be accommodated, and some pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I) were placed against mass order. The modern table arranges elements by increasing atomic number, has 18 groups and 7 periods, and is based on electronic configuration, divided into s, p, d and f blocks. It removes Mendeleev's defects, gives isotopes their natural single place, and explains periodicity as a consequence of repeating outer electronic configurations.

mcqs.q: A major benefit of the periodic table is that it:
options: Eliminates the need to study elements at all
Reduces the study of more than 100 elements to the study of a few groups and periods
mcqs.why: The periodic table organises all elements into one systematic arrangement in which position predicts properties. The study of more than 100 elements is reduced to the study of a few groups and periods, and trends such as metallic character, atomic size and valency become clear at a glance.

mcqs.q: The gaps left in the periodic table led to:
options: The invention of the discharge tube
The prediction and later discovery of new elements such as gallium and germanium
mcqs.why: Because position predicts properties, the gaps in the table allowed chemists to predict the properties of undiscovered elements; gallium and germanium were later discovered with properties matching the predictions - a triumph of the table.

mcqs.q: Lithium resembles magnesium in its behaviour because of:
options: Both having the same atomic number
The diagonal relationship - Li is diagonally related to Mg in the table
mcqs.why: Lithium, the first member of Group 1, has a very small atom with high charge density, making it behave partly like the element diagonally below-right, magnesium. This is the diagonal relationship; similarly beryllium resembles aluminium.

mcqs.q: Beryllium resembles which element diagonally related to it?
mcqs.why: Beryllium (Group 2, Period 2) resembles aluminium (Group 13, Period 3), the element diagonally below-right: both have small atoms, high charge density, form covalent compounds, and Be(OH)2 like Al(OH)3 is amphoteric.

mcqs.q: Lithium and beryllium differ from the rest of their groups mainly because their atoms are:
options: Very small, with high charge density and high ionization energies
In the last period of the table
mcqs.why: Li and Be are the first members of their groups and have only two shells, so their atoms are very small with high charge density. They form more covalent compounds and less ionic salts than the heavier members, and their hydroxides are weaker (Be(OH)2 is even amphoteric).

mcqs.q: The hydroxide of beryllium, Be(OH)2, is unusual for a Group 2 hydroxide because it is:
options: Insoluble in all liquids including acids
mcqs.why: Unlike the strongly basic hydroxides of the heavier Group 2 metals, Be(OH)2 is amphoteric - it reacts with both acids and alkalis - reflecting beryllium's diagonal resemblance to aluminium.

mcqs.q: Mendeleev's periodic table arranged the elements in increasing order of:
mcqs.why: Mendeleev arranged elements by increasing atomic mass in 8 groups, based on the formulae of oxides and hydrides. He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties, but his table could not accommodate isotopes and misplaced some pairs.

mcqs.q: The modern periodic table arranges the elements in increasing order of:
options: Atomic number, and is based on electronic configuration
mcqs.why: The modern table has 18 groups and 7 periods arranged by atomic number, divided into s, p, d and f blocks. It removes Mendeleev's defects and explains periodicity as the repetition of outer electronic configurations.

mcqs.q: A defect of Mendeleev's table was that:
options: Isotopes could not be accommodated and some pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni) stood against mass order
It was based on electronic configuration
mcqs.why: Because Mendeleev used atomic mass, isotopes of an element (same properties, different masses) had no proper place, and pairs like argon/potassium and cobalt/nickel had to be placed against mass order to keep them in the right groups. Hydrogen also had no proper place.

mcqs.q: In the modern table, isotopes of an element occupy:
options: A single place, because they have the same atomic number
mcqs.why: Isotopes have the same atomic number and the same outer electronic configuration, so in the modern (atomic number) table they naturally share the one place of their element - one of the defects of Mendeleev's mass-based table that the modern table removes.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1(i) Which halogen will have the least reactivity with alkaline earth metals?

(a) Chlorine (b) Iodine (c) Bromine (d) Fluorine
Correct answer: Iodine

Q: 1(ii) Which compound do you expect to be coloured?

(a) KCl (b) BaCl2 (c) AlCl3 (d) NiCl2
Correct answer: NiCl2

Q: 1(iii) In which element there exists the strongest forces of attraction between atoms?

(a) Mg (b) Ca (c) Sr (d) Ba
Correct answer: Mg

Q: 1(iv) Elements of which group are all coloured?

(a) Second group (b) Sixth group (c) Fourth group (d) Fifth group
Correct answer: Sixth group

Q: Note: Which group is really all coloured?

Strictly, the group whose elements are all coloured is Group 17, the halogens: F2 is pale yellow, Cl2 greenish yellow, Br2 reddish brown and I2 violet. 'Sixth group' in the book's options appears to be a misprint (probably for the seventh/halogen group), and option (b) is the intended answer.

Q: 1(v) Which halogen acid is unstable at room temperature?

(a) HBr (b) HI (c) HCl (d) HF
Correct answer: HI

Q: 1(vi) Which oxide is the most basic oxide?

(a) Na2O (b) Li2O (c) MgO (d) CO
Correct answer: Na2O

Q: 1(vii) Which group elements are the most reactive elements?

(a) Transition metal group (b) First group (c) Second group (d) Third group
Correct answer: First group

Q: 1(viii) The following solutions of a halogen and a sodium halide are mixed together. Which solution will turn dark because of a reaction?

(a) Br2 and NaCl (b) Br2 and NaF (c) Cl2 and NaF (d) Cl2 and NaI
Correct answer: Cl2 and NaI

Q: 1(ix) X is a monoatomic gas, which statement about this is correct?

(a) X burns in air (b) X is coloured (c) X is unreactive (d) X will displace iodine from it
Correct answer: X is unreactive

Q: 1(x) Which property is correct for group 1 elements?

(a) Low catalytic activity (b) High density (c) Low electrical conductivity (d) High melting point
Correct answer: Low catalytic activity

mcqs.q: 1(i) Which halogen will have the least reactivity with alkaline earth metals?
mcqs.why: The reactivity of the halogens decreases down the group (F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2) because the atoms get larger and attract the electron they need less strongly. Iodine, the least reactive halogen, therefore has the least reactivity with alkaline earth metals.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) Which compound do you expect to be coloured?
mcqs.why: Nickel is a transition metal, and transition-metal compounds are characteristically coloured because of their partly filled d sub-shells. NiCl2 is therefore coloured, while KCl, BaCl2 and AlCl3 - compounds of non-transition metals - are white/colourless.

mcqs.q: 1(iii) In which element there exists the strongest forces of attraction between atoms?
mcqs.why: Down Group 2 the atoms get bigger and the metallic bonding becomes weaker. Magnesium, the smallest atom of the four, has the strongest forces of attraction between its atoms, so Mg is the answer.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) Elements of which group are all coloured?
mcqs.why: As the Note after this question in the book explains: strictly, the group whose elements are all coloured is Group 17, the halogens (F2 pale yellow, Cl2 greenish yellow, Br2 reddish brown, I2 violet), which is not among the options. 'Sixth group' appears to be a misprint (probably for the halogen group), and option (b) is the intended answer.

mcqs.q: 1(v) Which halogen acid is unstable at room temperature?
mcqs.why: The thermal stability of the hydrogen halides decreases down the group (HF > HCl > HBr > HI) because the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker. Hydrogen iodide, HI, is the least stable and is unstable at room temperature.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) Which oxide is the most basic oxide?
mcqs.why: Basic character of oxides increases down a group and decreases across a period. Na2O is the oxide of a Group 1 metal and is more basic than Li2O (above it in the group) and than MgO (Group 2); CO is a neutral oxide. So Na2O is the most basic oxide here.

mcqs.q: 1(vii) Which group elements are the most reactive elements?
mcqs.why: Group 1 elements (alkali metals) are the most reactive elements: each has a single outer electron that is lost very easily, and reactivity increases down the group. They are more reactive than Group 2, Group 3 and the transition metals.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) The following solutions of a halogen and a sodium halide are mixed together. Which solution will turn dark because of a reaction?
mcqs.why: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salts. Chlorine is above iodine in Group 17, so Cl2 + 2NaI -> 2NaCl + I2; the liberated iodine makes the solution turn dark. Br2 cannot displace chlorine or fluorine, and Cl2 cannot displace fluorine.

mcqs.q: 1(ix) X is a monoatomic gas, which statement about this is correct?
options: X will displace iodine from it
mcqs.why: A monoatomic gas must be a noble gas (Group 18): its atoms already have complete outer shells, so X is unreactive. It does not burn in air, is colourless, and cannot displace iodine from anything.

mcqs.q: 1(x) Which property is correct for group 1 elements?
mcqs.why: Group 1 elements actually have LOW densities, LOW melting points and HIGH electrical conductivity, so those three options are wrong. The correct property is their low catalytic activity - unlike transition metals, the alkali metals are not used as catalysts.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) Why does it become easier to cut an alkali metal when we move from top to bottom in a group I?

Going down Group 1 the atomic size increases, so the single outer electron is held in a larger atom and the metallic bonding between the atoms becomes weaker (the interatomic attraction decreases). The metals therefore become softer down the group, and a softer metal is easier to cut with a knife.

Q: 2(ii) Predict the reactivity of potassium towards halogens.

Potassium is a very reactive alkali metal (more reactive than sodium and lithium because its outer electron is lost most easily among the common alkali metals), and halogens are very reactive non-metals. Potassium therefore reacts vigorously, even violently, with halogens to form the corresponding potassium halides, e.g. 2K + Cl2 -> 2KCl; with fluorine the reaction is explosive.

Q: 2(iii) In the following reaction, chlorine acts as an oxidising agent. Which is the reducing agent? Cl2(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + Br2(g)

The reducing agent is sodium bromide, NaBr (the bromide ions, Br-): they lose electrons and are themselves oxidised to Br2 while chlorine gains the electrons and is reduced. A reducing agent is the substance that donates electrons, so Br- / NaBr is the reducing agent.

Q: 2(iv) Why does iodine exist in the solid state at room temperature?

Iodine molecules, I2, are large and heavy, so the van der Waals forces between them are comparatively strong (much stronger than between the small molecules of chlorine or bromine). These forces hold the molecules in a solid lattice at room temperature; iodine even sublimes easily on gentle warming.

Q: 2(v) How does Ni catalyse the reaction involving hydrogenation of oil?

Finely divided nickel provides a large surface on which hydrogen molecules and the oil molecules are adsorbed. Adsorption weakens the H-H bonds and brings the reactants together, so hydrogen adds across the double bonds of the unsaturated oil at a much lower temperature than would otherwise be needed, converting it into saturated fat (ghee). The nickel is recovered unchanged at the end; it acts as a (heterogeneous) catalyst.

mcqs.q: It becomes easier to cut an alkali metal as we go down Group 1 because:
options: The atoms get smaller and harder
The metals gain more outer electrons
The atoms get larger and the metallic bonding between them becomes weaker
mcqs.why: Going down Group 1 the atomic size increases, so the single outer electron is held in a larger atom and the metallic bonding (interatomic attraction) becomes weaker. The metals therefore become softer down the group and easier to cut with a knife.

mcqs.q: Potassium reacts with halogens:
options: Vigorously, even violently, forming potassium halides (explosively with fluorine)
Only when a catalyst is added
mcqs.why: Potassium is a very reactive alkali metal - its outer electron is lost most easily among the common alkali metals - and halogens are very reactive non-metals. They react vigorously, e.g. 2K + Cl2 -> 2KCl; with fluorine the reaction is explosive.

mcqs.q: In the reaction Cl2(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + Br2, the reducing agent is:
mcqs.why: A reducing agent donates electrons. The bromide ions lose electrons and are oxidised to Br2, while chlorine gains the electrons and is reduced. So NaBr (Br-) is the reducing agent and chlorine is the oxidising agent.

mcqs.q: In the same reaction (Cl2 + 2NaBr), chlorine acts as the oxidising agent because it:
options: Loses electrons to the bromide ions
Gains electrons and is itself reduced
mcqs.why: An oxidising agent gains electrons. Chlorine molecules gain the electrons lost by bromide ions and are reduced to chloride ions (Cl2 -> 2Cl-), so chlorine is the oxidising agent and NaBr the reducing agent.

mcqs.q: Iodine exists as a solid at room temperature because:
options: It has hydrogen bonding between its molecules
Its molecules are joined by ionic bonds
Its large, heavy I2 molecules have comparatively strong van der Waals forces between them
mcqs.why: I2 molecules are large and heavy, so the van der Waals forces between them are much stronger than between the small molecules of chlorine or bromine. These forces hold iodine molecules in a solid lattice at room temperature.

mcqs.q: On gentle warming, solid iodine readily:
options: Sublimes - changes directly from solid to violet vapour
Reacts with air to form a gas
mcqs.why: The forces holding I2 molecules in the solid are not very strong, so on gentle warming iodine sublimes: it passes directly from the solid state to violet vapour without melting.

mcqs.q: Finely divided nickel catalyses the hydrogenation of oils because:
options: It reacts permanently with the oil
Its large surface adsorbs hydrogen and oil molecules, weakening the H-H bonds and bringing the reactants together
It supplies hydrogen from its own structure
It heats the oil by friction
mcqs.why: On the large surface of finely divided nickel, hydrogen molecules and oil molecules are adsorbed. Adsorption weakens the H-H bonds and brings the reactants together, so hydrogen adds across the double bonds of the unsaturated oil at a much lower temperature. The nickel is recovered unchanged.

mcqs.q: Hydrogenation of an unsaturated oil over a nickel catalyst converts it into:
mcqs.why: Hydrogen adds across the carbon-carbon double bonds of the unsaturated oil, saturating them. The liquid oil is thereby converted into a solid saturated fat - vegetable ghee.

mcqs.q: Potassium is more reactive than sodium and lithium towards halogens because:
options: It has more outer electrons than sodium
Its atoms are the smallest in the group
Its outer electron is lost most easily among the common alkali metals
mcqs.why: Down Group 1 the atoms get larger and the single outer electron is farther from the nucleus and lost more easily (ionization energy decreases). Potassium, below sodium and lithium, therefore reacts most vigorously of the three with halogens.

mcqs.q: A catalyst such as nickel in hydrogenation is recovered at the end of the reaction:
options: Unchanged - it only provides a surface and a lower-energy path
As part of the product fat
mcqs.why: Nickel acts as a heterogeneous catalyst: it takes part by adsorbing the reactants on its surface but is regenerated and recovered unchanged at the end, which is the defining behaviour of a catalyst.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) Which noble gas should have the lowest boiling point and why?

Helium should have the lowest boiling point. The noble gases are monoatomic and are held together only by very weak van der Waals forces, which are weakest for the smallest atom, helium; hence helium liquefies at the lowest temperature (about -269 degrees C).

Q: 3(ii) Compare the reactions of alkali metals with chlorine.

All alkali metals react with chlorine to give white ionic chlorides, MCl: 2Li + Cl2 -> 2LiCl, 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, 2K + Cl2 -> 2KCl. The vigour of the reaction increases down the group, because the outer electron is lost more and more easily: lithium reacts steadily on warming, sodium burns brightly in chlorine, and potassium reacts still more vigorously.

Q: 3(iii) Why are almost all the metals solids while non-metals generally exist as gases and solids?

Metal atoms are held together by strong metallic bonds in a close-packed lattice, which needs a great deal of energy to break, so almost all metals are solids with high melting points (mercury is the exception). Non-metal elements consist of small molecules (or single atoms) held by weak van der Waals forces, so they are gases, volatile liquids or low-melting solids; only the giant-structure non-metals like diamond are hard high-melting solids.

Q: 3(iv) Name any three elements in the periodic table which exist as liquids.

Three elements that are liquids at room temperature: mercury (Hg, a metal), bromine (Br2, a non-metal) and gallium (Ga, which melts just above room temperature, about 30 degrees C). Mercury and bromine are the two elements liquid under ordinary room conditions.

Q: 3(v) Why are transition elements different from normal elements?

Transition elements have their (n-1)d sub-shell being filled, whereas normal (representative) elements fill only s or p sub-shells. Because of the partly filled d sub-shell, transition elements differ: they show variable oxidation states, form coloured compounds, act as catalysts, form complex compounds and are generally hard metals with high melting points and densities, properties not shown by normal elements.

Q: 3(vi) Compare the reactivity of chlorine and bromine as an oxidising agent.

Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent. An oxidising agent gains electrons; chlorine atoms are smaller than bromine atoms, so chlorine attracts an incoming electron more strongly (higher electron affinity/electronegativity). That is why chlorine can oxidise bromide ions and displace bromine from its salts (Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2), but bromine cannot displace chlorine. Oxidising power of the halogens decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

Q: 3(vii) Which element is the most reactive and which is the least reactive among halogens? Give two reasons to explain your answer.

Most reactive: fluorine; least reactive: iodine. Reasons: (1) Reactivity of halogens depends on gaining one electron; fluorine's atom is the smallest, so the incoming electron is attracted most strongly by its nucleus, whereas in iodine the outer shell is far from the nucleus and shielded by many inner shells, so the attraction is weakest. (2) The bond in F2 and the energy terms favour reaction most for fluorine, and oxidising power decreases steadily down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

mcqs.q: The noble gas with the lowest boiling point is:
options: Helium, because its small atoms have the weakest van der Waals forces
Neon, because it is the lightest gas
Argon, because it is most abundant
Xenon, because its atoms are largest
mcqs.why: Noble gases are monoatomic and held together only by very weak van der Waals forces, which are weakest for the smallest atom, helium. Helium therefore liquefies at the lowest temperature, about -269 degrees C.

mcqs.q: All alkali metals react with chlorine to give:
mcqs.why: 2Li + Cl2 -> 2LiCl, 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, 2K + Cl2 -> 2KCl: in each case a white ionic chloride is formed, because the metal transfers its outer electron to chlorine.

mcqs.q: The vigour of the reaction of alkali metals with chlorine down the group:
options: Increases, because the outer electron is lost more and more easily
mcqs.why: Lithium reacts steadily on warming, sodium burns brightly in chlorine, and potassium reacts still more vigorously. Down the group the atoms grow larger, the outer electron is lost more easily (ionization energy falls), so reactivity increases.

mcqs.q: Almost all metals are solids with high melting points because:
options: Their atoms are held by strong metallic bonds in a close-packed lattice
mcqs.why: Strong metallic bonding in a close-packed lattice needs a great deal of energy to break, so almost all metals are solids with high melting points. Mercury is the exception - it is a liquid metal.

mcqs.q: Non-metal elements are generally gases or low-melting solids because:
options: They consist of small molecules or single atoms held by weak van der Waals forces
Their atoms are the largest in the table
mcqs.why: Non-metals are made of small molecules (like Cl2, O2) or single atoms (noble gases) attracted only by weak van der Waals forces, so little energy separates them: they are gases, volatile liquids or low-melting solids. Giant-structure non-metals like diamond are the exceptions.

mcqs.q: Three elements that are liquids at (or just above) room temperature are:
mcqs.why: Mercury (Hg) is a liquid metal and bromine (Br2) a liquid non-metal at room temperature; gallium (Ga) melts just above room temperature, at about 30 degrees C. Chlorine and iodine are a gas and a solid respectively, and sodium is a solid.

mcqs.q: The only two elements that are liquids under ordinary room conditions are:
mcqs.why: Mercury and bromine are the two elements liquid under ordinary room conditions. (Gallium melts at about 30 degrees C, just above a cool room temperature, so it is counted as a near-room-temperature liquid.)

mcqs.q: Transition elements differ from normal (representative) elements because in them:
options: The outer shell is completely filled
The (n-1)d sub-shell is being filled, giving variable oxidation states and coloured compounds
mcqs.why: Normal elements fill only s or p sub-shells, but transition elements have a partly filled (n-1)d sub-shell. As a result they show variable oxidation states, form coloured compounds and complex compounds, act as catalysts, and are hard metals with high melting points and densities.

mcqs.q: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine because:
options: Its smaller atoms attract an incoming electron more strongly, so it can displace bromine from bromides
It is a gas while bromine is a liquid
mcqs.why: An oxidising agent gains electrons. Chlorine atoms are smaller than bromine atoms, so chlorine attracts an incoming electron more strongly (higher electronegativity/electron affinity). Hence Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2, but bromine cannot displace chlorine. Oxidising power decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

mcqs.q: Among the halogens, the most reactive is fluorine and the least reactive is iodine because:
options: Fluorine is a liquid and iodine is a gas
Fluorine's small atom attracts the incoming electron most strongly, while iodine's outer shell is far from the nucleus and well shielded
mcqs.why: Halogen reactivity depends on gaining one electron. Fluorine's atom is the smallest, so the incoming electron is attracted most strongly by its nucleus. In iodine the outer shell is far from the nucleus and shielded by many inner shells, so the attraction is weakest. Reactivity and oxidising power fall steadily: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) Explain the role of catalytic converter in an automobile.

A catalytic converter, fitted in the exhaust system of an automobile, contains catalysts such as platinum, palladium and rhodium on a honeycomb support. It converts the harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones: carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide, unburnt hydrocarbons are oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, and oxides of nitrogen are reduced to nitrogen gas. It thus greatly reduces air pollution from vehicles.

Q: 4(ii) Why do the chemical reactivities of alkali metals increase down the group whereas they decrease down the group in case of halogens?

Alkali metals react by losing their single outer electron. Down the group the atoms grow larger, the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily (ionization energy decreases), so reactivity increases. Halogens react by gaining one electron. Down their group the atoms grow larger and the incoming electron is attracted less strongly (electron affinity/electronegativity decreases), so reactivity decreases. The opposite size effect on losing versus gaining electrons explains the opposite trends.

Q: 4(iii) Why are metals generally tough and strong whereas non-metals are neither tough nor strong?

In metals the atoms are packed closely in a lattice and held by strong metallic bonds in all directions; a large force is needed to separate the layers, so metals are tough and strong. Non-metals are made of small molecules held by weak van der Waals forces (or, like sulphur and phosphorus, weak covalent structures), so they are soft or brittle and neither tough nor strong.

Q: 4(iv) Both alkali metals and halogens are very reactive elements with roles opposite to each other. Explain.

Both are one electron away from a stable octet, which makes both extremely reactive, but in opposite senses. An alkali metal atom has one electron more than the octet and achieves stability by losing it (it is a strong reducing agent, electropositive). A halogen atom has one electron less than the octet and achieves stability by gaining one (it is a strong oxidising agent, electronegative). That is why they react so vigorously with each other to form ionic salts.

Q: 4(v) Why hydrogen bromide is thermally unstable as compared to hydrogen chloride?

The H-Br bond is longer and weaker than the H-Cl bond, because bromine is a larger atom than chlorine and the overlap of its orbital with hydrogen is less effective. Thermal stability of the hydrogen halides decreases down the group (HF > HCl > HBr > HI), so less heat is needed to break HBr into H2 and Br2; hence HBr is thermally less stable than HCl.

Q: 4(vi) Compare the properties of metals and non-metals.

Metals: good conductors of heat and electricity; lustrous; malleable and ductile; generally high melting points, densities and tensile strength; sonorous; form basic oxides; lose electrons to form positive ions (electropositive); mostly solids. Non-metals: poor conductors (insulators, except graphite); dull in appearance; brittle when solid, not malleable or ductile; generally low melting points and densities; form acidic or neutral oxides; gain or share electrons (electronegative); exist as solids, liquids and gases.

Q: 4(vii) V2O5 catalyst is preferred over platinum in the oxidation of sulphur dioxide. Give reasons.

In the Contact process, SO2 is oxidised to SO3 over the catalyst. Vanadium(V) oxide, V2O5, is preferred to platinum because: (1) it is much cheaper; (2) it is not easily poisoned (deactivated) by impurities such as arsenic compounds present in the gases, which rapidly poison platinum; and (3) it works efficiently at the operating temperature of about 450 degrees C, giving a high conversion.

mcqs.q: The catalysts used in an automobile's catalytic converter are:
options: Platinum, palladium and rhodium on a honeycomb support
mcqs.why: A catalytic converter contains platinum, palladium and rhodium spread on a honeycomb support to give a large surface area. These transition-metal catalysts convert harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.

mcqs.q: In a catalytic converter, carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen are converted into:
mcqs.why: The converter oxidises carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide and unburnt hydrocarbons to carbon dioxide and water, and reduces oxides of nitrogen to harmless nitrogen gas - greatly reducing air pollution from vehicles.

mcqs.q: The reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group because:
options: The atoms grow smaller down the group
Each metal gains an extra outer electron
The atoms grow larger and the outer electron is lost more easily (ionization energy decreases)
mcqs.why: Alkali metals react by losing their single outer electron. Down the group the atoms grow larger, the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and shielded by more shells, so it is lost more easily and reactivity increases.

mcqs.q: The reactivity of halogens decreases down the group because:
options: The atoms grow larger and the incoming electron is attracted less strongly
The atoms grow smaller down the group
Each halogen loses its outer electron
Their electron affinity increases down the group
mcqs.why: Halogens react by gaining one electron. Down the group the atoms grow larger, the outer shell is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so the incoming electron is attracted less strongly (electron affinity/electronegativity decreases) and reactivity falls - the opposite trend to the alkali metals.

mcqs.q: Metals are generally tough and strong because:
options: Their molecules are held by weak forces
Their atoms are packed closely and held by strong metallic bonds in all directions
mcqs.why: In a metal the close-packed ions are held by the electron sea in all directions; a large force is needed to separate the layers, so metals are tough and strong. Non-metals, made of small molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, are soft or brittle by comparison.

mcqs.q: An alkali metal atom achieves a stable octet by:
options: Losing its one outer electron - it is a strong reducing agent
mcqs.why: An alkali metal has one electron more than a stable octet, so it achieves stability by losing that electron, forming a positive ion. Losing electrons makes it a strong reducing agent (electropositive).

mcqs.q: A halogen atom achieves a stable octet by:
options: Gaining one electron - it is a strong oxidising agent
mcqs.why: A halogen has seven outer electrons - one less than the octet - so it gains one electron to complete the octet, forming a negative ion. Gaining electrons makes halogens strong oxidising agents (electronegative), which is why they react so vigorously with alkali metals to form ionic salts.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen bromide is thermally less stable than hydrogen chloride because:
options: The H-Br bond is longer and weaker than the H-Cl bond
The H-Cl bond does not exist
Hydrogen forms weaker bonds with all elements equally
mcqs.why: Bromine is a larger atom than chlorine, so the H-Br bond is longer and its orbital overlap with hydrogen less effective, making the bond weaker. Thermal stability of the hydrogen halides decreases down the group: HF > HCl > HBr > HI.

mcqs.q: The correct order of thermal stability of the hydrogen halides is:
mcqs.why: As the halogen atom gets bigger down the group, the H-X bond gets longer and weaker, so less heat is needed to break it. Thermal stability therefore falls steadily: HF is the most stable and HI the least.

mcqs.q: V2O5 is preferred over platinum as the catalyst for oxidising SO2 (Contact process) because it:
options: Works at a lower temperature than any catalyst
Is much cheaper and is not easily poisoned by impurities such as arsenic compounds
mcqs.why: In the Contact process, vanadium(V) oxide is preferred to platinum because it is much cheaper, it is not easily poisoned (deactivated) by impurities such as arsenic compounds in the gases - which rapidly poison platinum - and it works efficiently at the operating temperature of about 450 degrees C.

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) Explain the role of sodium as heat transfer agent in the atomic nuclear power plant. Which property of sodium is utilized in this role.?

Liquid sodium is used as the coolant/heat-transfer agent in some nuclear power plants: it absorbs the enormous heat produced in the reactor core and carries it to a heat exchanger where it raises steam for the turbines. The property utilised is sodium's excellent thermal conductivity (together with its low melting point, 98 degrees C, high boiling point and good heat capacity): as a metal it conducts heat very efficiently while remaining liquid over a wide temperature range.

Q: 5(ii) Why and how does lithium behave differently from the rest of the alkali metals?

Lithium differs because its atom and ion are exceptionally small, giving a high charge density. As a result: it resembles magnesium (diagonal relationship) more than sodium; it reacts less vigorously with water; its hydroxide and carbonate are less soluble and its hydroxide is a weaker base; it forms a nitride with nitrogen; and many of its compounds have covalent character. The small size of Li and Li+ (and their strong polarising power) is the root cause.

Q: 5(iii) Why aluminum metal is used in the manufacture of cooking utensils whereas magnesium is not considered useful for this purpose?

Aluminium is light, a good conductor of heat, does not rust, and is protected by a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that stops further corrosion, so it is ideal for cooking utensils. Magnesium, although also light, is a much more reactive metal: it tarnishes and corrodes readily, reacts with hot water and steam and with acidic foods, and thin magnesium can even catch fire; utensils of magnesium would not last and would be unsafe.

mcqs.q: In some nuclear power plants, liquid sodium is used as:
options: A coolant / heat-transfer agent in the reactor
mcqs.why: Liquid sodium absorbs the enormous heat produced in the reactor core and carries it to a heat exchanger, where it raises steam for the turbines. It is a heat-transfer agent (coolant), not the fuel.

mcqs.q: The property of sodium utilised in its role as a heat-transfer agent is its:
options: Excellent thermal conductivity (with a low melting point of 98 degrees C and a high boiling point)
mcqs.why: As a metal, sodium conducts heat very efficiently. It melts at only 98 degrees C and boils at a very high temperature, so it stays liquid over a wide range while carrying heat from the reactor core to the heat exchanger.

mcqs.q: Liquid sodium in a nuclear plant carries heat from the reactor core to:
options: A heat exchanger, where steam is raised for the turbines
mcqs.why: The hot liquid sodium flows from the reactor core to a heat exchanger, where its heat raises steam; the steam drives the turbines that generate electricity, and the cooled sodium returns to the core.

mcqs.q: Lithium behaves differently from the rest of the alkali metals mainly because:
options: Its atom and ion are exceptionally small, giving a high charge density
It is the heaviest alkali metal
It is a liquid at room temperature
mcqs.why: The small size of Li and Li+ gives them a high charge density and strong polarising power. This is the root cause of all lithium's unusual behaviour, including its resemblance to magnesium (diagonal relationship).

mcqs.q: Because of the diagonal relationship, lithium resembles:
mcqs.why: Lithium (Group 1, Period 2) resembles magnesium (Group 2, Period 3), the element diagonally below-right, in many properties - a consequence of their similar charge densities.

mcqs.q: Compared with the other alkali metals, lithium reacts with water:
options: Not at all - it is inert
mcqs.why: Because of its small size and higher ionization energy, lithium reacts with water steadily but less vigorously than sodium or potassium, another way in which it differs from the rest of Group 1.

mcqs.q: Lithium hydroxide differs from the other alkali-metal hydroxides in being:
options: A weaker base and less soluble (its carbonate is also less soluble)
mcqs.why: LiOH is a weaker base than NaOH or KOH, and lithium carbonate is much less soluble than the other alkali-metal carbonates - both effects of the small, highly polarising Li+ ion, and both resemble magnesium compounds.

mcqs.q: Unlike the other alkali metals, lithium reacts with nitrogen to form:
mcqs.why: Lithium combines directly with nitrogen to form lithium nitride, Li3N - a reaction shown by magnesium but not by the other alkali metals, again reflecting the diagonal relationship.

mcqs.q: Aluminium is used for cooking utensils because it:
options: Is light, conducts heat well and is protected by a thin tough layer of aluminium oxide that stops further corrosion
Has the highest melting point of all metals
mcqs.why: Aluminium is light and a good conductor of heat, and it does not rust: a thin, tough Al2O3 layer forms on its surface and protects the metal below from further corrosion. These properties make it ideal for cooking utensils.

mcqs.q: Magnesium is NOT used for cooking utensils because it:
options: Is a poor conductor of heat
Is too reactive - it tarnishes and corrodes readily, reacts with hot water, steam and acidic foods, and thin magnesium can catch fire
mcqs.why: Although light like aluminium, magnesium is a much more reactive metal: it corrodes readily, reacts with hot water and steam and with acidic foods, and thin magnesium can even catch fire. Utensils made of it would not last and would be unsafe.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1(i) Which gases are responsible for greenhouse effect?

(a) SO2, NO2 (b) NO2, CO (c) CO2, CH4 (d) O2, N2
Correct answer: CO2, CH4

Q: 1(ii) Indicate the source of sulphur which is responsible for the presence of oxides of sulphur in the atmosphere.

(a) Decomposition of vegetation (b) Waste gases from digestion of animals (c) Photochemical smog (d) Combustion of fossil fuels
Correct answer: Combustion of fossil fuels

Q: 1(iii) Concentration of which gas in the atmosphere is decreased by photosynthesis in plants?

(a) Oxygen (b) Nitrogen (c) Carbon dioxide (d) Water vapours
Correct answer: Carbon dioxide

Q: 1(iv) Which substance remains unaffected in the catalytic converter fixed in the exhaust of the automobiles?

(a) CO2 (b) CO (c) NO (d) NO2
Correct answer: CO2

Q: 1(v) People of which age groups are most affected by the air pollution?

(a) Young adults (b) Middle age people (c) Children (d) Both children and aged people
Correct answer: Both children and aged people

Q: 1(vi) In which area there is a greater possibility of acid rain?

(a) Around village (b) Around big cities (c) Around industrial area (d) Around water bodies
Correct answer: Around industrial area

Q: 1(vii) Why is smog not felt in summer?

(a) Because fog is not present in summer (b) Because due to heat of the Earth the smoke rises up (c) Because in summer smoke and fog cannot mix with each other (d) Because less fossil fuels are burnt in summer
Correct answer: Because fog is not present in summer

Q: 1(viii) Which catalyst is used in the catalytic converter fixed in the exhaust systems of automobiles?

(a) Ni (b) Cu (c) Pt, Pd and Rh (d) CaO
Correct answer: Pt, Pd and Rh

Q: 1(ix) Which components are essential for the formation of photochemical smog?

(a) CO, NO2, CO2 (b) NO2, volatile organic compounds, sunlight (c) CO2, NO2, sunlight (d) Volatile organic compounds, NO2, CO
Correct answer: NO2, volatile organic compounds, sunlight

Q: 1(x) Which gases contribute towards the formation of acid rain?

(a) Oxides of carbon (b) Oxides of sulphur (c) Oxides of nitrogen (d) Both the oxides of nitrogen and sulfur
Correct answer: Both the oxides of nitrogen and sulfur

mcqs.q: 1(i) Which gases are responsible for greenhouse effect?
mcqs.why: Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases: their molecules absorb the infrared (heat) radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and send part of it back, warming the planet. O2 and N2 do not absorb infrared, and SO2/NO2 are acid-rain gases.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) Indicate the source of sulphur which is responsible for the presence of oxides of sulphur in the atmosphere.
options: Waste gases from digestion of animals
mcqs.why: Coal and oil contain sulphur. When these fossil fuels are burnt in power stations, industries and vehicles, the sulphur is oxidised to sulphur dioxide and other oxides of sulphur, which enter the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: 1(iii) Concentration of which gas in the atmosphere is decreased by photosynthesis in plants?
mcqs.why: In photosynthesis plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and use it (with water and sunlight) to make food, releasing oxygen. Photosynthesis therefore decreases the concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) Which substance remains unaffected in the catalytic converter fixed in the exhaust of the automobiles?
mcqs.why: A catalytic converter oxidises CO to CO2 and unburnt hydrocarbons to CO2 and water, and reduces NO and NO2 to N2. Carbon dioxide is already the final, harmless-at-the-tailpipe product, so CO2 itself passes through unaffected.

mcqs.q: 1(v) People of which age groups are most affected by the air pollution?
mcqs.why: Children have developing lungs and breathe faster, while aged people have weaker lungs, hearts and immune systems. Both children and aged people are therefore the groups most affected by air pollution.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) In which area there is a greater possibility of acid rain?
mcqs.why: Industrial areas burn large amounts of fossil fuels and release SO2 and oxides of nitrogen, which dissolve in rain to form acids. Acid rain is therefore most likely around industrial areas (and big industrial cities).

mcqs.q: 1(vii) Why is smog not felt in summer?
options: Because fog is not present in summer
Because due to heat of the Earth the smoke rises up
Because in summer smoke and fog cannot mix with each other
Because less fossil fuels are burnt in summer
mcqs.why: Smog is a mixture of smoke and fog. In summer there is no fog - the air is hot and pollutants rise and disperse - so smog is not felt in summer; it forms in cold, foggy winter weather.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) Which catalyst is used in the catalytic converter fixed in the exhaust systems of automobiles?
mcqs.why: The catalytic converter uses the transition metals platinum (Pt), palladium (Pd) and rhodium (Rh) as catalysts, spread on a honeycomb support in the exhaust system.

mcqs.q: 1(ix) Which components are essential for the formation of photochemical smog?
mcqs.why: Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen dioxide and volatile organic compounds (hydrocarbons) react in the presence of strong sunlight, producing ozone and other irritating products. Sunlight is essential - hence 'photochemical'.

mcqs.q: 1(x) Which gases contribute towards the formation of acid rain?
options: Both the oxides of nitrogen and sulfur
mcqs.why: Acid rain is caused by both sets of acidic gases: oxides of sulphur (SO2, SO3) forming sulphuric acid, and oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO2) forming nitric acid, dissolved in rain water. Oxides of carbon do not cause acid rain in this way.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) What is the main objective of environmental education?

The main objective of environmental education is to create awareness and understanding of the environment and of how human activities affect it, so that people develop responsible attitudes and practical habits: conserving resources, reducing pollution and waste, and protecting ecosystems for present and future generations.

Q: 2(ii) How is particulate matter released in the atmosphere?

Particulate matter (tiny solid particles and liquid droplets: dust, soot, smoke and ash) is released by the burning of fossil fuels in vehicles, factories and power stations, by burning of crop residues and garbage, by construction work, dust storms and industrial processes such as cement making, and by volcanic eruptions.

Q: 2(iii) Which gas is more poisonous, CO2 or CO?

Carbon monoxide, CO, is far more poisonous. It binds with the haemoglobin of blood about 250 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and preventing the blood from carrying oxygen to the tissues, which can cause death. CO2 is not directly poisonous at ordinary concentrations; it is harmful mainly as a greenhouse gas.

Q: 2(iv) How does acid rain affect forests?

Acid rain washes the nutrients (calcium, magnesium, potassium) out of the soil and makes the soil acidic, releasing toxic aluminium that damages tree roots. It also directly injures the leaves and bark of trees. Forests therefore grow poorly, their leaves yellow and fall, and whole forest areas die, especially at high altitudes.

Q: 2(v) In what way sulphur present in fossil fuels becomes dangerous?

When fossil fuels containing sulphur (coal and oil) are burnt, the sulphur is oxidised to sulphur dioxide, SO2, which is released into the air. SO2 irritates and damages the respiratory system, and in the atmosphere it is further oxidised and dissolved in moisture to form sulphuric acid, a main component of acid rain.

Q: 2(vi) Name any three major sources responsible for the greenhouse effect.

Three major sources of the greenhouse gases: (1) burning of fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas) in power stations, industries and vehicles, releasing CO2; (2) deforestation, which removes the trees that absorb CO2 and adds CO2 when the wood is burnt or decays; (3) agriculture and waste, including methane from livestock, rice fields and landfills (and nitrous oxide from fertilisers).

Q: 2(vii) How is wind energy useful for us?

Wind energy turns windmills and turbines: it generates electricity without fuel or pollution, pumps water for irrigation, and was traditionally used for grinding grain and sailing ships. It is a renewable and clean source of energy.

mcqs.q: The main objective of environmental education is to:
options: Create awareness of how human activities affect the environment, so people adopt responsible, pollution-reducing habits
Teach the names of all pollutants
Train people only for industrial jobs
mcqs.why: Environmental education aims at awareness and understanding of the environment and of how human activities affect it, so that people develop responsible attitudes: conserving resources, reducing pollution and waste, and protecting ecosystems for present and future generations.

mcqs.q: Particulate matter is released into the atmosphere by:
options: Burning of fossil fuels, crop residues and garbage, construction work and industrial processes such as cement making
mcqs.why: Particulate matter - tiny solid particles and liquid droplets such as dust, soot, smoke and ash - comes from burning fossil fuels in vehicles, factories and power stations, burning of crop residues and garbage, construction work, dust storms, cement making and volcanic eruptions.

mcqs.q: Carbon monoxide is far more poisonous than carbon dioxide because CO:
options: Turns into acid in the lungs
Binds with haemoglobin about 250 times more strongly than oxygen, preventing the blood from carrying oxygen
mcqs.why: CO combines with the haemoglobin of blood about 250 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. The blood can then no longer carry oxygen to the tissues, which can cause death. CO2 is not directly poisonous at ordinary concentrations; it is harmful mainly as a greenhouse gas.

mcqs.q: The compound formed when CO binds with haemoglobin is called:
mcqs.why: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin forming carboxyhaemoglobin, which is stable and blocks the haemoglobin from picking up oxygen - the reason CO is such a dangerous, silent poison.

mcqs.q: Acid rain damages forests mainly by:
options: Washing nutrients out of the soil and releasing toxic aluminium that damages tree roots
Burning the leaves with strong acid directly
mcqs.why: Acid rain washes nutrients (calcium, magnesium, potassium) out of the soil and makes it acidic, releasing toxic aluminium that damages tree roots; it also injures leaves and bark directly. Forests then grow poorly, leaves yellow and fall, and whole forest areas die, especially at high altitudes.

mcqs.q: Sulphur present in fossil fuels becomes dangerous because, on burning, it forms:
options: Sulphur dioxide, which damages the respiratory system and forms sulphuric acid in acid rain
Hydrogen sulphide in the fuel tank
mcqs.why: When coal and oil containing sulphur are burnt, the sulphur is oxidised to SO2 and released into the air. SO2 irritates and damages the respiratory system and, in the atmosphere, is further oxidised and dissolved in moisture to form sulphuric acid - a main component of acid rain.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a major source of greenhouse gases?
options: Burning of fossil fuels in power stations, industries and vehicles, releasing CO2
mcqs.why: The three major sources are: (1) burning fossil fuels, releasing CO2; (2) deforestation, which removes CO2-absorbing trees and adds CO2 when wood burns or decays; (3) agriculture and waste, giving methane from livestock, rice fields and landfills and nitrous oxide from fertilisers.

mcqs.q: Deforestation increases the greenhouse effect because it:
options: Increases the oxygen in the air
Removes the trees that absorb CO2, and adds CO2 when the wood is burnt or decays
mcqs.why: Trees are a natural sink for carbon dioxide through photosynthesis. Cutting and burning forests both removes this sink and releases the stored carbon as CO2, so deforestation strengthens the greenhouse effect in two ways.

mcqs.q: Methane, a greenhouse gas, is released from:
mcqs.why: Methane comes from agriculture and waste: the digestion of livestock, the flooded rice fields, and the decomposition of waste in landfills. Nitrous oxide from fertilisers is another agricultural greenhouse gas.

mcqs.q: Wind energy is useful because it:
options: Generates electricity without fuel or pollution and can pump water for irrigation
mcqs.why: Wind turns windmills and turbines: it generates electricity without fuel or pollution, pumps water for irrigation, and was traditionally used for grinding grain and sailing ships. It is a renewable and clean source of energy.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) How is the excessive use of insecticides and pesticides harmful for birds?

Insecticides and pesticides enter food chains and accumulate in the bodies of birds (biomagnification). Classic examples such as DDT make the egg shells of birds thin and fragile, so the eggs break before hatching and the populations decline; the chemicals also kill the insects that many birds feed on and can poison birds directly, upsetting the ecosystem.

Q: 3(ii) Percentage of CO2 in air is only 0.04%. Then how does it become harmful for the ecosystem?

Although CO2 is only 0.04% of the air, it is a powerful absorber of the infrared (heat) radiation given out by the Earth. Human activities keep adding to this small amount, and even a small increase strengthens the greenhouse blanket significantly, raising the Earth's temperature. The natural carbon balance is delicate: plants and oceans can absorb only a limited amount, so the excess accumulates year after year and disturbs the whole ecosystem through climate change.

Q: 3(iii) Why only some pollutant gases present in the atmosphere cause green house effect while others do not?

Only those gases cause the greenhouse effect whose molecules can absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions, sending part of it back to the surface. CO2, CH4, water vapour, N2O and ozone have the right molecular vibrations for this. The main gases N2 and O2 are made of two similar atoms and do not absorb infrared radiation, so they do not contribute to the greenhouse effect.

Q: 3(iv) How can you reduce the emission of CO present in the gases emitted by the burning of fuel in the automobile engines?

CO is formed by the incomplete combustion of fuel. Its emission is reduced by: ensuring complete combustion through proper tuning of the engine and a correct air-fuel mixture; fitting a catalytic converter in the exhaust, which oxidises CO to CO2; regular maintenance of vehicles; and shifting to cleaner fuels and electric vehicles.

Q: 3(v) Mention three different ways in which solar energy can be useful for us.

(1) Solar cells (photovoltaic panels) convert sunlight directly into electricity. (2) Solar water heaters, cookers and dryers use the Sun's heat directly. (3) Through photosynthesis, sunlight grows our food crops, and it also drives the water cycle and winds that we use for hydro and wind power. (Also: solar furnaces and solar desalination.)

mcqs.q: Insecticides such as DDT harm birds mainly because they:
options: Accumulate in birds' bodies (biomagnification) and make their egg shells thin and fragile, so eggs break before hatching
mcqs.why: Pesticides enter food chains and accumulate in the bodies of birds at the top - biomagnification. DDT makes egg shells thin and fragile so the eggs break before hatching and bird populations decline; the chemicals also kill the insects birds feed on and can poison birds directly.

mcqs.q: The process by which pesticides become more concentrated in animals higher up a food chain is called:
mcqs.why: As each animal eats many contaminated organisms, the pesticide is stored in its body and passed on in higher concentration to its predator. This build-up along the food chain is biomagnification, and it is why top predators such as birds of prey are harmed most.

mcqs.q: CO2 is only 0.04% of the air, yet it harms the ecosystem because:
options: It replaces oxygen in the air
It destroys the ozone layer directly
It is a powerful absorber of infrared radiation, so even a small increase strengthens the greenhouse blanket significantly
mcqs.why: Carbon dioxide strongly absorbs the infrared (heat) radiation given out by the Earth. Human activities keep adding to the small natural amount, and even a small increase traps much more heat, raising the Earth's temperature and disturbing the whole ecosystem through climate change.

mcqs.q: Excess CO2 accumulates in the atmosphere year after year because:
options: Plants and oceans can absorb only a limited amount of it
CO2 cannot be absorbed by anything
There are no plants left on Earth
CO2 is produced only by volcanoes
mcqs.why: The natural carbon balance is delicate: photosynthesis and the oceans absorb CO2, but only at a limited rate. The extra CO2 from burning fossil fuels exceeds this capacity, so the excess accumulates and the greenhouse effect keeps strengthening.

mcqs.q: Nitrogen and oxygen, the main gases of the air, do NOT cause the greenhouse effect because their molecules:
options: Are present in very small amounts
Absorb all radiation including visible light
mcqs.why: Only gases whose molecules can absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions cause the greenhouse effect - CO2, CH4, water vapour, N2O and ozone. N2 and O2, made of two similar atoms, do not absorb infrared, so they play no part.

mcqs.q: Greenhouse gases warm the Earth by absorbing:
options: The ultraviolet radiation from space stations
Visible light before it reaches the Earth
The infrared (heat) radiation emitted by the Earth's surface
mcqs.why: The Earth's surface, warmed by the Sun, emits infrared radiation. Greenhouse gas molecules absorb this outgoing radiation and re-emit it in all directions, sending part of it back to the surface - the essence of the greenhouse effect.

mcqs.q: Carbon monoxide emission from automobile engines can be reduced by:
options: Ensuring complete combustion through proper engine tuning and a correct air-fuel mixture
mcqs.why: CO is formed by the incomplete combustion of fuel. Proper tuning of the engine and the correct air-fuel mixture ensure complete combustion to CO2 instead; fitting a catalytic converter, regular maintenance, and shifting to cleaner fuels and electric vehicles reduce CO further.

mcqs.q: A catalytic converter reduces CO emission by:
mcqs.why: In the exhaust, the catalysts (Pt, Pd, Rh) oxidise the poisonous carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide, and also oxidise unburnt hydrocarbons and reduce nitrogen oxides to nitrogen.

mcqs.q: Solar cells (photovoltaic panels) are useful because they:
mcqs.why: Solar cells convert the Sun's light directly into electrical energy - a clean, renewable source of electricity. Solar energy is also used directly for heating water, cooking and drying, and through photosynthesis it grows our food crops.

mcqs.q: Besides making electricity and heat, solar energy also helps us by:
options: Growing food crops through photosynthesis and driving the water cycle and winds
mcqs.why: Through photosynthesis, sunlight grows the crops we eat; it also drives the water cycle (giving hydro power) and the winds (giving wind power). Solar furnaces and solar desalination are further uses.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) Describe the harmful effects of the major pollutants present in the air.

Oxides of carbon: CO is a poisonous gas that reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood; excess CO2 causes the greenhouse effect. Oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO2): irritate the lungs, form photochemical smog and contribute to acid rain. Oxides of sulphur (SO2, SO3): cause respiratory diseases and acid rain that damages buildings, crops and aquatic life. Methane: a strong greenhouse gas. Particulate matter: penetrates deep into the lungs and causes asthma, bronchitis, heart disease and cancer. Overall, these pollutants damage human health, crops, forests, water bodies and buildings.

Q: 4(ii) Explain greenhouse effect. How is global warming dangerous for us?

Greenhouse effect: the Sun's radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface, which then emits infrared (heat) radiation. Greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4 and others) absorb this outgoing radiation and re-emit it in all directions, so part of the heat is returned to the surface instead of escaping to space: the atmosphere acts like the glass of a greenhouse and the Earth stays warmer. Global warming is dangerous because the extra warming melts glaciers and polar ice (raising sea levels and flooding coastal areas), disturbs rainfall and causes floods and droughts, spreads diseases, damages crops and ecosystems, and makes heatwaves more severe.

Q: 4(iii) What is air quality index? What information does it convey?

The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a rating system that reports how polluted the air is at a place and time, based mainly on the levels of particulate matter and the key pollutant gases. It converts the measurements into a single number and category: an AQI under 50 is good and safe, while a value over 300 is hazardous to health. It tells people, especially the high-risk groups, whether it is safe to spend time outdoors and what precautions to take.

Q: 4(iv) Who are high risk groups and why is pollution more dangerous for them?

High-risk groups are children under 18, adults over 65, people with chronic heart or lung disease, diabetic patients, and outdoor workers. Pollution is more dangerous for them because children's lungs are still developing and they breathe faster, the elderly and the sick have weaker lungs, hearts and immune systems, and outdoor workers inhale polluted air for long periods. In them, pollutants entering the blood stream can quickly cause serious illness, hospitalisation and even premature death.

Q: 4(v) Describe three strategies to address environmental issues.

Three strategies: (1) Reduce emissions at source: discourage fossil fuels, shift to renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro), use cleaner public transport and enforce emission standards for vehicles and industries, including catalytic converters and filters. (2) Restore the natural balance: plant trees on a large scale and protect forests, which absorb CO2 and trap dust. (3) Manage waste and raise awareness: proper disposal and recycling of waste instead of burning, and environmental education so that individuals and industries adopt cleaner habits, supported by laws and monitoring such as the AQI.

mcqs.q: Oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO2) harm us because they:
options: Increase the oxygen in the blood
Irritate the lungs, form photochemical smog and contribute to acid rain
mcqs.why: NO and NO2 irritate the lungs and respiratory system, react in sunlight to form photochemical smog, and dissolve in rain as nitric acid, contributing to acid rain.

mcqs.q: Particulate matter is dangerous to health because it:
options: Penetrates deep into the lungs and causes asthma, bronchitis, heart disease and cancer
