mcqs.why: The tiny particles of particulate matter are inhaled deep into the lungs and can enter the blood, causing asthma, bronchitis, heart disease and cancer. Together with SO2 (respiratory diseases, acid rain) and CO (poisoning), they make air pollution a major health hazard.

mcqs.q: In the greenhouse effect, the atmosphere acts like the glass of a greenhouse because greenhouse gases:
options: Let the Sun's radiation in but absorb the outgoing infrared radiation and return part of it to the surface
mcqs.why: The Sun's radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface, which emits infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb this outgoing radiation and re-emit it in all directions, so part of the heat returns to the surface instead of escaping to space, keeping the Earth warmer.

mcqs.q: Global warming is dangerous because the melting of glaciers and polar ice will:
options: Increase the land area of continents
Raise sea levels and flood coastal areas
Make more fresh water available everywhere permanently
mcqs.why: Extra warming melts glaciers and polar ice, raising sea levels and flooding coastal areas. It also disturbs rainfall (floods and droughts), spreads diseases, damages crops and ecosystems, and makes heatwaves more severe.

mcqs.q: The Air Quality Index (AQI) tells us:
options: How polluted the air is - below 50 is good and safe, above 300 is hazardous to health
mcqs.why: The AQI converts measurements of particulate matter and key pollutant gases into a single number and category. An AQI under 50 is good and safe, while over 300 is hazardous; it tells people, especially high-risk groups, whether it is safe to be outdoors and what precautions to take.

mcqs.q: High-risk groups for air pollution include:
options: People who live in villages only
Children under 18, adults over 65, people with chronic heart or lung disease, diabetics and outdoor workers
mcqs.why: Pollution is more dangerous for these groups: children's lungs are still developing and they breathe faster, the elderly and the sick have weaker lungs, hearts and immune systems, and outdoor workers inhale polluted air for long periods - so illness, hospitalisation and even premature death can follow quickly.

mcqs.q: Air pollution is especially dangerous for children because:
options: Their lungs are still developing and they breathe faster than adults
mcqs.why: Children's lungs are still growing and, being active and breathing faster, they inhale more polluted air for their body size. Pollutants entering their blood stream can therefore cause serious illness quickly.

mcqs.q: One strategy to address environmental issues is to reduce emissions at source by:
options: Shifting to renewable energy, using cleaner public transport and enforcing emission standards for vehicles and industries
mcqs.why: Reducing emissions at source means discouraging fossil fuels, shifting to renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro), using cleaner public transport, and enforcing emission standards - including catalytic converters and filters - for vehicles and industries.

mcqs.q: Planting trees on a large scale helps the environment because trees:
options: Absorb CO2 and trap dust, restoring the natural balance
mcqs.why: Afforestation and protecting forests restore the natural balance: trees absorb carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and their leaves trap dust and particulate matter, cleaning the air.

mcqs.q: Proper waste management helps the environment because it:
options: Increases the amount of garbage burnt
Produces more methane in the open air
Has no connection with air quality
Replaces open burning of waste with disposal and recycling, reducing smoke and pollution
mcqs.why: Burning garbage is a major source of smoke and particulate matter. Proper disposal and recycling of waste instead of burning, together with environmental education and laws monitored through measures like the AQI, are key strategies against pollution.

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) Major Pakistani cities experience a very high AQI in winter which renders them the most polluted cities in the world. Point out some of the major causes of high AQI in these cities.

Major causes: the huge number of vehicles with poorly maintained engines; industrial emissions and brick kilns; burning of crop residues (stubble) in the surrounding fields in the winter season; burning of garbage and solid fuel for heating; construction dust; and the winter weather itself: cold, still air and temperature inversion trap the pollutants near the ground, while fog mixes with smoke to form dense smog. Together these push the AQI of cities like Lahore to hazardous levels in winter.

Q: 5(ii) Why does AQI not rise in Pakistan in hot days of summer?

In hot summer days the ground and the air near it are strongly heated, so the warm air (with the pollutants) rises and disperses into the upper atmosphere; winds and convection mix the air vertically. There is no temperature inversion layer to trap pollution, no fog for smog formation, and rain in the monsoon season washes particles out of the air. Hence the AQI stays much lower than in winter.

Q: 5(iii) How has climate change affected Pakistan during the last five years?

In the last five years Pakistan has faced the visible effects of climate change: the catastrophic floods of 2022, which affected about 33 million people and caused huge losses of life, homes and crops; record-breaking heatwaves, with cities like Jacobabad among the hottest places on Earth; faster melting of the northern glaciers with glacial lake outburst floods; erratic monsoon rains and longer dry spells causing drought in parts of Sindh and Balochistan; and longer, more severe smog seasons in the plains. These events have damaged agriculture, water supplies and public health.

mcqs.q: A major cause of very high AQI in Pakistani cities in winter is:
options: Too many trees in the cities
The huge number of vehicles with poorly maintained engines, together with industrial emissions and brick kilns
mcqs.why: Vehicle exhaust from poorly maintained engines, industrial emissions and brick kilns pour out pollutants; to these are added stubble burning, garbage burning, solid fuel heating and construction dust - the sources that push city AQI to hazardous levels.

mcqs.q: Burning of crop residues (stubble) in surrounding fields contributes to winter smog because it:
options: Releases large amounts of smoke and particulate matter into the still winter air
Cools the air so fog cannot form
mcqs.why: In the winter season, farmers burn crop stubble in the fields around cities. The smoke drifts into the cities, where cold, still air traps it near the ground and it mixes with fog to form dense smog.

mcqs.q: Winter weather itself raises the AQI because:
options: Winter air is thinner and cleaner
Cold, still air and temperature inversion trap the pollutants near the ground
Strong winter winds blow pollution into the cities from deserts only
There is more sunlight in winter
mcqs.why: In winter a temperature inversion layer acts like a lid: the air near the ground is colder and still, so pollutants cannot rise and disperse. Fog mixes with the trapped smoke to form dense smog, and the AQI reaches hazardous levels.

mcqs.q: Smog in Pakistani cities is at its worst in winter because it needs:
options: Fog to mix with the trapped smoke
mcqs.why: Smog = smoke + fog. Fog forms in cold winter weather; combined with pollutants trapped by temperature inversion, it produces the dense smog for which cities like Lahore become notorious in winter.

mcqs.q: The AQI does NOT rise on hot summer days because:
options: No fuel is burnt in summer
Pollutants are not produced in summer
The strongly heated air rises and disperses the pollutants into the upper atmosphere
mcqs.why: On hot days the ground and the air near it are strongly heated, so the warm air - with its pollutants - rises and disperses; winds and convection mix the air vertically. There is no inversion layer to trap pollution near the ground.

mcqs.q: Monsoon rain lowers the AQI because rain:
options: Washes the particles out of the air
mcqs.why: Rain droplets capture dust and particulate matter and bring them down to the ground, cleaning the air. Together with rising warm air and no fog, this keeps the summer (monsoon) AQI much lower than in winter.

mcqs.q: Climate change in Pakistan in recent years was shown most catastrophically by:
options: An increase in snowfall in Karachi
The floods of 2022, which affected about 33 million people
mcqs.why: The catastrophic floods of 2022 affected about 33 million people and caused huge losses of life, homes and crops - the most visible recent effect of climate change in Pakistan, alongside record heatwaves and glacial melt.

mcqs.q: Record-breaking heatwaves in Pakistan have made which city famous as one of the hottest places on Earth?
mcqs.why: Cities like Jacobabad in Sindh have recorded some of the highest temperatures on Earth during the recent record-breaking heatwaves - a direct effect of climate change on Pakistan.

mcqs.q: Faster melting of Pakistan's northern glaciers causes:
options: A permanent increase in river flow with no risk
mcqs.why: Warming melts the northern glaciers faster, forming unstable glacial lakes that can burst and cause glacial lake outburst floods in the valleys below, while in the long run the water supply itself is threatened.

mcqs.q: Erratic monsoon rains and longer dry spells due to climate change have caused, in parts of Sindh and Balochistan:
options: Drought, damaging agriculture, water supplies and public health
Permanent flooding of the whole provinces
mcqs.why: Climate change has made the monsoon erratic and dry spells longer, producing drought in parts of Sindh and Balochistan, while other areas flood. Together with heatwaves and worse smog seasons, these events damage agriculture, water supplies and public health.

lessons.title: In-text Exercise
lessons.notes_html:
Q: In-text Exercise (1): In the reduction of alkyl halides with Zn / HCl, alkyl halide is being reduced. Which species in this reaction is being oxidized?

Zinc metal is being oxidised: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-. The zinc dissolves in the acid as zinc chloride while it supplies the electrons (through the nascent/atomic hydrogen formed) that reduce the alkyl halide to the alkane. Oxidation and reduction always go together; here the alkyl halide gains hydrogen (reduction) and zinc loses electrons (oxidation).

Q: In-text Exercise (2): During the combustion reaction of ethane, which bonds are being broken and which are being formed?

Bonds broken: the C-C bond and the C-H bonds of ethane, and the O=O bonds of oxygen. For complete combustion, 2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 4CO2 + 6H2O: broken are 2 C-C bonds, 12 C-H bonds and 7 O=O bonds. Bonds formed: the C=O bonds in carbon dioxide (8 of them) and the O-H bonds in water (12 of them). The energy released in forming the new bonds is greater than the energy absorbed in breaking the old ones, so the reaction is exothermic.

Q: In-text Exercise (3): What products other than CH3Cl are formed when methane reacts with chlorine gas?

Besides chloromethane, CH3Cl, the reaction continues by substitution of the remaining hydrogens, giving dichloromethane, CH2Cl2, trichloromethane (chloroform), CHCl3, and tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride), CCl4, together with hydrogen chloride, HCl, at each step.

mcqs.q: When an alkyl halide is reduced with Zn/HCl, the species that is OXIDISED is:
mcqs.why: Oxidation and reduction always go together. The alkyl halide gains hydrogen (reduction), while zinc loses electrons and dissolves in the acid as zinc chloride: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-. Zinc is therefore the species oxidised (it supplies the electrons through the nascent hydrogen formed).

mcqs.q: In the Zn/HCl reduction, the alkyl halide is reduced because it:
options: Gains hydrogen and loses the halogen
mcqs.why: Reduction of an alkyl halide means the C-X bond is replaced by a C-H bond: the halide gains hydrogen (through the atomic hydrogen from Zn/HCl) and the halogen leaves as halide ion, giving the alkane.

mcqs.q: During the complete combustion of ethane, the bonds broken in the ethane molecule are:
options: The C-C bond and the C-H bonds
mcqs.why: Bonds broken: the C-C bond and the C-H bonds of ethane, and the O=O bonds of oxygen. Bonds formed: the C=O bonds in carbon dioxide and the O-H bonds in water. For 2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 4CO2 + 6H2O: broken are 2 C-C, 12 C-H and 7 O=O bonds; formed are 8 C=O and 12 O-H bonds.

mcqs.q: The balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethane is:
mcqs.why: Balance C: 2C2H6 gives 4CO2. Balance H: 2C2H6 gives 6H2O. Oxygen needed: 4CO2 needs 8 O atoms and 6H2O needs 6 O atoms, total 14 O atoms = 7O2. So 2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 4CO2 + 6H2O. The energy released in forming the new bonds exceeds that absorbed in breaking the old ones, so combustion is exothermic.

mcqs.q: In the combustion of two molecules of ethane, the number of O=O bonds broken is:
mcqs.why: From the balanced equation 2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 4CO2 + 6H2O, seven oxygen molecules are used for two ethane molecules, so 7 O=O bonds are broken (along with 2 C-C and 12 C-H bonds).

mcqs.q: When methane reacts with chlorine, the product formed after chloromethane by further substitution is:
mcqs.why: Substitution continues step by step: CH4 -> CH3Cl (chloromethane) -> CH2Cl2 (dichloromethane) -> CHCl3 (trichloromethane, chloroform) -> CCl4 (tetrachloromethane), with HCl formed at each step.

mcqs.q: The final, fully substituted product of methane with excess chlorine is:
mcqs.why: With excess chlorine all four hydrogens of methane are replaced one by one, ending at tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride), CCl4, with hydrogen chloride formed at every step.

mcqs.q: At each step of the chlorination of methane, the other product formed (besides the chlorinated methane) is:
mcqs.why: In each substitution step a chlorine atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom; the removed hydrogen combines with the second chlorine atom to give HCl. So CH3Cl, CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4 are each accompanied by HCl.

mcqs.q: Zinc dissolves in hydrochloric acid during the reduction of alkyl halides as:
mcqs.why: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + 2[H]. The zinc is oxidised to Zn2+ and passes into solution as zinc chloride, while the nascent (atomic) hydrogen produced reduces the alkyl halide to the alkane.

mcqs.q: Combustion reactions are exothermic because:
options: No bonds are broken in combustion
The energy released in forming the new bonds is greater than the energy absorbed in breaking the old bonds
Oxygen releases energy on its own
mcqs.why: Breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming bonds releases energy. In combustion, forming the strong C=O bonds of CO2 and O-H bonds of water releases more energy than is needed to break the C-C, C-H and O=O bonds, so the excess appears as heat (and light).

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1(i) Which other atom is almost always present along with carbon atom in all organic compounds?

(a) Oxygen (b) Nitrogen (c) Hydrogen (d) Halogen
Correct answer: Hydrogen

Q: 1(ii) Which other metal can be used to reduce alkyl halides?

(a) Al (b) Mg (c) Ni (d) Co
Correct answer: Mg

Q: 1(iii) If naphtha undergoes a combustion reaction what products do you expect it to form?

(a) Alkanes (b) Alkenes (c) CO2 and H2O (d) Both alkanes and alkenes
Correct answer: CO2 and H2O

Q: 1(iv) Why does a mixture of zinc and hydrochloric acid acts as a reducing agent?

(a) Because zinc acts as a reducing agent. (b) Because atomic hydrogen is produced with Zn / HCl which acts as a reducing agent. (c) Because molecular hydrogen is produced with Zn / HCl which acts as a reducing agent. (d) Because chloride ions are produced with Zn / HCl which act as a reducing agent.
Correct answer: Because atomic hydrogen is produced with Zn / HCl which acts as a reducing agent.

Q: 1(v) Which alkane will evolve the most amount of heat when it is burnt with oxygen?

(a) Ethane (b) Propane (c) n-Butane (d) iso-Butane
Correct answer: n-Butane

Q: 1(vi) Which reaction is not given by alkanes?

(a) Substitution (b) Combustion (c) Addition (d) Cracking
Correct answer: Addition

Q: 1(vii) Which hydrocarbon is responsible for explosions in coal mines?

(a) Butane (b) Pentane (c) Methane (d) Ethene
Correct answer: Methane

Q: 1(viii) Which product will be formed when ethyl bromide (CH3 CH2 Br) is treated with Zn/HCl

(a) CH4 (b) CH3 - CH3 (c) CH3 - CH2 - CH2 - CH3 (d) CH3 - CH2 - CH3
Correct answer: CH3 - CH3

Q: 1(ix) Which of the following is not a process of halogenation of alkanes?

(a) Cracking (b) Chlorination (c) Bromination (d) Iodination
Correct answer: Cracking

Q: 1(x) How many moles of oxygen will be required to completely burn propane?

(a) 4 moles (b) 5 moles (c) 3 moles (d) 6 moles
Correct answer: 5 moles

mcqs.q: 1(i) Which other atom is almost always present along with carbon atom in all organic compounds?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen is almost always present along with carbon in organic compounds - hydrocarbons contain only C and H, and most other organic compounds (alcohols, acids, sugars) also contain hydrogen. Oxygen, nitrogen and halogens occur only in some organic compounds.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) Which other metal can be used to reduce alkyl halides?
mcqs.why: Besides zinc, magnesium can also be used to reduce alkyl halides (for example with dry ether it forms organomagnesium compounds, and it supplies electrons for reduction). Aluminium, nickel and cobalt are not used for this reduction in the book's method.

mcqs.q: 1(iii) If naphtha undergoes a combustion reaction what products do you expect it to form?
mcqs.why: Naphtha is a mixture of hydrocarbons. Complete combustion of any hydrocarbon gives only carbon dioxide and water: hydrocarbon + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. Alkanes and alkenes are fuels here, not products.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) Why does a mixture of zinc and hydrochloric acid acts as a reducing agent?
options: Because zinc acts as a reducing agent.
Because atomic hydrogen is produced with Zn / HCl which acts as a reducing agent.
Because molecular hydrogen is produced with Zn / HCl which acts as a reducing agent.
Because chloride ions are produced with Zn / HCl which act as a reducing agent.
mcqs.why: Zn + HCl produces nascent (atomic) hydrogen, [H], which is a much stronger reducing agent than ordinary molecular hydrogen H2. It is this atomic hydrogen that reduces the alkyl halide to the alkane.

mcqs.q: 1(v) Which alkane will evolve the most amount of heat when it is burnt with oxygen?
mcqs.why: The heat evolved on burning increases with the size of the alkane molecule (more C-C and C-H bonds are oxidised). Among ethane (C2), propane (C3) and the butanes (C4), a butane evolves the most heat, and the book's key takes n-butane above its branched isomer iso-butane.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) Which reaction is not given by alkanes?
mcqs.why: Alkanes are saturated compounds - all their bonds are single - so they cannot add more atoms across a bond. They give substitution, combustion and cracking reactions, but NOT addition reactions (addition is characteristic of unsaturated alkenes and alkynes).

mcqs.q: 1(vii) Which hydrocarbon is responsible for explosions in coal mines?
mcqs.why: Methane leaking from coal seams mixes with air to form 'firedamp', an explosive mixture responsible for explosions in coal mines. This is why mine safety lamps and ventilation are essential underground.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) Which product will be formed when ethyl bromide (CH3 CH2 Br) is treated with Zn/HCl
mcqs.why: Zn/HCl replaces the halogen of an alkyl halide by hydrogen (reduction). Ethyl bromide CH3-CH2Br therefore gives ethane, CH3-CH3: the Br is removed and H takes its place.

mcqs.q: 1(ix) Which of the following is not a process of halogenation of alkanes?
mcqs.why: Halogenation of alkanes means introducing halogen atoms: chlorination (Cl2), bromination (Br2) and iodination (I2). Cracking is a completely different process - the breaking of large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller ones by heat - so it is not a halogenation process.

mcqs.q: 1(x) How many moles of oxygen will be required to completely burn propane?
mcqs.why: Propane burns completely as: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O. Check: C 3 = 3; H 8 = 8; O: 3CO2 + 4H2O needs 6 + 4 = 10 O atoms = 5 O2 molecules. So 5 moles of oxygen are required per mole of propane.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) Differentiate between an organic and an inorganic compound.

Organic compounds are the compounds of carbon, obtained originally from living sources; they are covalent, generally have low melting and boiling points, are inflammable, are mostly insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents, and exist in very large numbers. Inorganic compounds come from non-living (mineral) sources; they are often ionic, have high melting and boiling points, are generally non-inflammable, are often soluble in water, and are far fewer in number.

Q: 2(ii) Why are organic compounds found in large numbers?

Because of the unique property of carbon called catenation: carbon atoms can join with one another in long chains, branched chains and rings, and can form single, double and triple bonds, combining with H, O, N, halogens and many other elements. This produces millions of possible structures, so organic compounds are found in enormous numbers.

Q: 2(iii) Name the products which are obtained when natural gas is oxidized under controlled conditions.

Under controlled conditions natural gas (methane) is oxidised to useful products instead of burning completely: it gives methanol (CH3OH) and formaldehyde/methanal (HCHO); with steam over a catalyst it gives synthesis gas, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, CO + H2, used for making ammonia and methanol.

Q: 2(iv) How naphtha fraction is decomposed to give lower hydrocarbons?

By cracking: the naphtha fraction is heated strongly (at high temperature, in the absence of air and often over a catalyst), so that its long-chain hydrocarbon molecules break up (decompose) into smaller, more useful hydrocarbons, e.g. lower alkanes and alkenes such as ethene and propene.

Q: 2(v) Write down the molecular formula, structural formula and the condensed structural formula for iso-butane.

Iso-butane: molecular formula C4H10. Structural formula: a central CH group joined to three CH3 groups, CH(CH3)3. Condensed structural formula: (CH3)3CH. Its IUPAC name is 2-methylpropane.

Q: 2(vi) How are organic compounds useful for us?

Organic compounds are essential to life and daily living: our food (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins), medicines, fuels (petrol, gas, coal), clothing fibres, plastics, rubber, soaps and detergents, dyes, perfumes, pesticides and fertilisers are all organic compounds.

Q: 2(vii) Write down the names of five such organic compounds which exist naturally?

Five naturally occurring organic compounds: glucose (sugar), starch, cellulose, urea and natural rubber. (Also: proteins, fats/oils, citric acid, lactic acid.)

Q: 2(viii) Give IUPAC name to the following compound. CH3 - CH(CH3) - CH2 - CH3 (a CH3 group is attached below the second carbon).

The longest continuous chain has 4 carbon atoms (butane). A methyl group (-CH3) is attached to the second carbon atom. The IUPAC name is 2-methylbutane.

Q: 2(ix) How do the melting and boiling points of alkanes change when we move from lower members to higher members?

They increase regularly. As we go from lower to higher alkanes the molecules become larger and heavier, the van der Waals forces between them become stronger, and more heat energy is needed to separate them; so melting points and boiling points rise with the size of the molecule (the first four members are gases, the middle ones liquids and the higher ones solids).

mcqs.q: Which set of properties belongs to most organic compounds?
options: Ionic, very high melting points, non-inflammable
Always soluble in water and insoluble in petrol
Covalent, low melting and boiling points, inflammable, mostly insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents
Fewer in number than inorganic compounds
mcqs.why: Organic compounds are compounds of carbon, originally obtained from living sources. They are covalent, generally have low melting and boiling points, are inflammable, are mostly insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents, and exist in very large numbers.

mcqs.q: Inorganic compounds differ from organic compounds in that they are generally:
options: Made only of carbon and hydrogen
Often ionic, with high melting and boiling points, non-inflammable and often soluble in water
mcqs.why: Inorganic compounds come from non-living (mineral) sources. They are often ionic, have high melting and boiling points, are generally non-inflammable, are often soluble in water, and are far fewer in number than organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Catenation is the property of carbon by which:
options: Carbon atoms join with one another in long chains, branched chains and rings
mcqs.why: Catenation is carbon's unique self-linking property: carbon atoms join in long chains, branched chains and rings, forming single, double and triple bonds and combining with H, O, N, halogens and many other elements - producing millions of structures.

mcqs.q: Organic compounds exist in enormous numbers mainly because carbon can:
options: Form chains, branches and rings with single, double and triple bonds to many other elements
Form ionic compounds with metals only
mcqs.why: Because of catenation and its four valency, carbon builds an almost unlimited variety of skeletons and combines with many other elements. This produces millions of possible structures, so organic compounds are found in enormous numbers.

mcqs.q: Under controlled conditions, oxidation of natural gas (methane) gives the useful products:
mcqs.why: Instead of burning completely, methane oxidised under controlled conditions gives methanol and formaldehyde. With steam over a catalyst it gives synthesis gas (CO + H2), used for making ammonia and methanol.

mcqs.q: Synthesis gas, obtained from natural gas with steam over a catalyst, is a mixture of:
options: Carbon monoxide and hydrogen, CO + H2
mcqs.why: Passing methane and steam over a hot catalyst gives synthesis gas, CO + H2. This mixture is industrially important for making ammonia (with N2) and methanol.

mcqs.q: Cracking is the process in which:
options: Long-chain hydrocarbons are heated strongly (in the absence of air, often over a catalyst) so they break into smaller, more useful hydrocarbons
Small hydrocarbons join to form polymers
Hydrocarbons are burnt in excess oxygen
mcqs.why: In cracking, fractions such as naphtha are heated strongly at high temperature, in the absence of air and often over a catalyst. The long molecules decompose into lower alkanes and alkenes such as ethene and propene, which are in greater demand.

mcqs.q: Cracking of the naphtha fraction produces, among other products:
options: Lower alkenes such as ethene and propene
mcqs.why: The naphtha fraction's long-chain molecules break up into smaller hydrocarbons - lower alkanes plus valuable alkenes like ethene and propene, which are starting materials for plastics and other chemicals.

mcqs.q: The molecular formula of iso-butane is:
mcqs.why: Iso-butane is a butane isomer: four carbons in a branched arrangement still hold ten hydrogens, C4H10 - the same molecular formula as n-butane, but a different structure (2-methylpropane).

mcqs.q: The condensed structural formula of iso-butane is:
mcqs.why: Iso-butane has a central CH group joined to three CH3 groups: CH(CH3)3, written in condensed form as (CH3)3CH. Its IUPAC name is 2-methylpropane.

mcqs.q: The IUPAC name of iso-butane is:
mcqs.why: Taking the longest chain as propane (3 carbons) with a methyl group on carbon 2 gives 2-methylpropane - the systematic name of the branched butane commonly called iso-butane.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a naturally occurring organic compound?
mcqs.why: Naturally occurring organic compounds include glucose (sugar), starch, cellulose, urea and natural rubber (also proteins, fats/oils, citric acid and lactic acid). Sodium chloride, sulphuric acid and calcium carbonate are inorganic.

mcqs.q: The IUPAC name of CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3 is:
mcqs.why: The longest continuous chain has 4 carbon atoms (butane). A methyl group (-CH3) is attached to the second carbon. Numbering from the nearer end gives the substituent position 2, so the name is 2-methylbutane.

mcqs.q: In naming the compound CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3, the parent chain is chosen as:
options: The shortest chain of two carbons
The chain containing the branch only
The longest continuous carbon chain - four carbons, giving butane
mcqs.why: IUPAC rule: select the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent. Here it has 4 carbons (butane); the remaining CH3 is a methyl substituent on carbon 2, giving 2-methylbutane.

mcqs.q: As we go from lower to higher alkanes, their melting and boiling points:
options: Increase regularly, because the larger molecules have stronger van der Waals forces
mcqs.why: Higher alkanes have larger, heavier molecules; the van der Waals forces between them are stronger, so more heat energy is needed to separate them. Hence melting and boiling points rise with molecular size: the first four members are gases, the middle ones liquids and the higher ones solids.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) Why do alkanes show little reactivity towards the other reagents?

All the bonds in alkanes are strong single covalent bonds (C-C and C-H), and the molecules are almost non-polar, so there is no weak point or reactive site for reagents to attack. Breaking these bonds needs a lot of energy (light or high temperature), so at ordinary conditions alkanes are quite unreactive (they were called 'paraffins', meaning little affinity).

Q: 3(ii) Why does a mixture of natural gas and air explode?

Natural gas (mainly methane) escaping into air forms an explosive mixture: within certain limits of proportion, the mixture burns extremely rapidly when ignited by a spark or flame, because the combustion of methane is highly exothermic and the hot gases expand suddenly. The rapid expansion of gases in a confined space is the explosion.

Q: 3(iii) How do you compare the melting and boiling points of inorganic and organic compounds?

Inorganic compounds are often ionic or have strong intermolecular forces, so their melting and boiling points are high. Organic compounds are covalent molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, so their melting and boiling points are generally much lower than those of inorganic compounds.

Q: 3(iv) Reactions of alkanes with chlorine takes place in the presence of sunlight. What is the role of sunlight in the reaction?

Sunlight provides the energy needed to break the Cl-Cl bond into free chlorine atoms (free radicals), which start and carry on the substitution reaction with the alkane. In the dark the Cl2 molecules cannot be split, so the reaction does not take place; sunlight acts as the initiator of the free-radical chain reaction.

Q: 3(v) How do you compare the boiling point of n - butane with that of iso - butane?

n-Butane has the higher boiling point (about -0.5 degrees C) than iso-butane (about -12 degrees C). The straight-chain molecules of n-butane pack closely and have a larger surface of contact, so their van der Waals forces are stronger; the branched, more compact molecules of iso-butane touch less effectively, so less energy is needed to separate them.

Q: 3(vi) Why are organic compounds not generally soluble in water?

Most organic compounds are covalent and non-polar (or only weakly polar), while water is a strongly polar solvent. The weak forces between organic molecules cannot be replaced by strong attractions to water molecules, so the compounds do not dissolve; they dissolve instead in non-polar organic solvents such as petrol, benzene and ether ('like dissolves like').

mcqs.q: Alkanes show little reactivity towards other reagents because:
options: All their bonds are strong single covalent bonds and the molecules are almost non-polar, leaving no weak point to attack
mcqs.why: Breaking the strong C-C and C-H single bonds of alkanes needs a lot of energy (light or high temperature). With no polar or weak site for reagents to attack, alkanes are quite unreactive at ordinary conditions - they were called 'paraffins', meaning little affinity.

mcqs.q: A mixture of natural gas and air explodes when ignited because:
options: The mixture burns extremely rapidly and the hot gases expand suddenly in a confined space
The gas turns into a solid
mcqs.why: Natural gas (mainly methane) mixed with air in certain proportions forms an explosive mixture: combustion is highly exothermic and almost instantaneous on ignition, and the sudden expansion of the hot gases in a confined space is the explosion.

mcqs.q: Organic compounds generally have LOWER melting and boiling points than inorganic compounds because:
options: Organic molecules are covalent and held by weak van der Waals forces, while many inorganic compounds are ionic with strong forces
Organic compounds are heavier in every case
mcqs.why: Ionic inorganic compounds are held by strong electrostatic forces and need much heat to melt or boil. Covalent organic molecules are held only by weak van der Waals forces, so their melting and boiling points are generally much lower.

mcqs.q: Sunlight is needed for the reaction of alkanes with chlorine because it:
options: Heats the alkane until it melts
Provides the energy to break the Cl-Cl bond into free chlorine atoms (free radicals) that start the reaction
Removes hydrogen from the alkane directly
mcqs.why: Ultraviolet light in sunlight splits Cl2 molecules into reactive chlorine free radicals, which start and carry on the substitution chain reaction with the alkane. In the dark the Cl-Cl bond is not broken, so the reaction does not take place.

mcqs.q: In the dark, chlorine does not react with an alkane because:
options: Alkanes become ionic in the dark
The temperature always falls to zero
The Cl2 molecules cannot be split into free radicals without light energy
mcqs.why: The chain reaction is initiated by chlorine free radicals, formed only when light supplies the bond-breaking energy. Without light there are no radicals, so no substitution occurs.

mcqs.q: n-Butane has a higher boiling point (about -0.5 C) than iso-butane (about -12 C) because:
options: Straight-chain n-butane molecules pack closely with a larger surface of contact, giving stronger van der Waals forces
iso-Butane has stronger covalent bonds inside the molecule
mcqs.why: Both are C4H10, but shape matters: n-butane's straight chains lie close together with more contact area, so intermolecular forces are stronger and more energy is needed to boil it. Branched iso-butane molecules are compact and touch less effectively.

mcqs.q: Branched alkanes generally boil at lower temperatures than their straight-chain isomers because branched molecules:
options: Are more compact and touch neighbouring molecules less effectively, so less energy separates them
mcqs.why: Branching makes the molecule ball-shaped rather than rod-shaped. The reduced surface contact weakens the van der Waals attractions, so branched isomers (like iso-butane) boil lower than straight-chain ones (like n-butane).

mcqs.q: Most organic compounds do not dissolve in water because:
options: Water repels all carbon compounds chemically
They are covalent and non-polar, while water is a strongly polar solvent - 'like dissolves like'
mcqs.why: The weak forces between non-polar organic molecules cannot be replaced by strong attractions to water molecules, so the compounds stay undissolved in water. They dissolve instead in non-polar organic solvents such as petrol, benzene and ether.

mcqs.q: A typical organic compound will dissolve best in:
options: A non-polar organic solvent such as petrol, benzene or ether
mcqs.why: Following 'like dissolves like', non-polar covalent organic compounds dissolve in non-polar solvents - petrol, benzene and ether are standard examples - rather than in polar water.

mcqs.q: Breaking the bonds of an alkane requires a lot of energy, which is why alkane reactions usually need:
options: Light or high temperature to get started
Nothing at all - they react instantly
mcqs.why: The C-C and C-H bonds are strong, so an input of energy - sunlight for chlorination, a spark or flame for combustion, high temperature for cracking - is needed to break the first bonds and start the reaction.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) Describe the importance of organic compounds in daily life.

Organic compounds form the basis of daily life. Food: carbohydrates, proteins, fats and vitamins give us energy and build the body. Health: medicines such as aspirin, paracetamol and antibiotics are organic compounds. Clothing: cotton, wool, silk and synthetic fibres. Fuels: petrol, diesel, kerosene, natural gas and coal run our vehicles and homes. Household articles: plastics, soaps, detergents, cosmetics, dyes, paints and rubber. Agriculture: fertilisers, pesticides and insecticides. Life itself is built on organic compounds, since the bodies of all living things are made of them.

Q: 4(ii) Why is carbon so important as an element that the whole branch of chemistry is based on it?

Carbon is tetravalent and has the unique power of catenation: it can form four strong covalent bonds and can link with itself in long chains, branches and rings, and with many other elements, making millions of compounds. It is also the backbone of all living matter: proteins, carbohydrates, fats and nucleic acids are carbon compounds. Because of this unmatched versatility, an entire branch of chemistry, organic chemistry, is devoted to the compounds of carbon.

Q: 4(iii) A carbon-carbon single bond (C - C) in alkanes does not behave as a functional group but a carbon carbon double bond (C = C) in alkenes does. Explain.

A functional group is the atom or group of atoms that gives a compound its characteristic reactions. The C-C single bond is present in all alkanes and is strong and non-polar; it does not react in any characteristic way, so it is not a functional group: alkanes as a class are unreactive. The C=C double bond in alkenes, however, is a centre of reactivity: its pi electrons are exposed and readily take part in addition reactions, which are the characteristic reactions of alkenes. Hence C=C behaves as a functional group while C-C does not.

Q: 4(iv) Explain IUPAC system of nomenclature for alkanes.

In the IUPAC system for alkanes: (1) Select the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent chain; its length gives the base name (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex- ... -ane). (2) Number the chain from the end that gives the side groups (substituents) the lowest possible numbers. (3) Name each side group as an alkyl group (methyl, ethyl, etc.) with its position number, listed alphabetically before the parent name. (4) If the same group occurs more than once, use di-, tri-, tetra- prefixes. Example: CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3 is 2-methylbutane.

Q: 4(v) How combustion reaction of alkanes is useful for us?

Combustion of alkanes is strongly exothermic and is our main source of energy: methane (natural gas) is used for cooking, heating and generating electricity; propane and butane (LPG) are used as domestic and vehicle fuels; petrol and diesel (mixtures of alkanes) run vehicles; and kerosene is used in lamps, stoves and jet engines. The useful products are heat, light and mechanical/electrical energy, with CO2 and water as the end products.

mcqs.q: Which of the following medicines are organic compounds?
options: Aspirin, paracetamol and antibiotics such as penicillin
mcqs.why: Almost all modern medicines are organic compounds: aspirin, paracetamol and antibiotics are carbon compounds designed from organic chemistry. Food, fuels, fibres, plastics, soaps, dyes and fertilisers are likewise organic.

mcqs.q: Carbon is given a whole branch of chemistry (organic chemistry) mainly because of:
options: Its great hardness as diamond only
Its tetravalency and unique power of catenation, forming millions of compounds in chains, branches and rings
Its presence in the air as CO2
mcqs.why: Carbon forms four strong covalent bonds and links with itself and with many other elements in an unmatched variety of structures - millions of compounds. It is also the backbone of all living matter (proteins, carbohydrates, fats, nucleic acids), so an entire branch of chemistry is devoted to it.

mcqs.q: The compounds that form the backbone of all living matter - proteins, carbohydrates, fats and nucleic acids - are compounds of:
mcqs.why: Every living organism is built from carbon compounds: proteins, carbohydrates, fats and nucleic acids all have carbon skeletons. This is a second reason carbon holds a unique place in chemistry.

mcqs.q: A functional group is:
options: Any carbon atom in a chain
The longest chain in a molecule
A group of compounds with the same colour
The atom or group of atoms that gives a compound its characteristic reactions
mcqs.why: The functional group determines how a compound reacts: -OH makes alcohols behave alike, C=C makes alkenes give addition reactions, and so on. Compounds are classified into families by their functional groups.

mcqs.q: The C=C double bond in alkenes behaves as a functional group because:
options: Its exposed pi electrons readily take part in addition reactions, the characteristic reactions of alkenes
It is present in all alkanes too
mcqs.why: The pi bond of C=C sticks out from the molecule and its electrons are easily attacked by reagents, so alkenes undergo addition across the double bond. This characteristic reactivity makes C=C a true functional group.

mcqs.q: The C-C single bond in alkanes does NOT behave as a functional group because it:
options: Is strong and non-polar and takes part in no characteristic reaction - alkanes as a class are unreactive
mcqs.why: Every alkane contains C-C single bonds, yet they give the molecule no special reactivity - the bond is strong, non-polar and inert. A functional group must confer characteristic reactions, which the C-C bond does not.

mcqs.q: In IUPAC nomenclature of alkanes, the base name comes from:
options: The number of hydrogen atoms only
The longest continuous carbon chain (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex- ... -ane)
mcqs.why: Step 1 of IUPAC naming: select the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent; its length fixes the base name (1 = meth-, 2 = eth-, 3 = prop-, 4 = but-, 5 = pent-, 6 = hex-, with the ending -ane for alkanes).

mcqs.q: When numbering the parent chain of an alkane, you number from the end that:
options: Gives the substituents the highest numbers
Is nearest to the alphabetically first group name only
Gives the side groups (substituents) the lowest possible numbers
mcqs.why: Step 2: number the chain from the end giving substituents the lowest locants. Then name each alkyl side group with its position, listed alphabetically before the parent name.

mcqs.q: If the same alkyl group occurs more than once in an alkane, its name uses the prefix:
options: di-, tri- or tetra- (for two, three or four groups)
mcqs.why: Repeated substituents are counted with multiplying prefixes: two = di-, three = tri-, four = tetra- (e.g. 2,3-dimethylbutane has two methyl groups). Each position number is still listed.

mcqs.q: The combustion of alkanes is useful to us mainly because it:
options: Is strongly exothermic - methane, LPG, petrol, diesel and kerosene supply our heat, light and power
mcqs.why: Burning alkanes releases large amounts of energy: methane (natural gas) for cooking, heating and electricity; propane and butane (LPG) as domestic and vehicle fuels; petrol and diesel for vehicles; kerosene for lamps, stoves and jet engines - with CO2 and water as end products.

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) When natural gas valve is kept open in the kitchen, the gas spreads through the whole kitchen. This may cause an explosion. What is the reason of this explosion and how can you avoid it?

The leaking natural gas (methane) diffuses and mixes with the air of the kitchen, forming an explosive mixture. Any spark or flame (from a match, a switch or the stove) ignites it, and the whole mixture burns almost instantaneously with a sudden expansion of hot gases: an explosion. To avoid it: never leave a gas valve open without a flame, keep the kitchen ventilated, check pipes and connections for leaks, close the cylinder/regulator valve when not in use, and if gas is smelt, do not light a match or switch on electrical appliances; open the doors and windows and close the supply first.

Q: 5(ii) "Neem" is a common tree grown throughout our country. Comment on the medicinal benefits of this tree.

Neem is called a village pharmacy. Its leaves, bark, seeds and oil (containing compounds such as azadirachtin and nimbin) have antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral and anti-inflammatory properties. Neem is traditionally used for skin diseases, wounds, dental care (neem twigs as toothbrushes), fever and as a blood purifier; neem extracts are also used as a natural insecticide and in soaps and cosmetics. Its wide availability and low cost make it valuable in our country.

Q: 5(iii) Name a few popular medicines which are, in fact, organic compounds?

Popular medicines that are organic compounds: paracetamol (pain and fever), aspirin (pain, fever and heart protection), ibuprofen, penicillin and other antibiotics, antihistamines, and vitamins such as vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Almost all modern medicines are organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Gas leaking from an open valve fills the whole kitchen and may explode because the methane:
options: Diffuses and mixes with air to form an explosive mixture that any spark can ignite
mcqs.why: Methane diffuses through the kitchen air forming an explosive mixture. A spark or flame - from a match, a switch or the stove - ignites the whole mixture almost instantaneously, and the sudden expansion of hot gases is the explosion.

mcqs.q: If you smell leaked gas in the kitchen, the SAFE action is to:
options: Light a candle to find the leak
Open doors and windows and close the gas supply - without lighting a match or switching electrical appliances
Turn on the stove to burn the gas away
mcqs.why: Any spark - even from an electrical switch - can ignite the explosive gas-air mixture. First close the supply valve, then ventilate by opening doors and windows; never strike a match or operate switches until the gas has cleared.

mcqs.q: Explosions from leaked gas can be prevented by:
options: Storing extra cylinders beside the stove
Keeping the kitchen ventilated, checking pipes and connections for leaks, and closing the cylinder/regulator valve when not in use
mcqs.why: Prevention is simple: never leave a gas valve open without a flame, ventilate the kitchen, check pipes and connections regularly for leaks, and close the cylinder or regulator valve whenever the gas is not in use.

mcqs.q: Neem is called a 'village pharmacy' because its leaves, bark, seeds and oil have:
options: Antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral and anti-inflammatory properties
mcqs.why: Neem's parts contain compounds such as azadirachtin and nimbin with antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral and anti-inflammatory action. Neem is traditionally used for skin diseases, wounds, dental care, fever and as a blood purifier, and its extracts serve as a natural insecticide and in soaps and cosmetics.

mcqs.q: Azadirachtin, obtained from neem, is used as:
mcqs.why: Azadirachtin from neem seeds is a well-known natural (botanical) insecticide - it repels and disrupts insect pests without the pollution of synthetic pesticides, one of neem's most valuable uses in our country.

mcqs.q: Neem twigs are traditionally used in our villages for:
mcqs.why: Chewing neem twigs cleans the teeth and fights the bacteria of dental disease - a traditional, free toothbrush. Neem is also used for skin diseases, wounds, fever and as a blood purifier.

mcqs.q: Paracetamol, used for pain and fever, is an example of:
options: An organic compound used as a medicine
mcqs.why: Popular medicines that are in fact organic compounds include paracetamol (pain and fever), aspirin (pain, fever and heart protection), ibuprofen, penicillin and other antibiotics, antihistamines and vitamins such as vitamin C (ascorbic acid).

mcqs.q: Aspirin is an organic medicine used for:
options: Pain, fever and protection of the heart
mcqs.why: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) relieves pain and fever and, in small regular doses, protects the heart by preventing clots. Like almost all modern medicines, it is an organic compound.

mcqs.q: Vitamin C, an organic compound, is also known by its chemical name:
mcqs.why: Vitamin C is ascorbic acid - a carbon compound essential in the diet. Its presence in the list of 'medicines' shows how completely daily health depends on organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Neem extracts are also used in:
options: Soaps and cosmetics, besides medicines and insecticides
mcqs.why: Because of its antibacterial and skin-friendly properties, neem is added to soaps, creams and other cosmetics. Its wide availability and low cost make this common tree especially valuable in our country.

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Empirical Data Collection and Analysis

lessons.title: In-text Exercise & Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: In-text Exercise 1: A student weighs a given substance three times, and each time he gets the reading 5.2g. The true weight of the substance is, however, 5.0g. Is the work done by the student (i) precise and accurate (ii) accurate but not precise (iii) precise but not accurate?

The work is (iii) precise but not accurate. All three readings are identical (5.2 g), so they agree closely with each other: the work is precise. But every reading differs from the true weight (5.0 g) by 0.2 g, so the work is not accurate. The constant difference suggests a systematic error, e.g. the balance was not zeroed.

Q: In-text Exercise 2: How will you avoid systematic and random errors?

Systematic errors are avoided by calibrating and zeroing the instruments before use, using standard/certified apparatus, and applying the known constant correction to every reading. Random errors cannot be removed completely, but they are reduced by taking several repeated measurements and using their average, by working carefully with a consistent technique (e.g. reading the meniscus at eye level), and by controlling environmental disturbances such as draughts on a balance.

Q: 1(i) Which of the following pairs of quantities may be measured in the same unit?

(a) Heat and temperature (b) Temperature and area (c) Heat and work (d) Length and work
Correct answer: Heat and work

Q: 1(ii) In which unit we usually measure the energy present in the food?

(a) Kilojoules (b) Megajoules (c) Calorie (d) Joule
Correct answer: Calorie

Q: 1(iii) What prefix is used for 10^-12?

(a) Mega (b) Pico (c) Giga (d) Tessa
Correct answer: Pico

Q: 1(iv) In SI unit of pressure is expressed in:

(a) Newton per metre (b) Newton per metre square (c) Joule (d) Pascal
Correct answer: Pascal

Q: 1(v) Which symbol is used for kilogram in SI units?

(a) K (b) k (c) Kgm (d) kg
Correct answer: kg

Q: 1(vi) What does a mole represent?

(a) Number (b) Mass (c) Volume (d) Length
Correct answer: Number

Q: 1(vii) Which unit of volume should usually be used in Chemistry?

(a) Millilitre (b) Litre (c) Cubic centimetre (d) Cubic metre
Correct answer: Cubic centimetre

Q: 1(viii) Express 0.000840 in scientific notation:

(a) 8.40 x 10^-3 (b) 840 x 10^-6 (c) 8.40 x 10^-4 (d) 84.0 x 10^-5
Correct answer: 8.40 x 10^-4

Q: 1(ix) In SI units prefix nano means:

(a) 10^-9 (b) 10^-8 (c) 10^-11 (d) 10^-12
Correct answer: 10^-9

Q: 1(x) 65 degrees C is equivalent to:

(a) 208 K (b) 338 K (c) 403 K (d) 300 K
Correct answer: 338 K

mcqs.q: 1(i) Which of the following pairs of quantities may be measured in the same unit?
mcqs.why: Heat and work are both forms of energy, so both are measured in the same unit, the joule (J). Temperature is measured in kelvin/degrees Celsius and area in square metres - different kinds of quantity cannot share a unit.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) In which unit we usually measure the energy present in the food?
mcqs.why: The energy present in food is usually expressed in calories (in practice kilocalories on food labels). The joule and kilojoule are the SI units of energy, but the calorie remains the customary unit for food energy, as the book states.

mcqs.q: 1(iii) What prefix is used for 10^-12?
mcqs.why: The prefix pico stands for 10^-12 (one trillionth). For comparison: giga = 10^9, mega = 10^6 and nano = 10^-9. ('Tessa' is not an SI prefix.)

mcqs.q: 1(iv) In SI unit of pressure is expressed in:
mcqs.why: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), which equals one newton per square metre (1 Pa = 1 N/m2). Although 'newton per metre square' describes the same quantity, the official SI unit name asked for is the pascal.

mcqs.q: 1(v) Which symbol is used for kilogram in SI units?
mcqs.why: Unit symbols are exact: the kilogram is written kg - small k for the prefix kilo and small g for gram. 'K' alone is the symbol of kelvin, and 'Kgm' is not an SI symbol.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) What does a mole represent?
mcqs.why: A mole represents a NUMBER of particles: one mole contains 6.022 x 10^23 particles (atoms, molecules or ions) - the Avogadro number. It is the SI unit for amount of substance, not a mass, volume or length.

mcqs.q: 1(vii) Which unit of volume should usually be used in Chemistry?
mcqs.why: In chemistry the volumes handled are small, so the cubic centimetre (cm3, equal to 1 mL) is the unit usually used, rather than the litre or the cubic metre.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) Express 0.000840 in scientific notation:
mcqs.why: Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit stands before it: 0.000840 -> 8.40, and the point has moved 4 places to the right, so the power is -4: 0.000840 = 8.40 x 10^-4. The trailing zero is kept because it is a significant figure.

mcqs.q: 1(ix) In SI units prefix nano means:
mcqs.why: In SI units the prefix nano means 10^-9 (one thousand-millionth), e.g. a nanometre is 10^-9 m. Pico is smaller still at 10^-12.

mcqs.q: 1(x) 65 degrees C is equivalent to:
mcqs.why: To convert Celsius to kelvin, add 273: T(K) = 65 + 273 = 338 K. Kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size; only their zero points differ.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) What is consistency of results?

Consistency of results means that repeated measurements or repeated experiments give the same (or very nearly the same) results: the results are reproducible and agree with one another. It is the sign of precise work and reliable technique.

Q: 2(ii) Why SI units are user friendly?

SI units are user friendly because they form one coherent, decimal system: all multiples and sub-multiples are in powers of ten (kilo, centi, milli...), so conversions are simple; the same units are understood all over the world; and all derived units are built directly from the seven base units without awkward conversion factors.

Q: 2(iii) Define systematic error and random error.

A systematic error is a constant error in the same direction in every measurement, caused by the instrument or method itself (e.g. a pipette that always delivers slightly less than its marked volume, or an unzeroed balance); it affects accuracy and can be corrected by calibration. A random error is an unpredictable, small variation that differs from one measurement to the next, caused by slight changes in conditions or technique; it affects precision and is reduced by averaging repeated readings.

Q: 2(iv) What is reason behind a random error?

Random errors arise from unpredictable small changes during an experiment: limitations of the instrument, environmental factors such as air currents or temperature fluctuations, and slight variations in the observer's procedure, e.g. reading a measuring cylinder from a slightly different angle each time.

Q: 2(v) Does systematic error affect the accuracy?

Yes. A systematic error shifts every measurement by the same amount away from the true value, so the results are consistently wrong: accuracy is exactly what a systematic error destroys. (It does not spoil precision, because the readings still agree with each other.)

Q: 2(vi) Which other systems of measurements are used apart from SI units?

Besides SI, other systems in use are the CGS system (centimetre-gram-second), the MKS system (metre-kilogram-second, from which SI grew), the FPS or Imperial system (foot-pound-second: inches, feet, pounds, gallons, still common in some countries), and local/indigenous units used in trade in our country.

Q: 2(vii) Define metre.

The metre is the SI base unit of length. It is defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second. (Originally it was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole.)

Q: 2(viii) Mention two benefits scientists get by using SI units.

(1) Communication: scientists everywhere understand the same units, so results can be shared, compared and repeated without confusion or conversion errors. (2) Convenience and coherence: SI is decimal and coherent, so calculations are simpler and derived units follow directly from the base units, making experimental work faster and more reliable.

mcqs.q: Consistency of results means that:
options: Results always equal the true value exactly
Only one measurement is ever taken
Repeated measurements or experiments give the same, or very nearly the same, results
mcqs.why: Consistency means the results are reproducible and agree with one another when the measurement or experiment is repeated. It is the sign of precise work and reliable technique.

mcqs.q: SI units are user friendly because they form:
options: One coherent decimal system, with multiples and sub-multiples in powers of ten, understood all over the world
A different system for every country
A system based on the number 12
A system with no derived units
mcqs.why: All SI multiples and sub-multiples are powers of ten (kilo, centi, milli...), so conversions are simple; the same units are understood worldwide; and all derived units are built directly from the seven base units without awkward conversion factors.

mcqs.q: A systematic error is:
options: A different random mistake each time
A constant error in the same direction in every measurement, caused by the instrument or method itself
An error that cancels itself out
An error found only in calculations
mcqs.why: Examples: a pipette that always delivers slightly less than its marked volume, or an unzeroed balance. A systematic error affects accuracy and can be corrected by calibration - unlike a random error, it does not average away.

mcqs.q: A random error is:
options: The same error repeated in every reading
An error caused by a broken instrument
An unpredictable small variation that differs from one measurement to the next
A mistake in writing the units
mcqs.why: Random errors come from slight changes in conditions or technique during the experiment. They affect precision and are reduced (not removed) by repeating the measurement several times and averaging.

mcqs.q: Random errors arise from causes such as:
options: A pipette with a constant fault
Instrument limitations, air currents, temperature fluctuations and slight variations in the observer's reading technique
mcqs.why: Reading a measuring cylinder from a slightly different angle each time, draughts on a balance and small temperature changes all introduce unpredictable variations - the sources of random error. (An unzeroed balance or faulty pipette causes systematic, not random, error.)

mcqs.q: A systematic error destroys accuracy because it:
options: Shifts every measurement by the same amount away from the true value, so the results are consistently wrong
mcqs.why: Because every reading is shifted in the same direction, the average is also shifted: accuracy is exactly what a systematic error destroys. Precision is not spoilt, since the readings still agree with each other - as with the balance that read 5.2 g every time for a 5.0 g mass.

mcqs.q: Apart from SI, another system of measurement in use is the:
options: CGS system (centimetre-gram-second) - and also MKS, FPS/Imperial and local units
mcqs.why: Other systems include CGS (centimetre, gram, second), MKS (metre, kilogram, second - from which SI grew), the FPS or Imperial system (foot, pound, second: inches, feet, pounds, gallons) and local indigenous units used in trade.

mcqs.q: The metre is defined as:
options: The length of the King's arm
The length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during 1/299,792,458 of a second
The distance from the equator to the pole
mcqs.why: The modern SI definition fixes the metre by the speed of light: light travels exactly 299,792,458 metres in one second in vacuum, so the metre is the distance light covers in 1/299,792,458 s. (Originally it was one ten-millionth of the equator-to-pole distance.)

mcqs.q: One benefit scientists get from using SI units is better communication, because:
options: Each scientist can invent personal units
Units need not be written with results
Conversion errors become impossible in daily life
Scientists everywhere understand the same units, so results can be shared, compared and repeated without confusion
mcqs.why: A result stated in SI units means the same thing in every laboratory in the world, so experiments can be repeated and data combined without conversion mistakes - a key reason SI is the language of science.

mcqs.q: SI units make calculations simpler because the system is:
options: Decimal and coherent - derived units follow directly from the base units with no awkward conversion factors
mcqs.why: Coherence means derived units are simple products/quotients of base units (e.g. pressure = force/area = N/m2 = Pa), and decimal prefixes handle all sizes. Experimental work becomes faster and more reliable.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) Compare the units in SI system with those in MKS system?

The MKS system uses three base units: metre, kilogram and second. The SI system grew out of MKS but is larger and fully coherent: it has seven base units (metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela) and a complete set of derived units built from them with prefixes in powers of ten. For the quantities common to both (length, mass, time) the units are identical; SI simply extends MKS to electricity, temperature, amount of substance and light, and standardises symbols and prefixes.

Q: 3(ii) What are five basic SI units which are used in Chemistry?

The five base SI units generally used in Chemistry are: metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, kelvin (K) for temperature and mole (mol) for amount of substance. (The other two base units, ampere and candela, are rarely needed in chemistry.)

Q: 3(iii) Explain the three units derived for the basic SI units.

The three derived units most used in Chemistry are built from the base units: (1) Volume: the cubic metre (m3), in practice the cubic centimetre (cm3), obtained from length cubed. (2) Pressure: the pascal (Pa), one newton per square metre, built from mass, length and time. (3) Density: kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m3), practically gram per cubic centimetre, built from mass divided by volume. (Energy in joules is another common derived unit.)

Q: 3(iv) Explain why do we prefer to use smaller units of mass and volume in Chemistry?

In the laboratory we work with small quantities of chemicals: a few grams of a solid and a few cubic centimetres of a liquid. Expressing these in kilograms and cubic metres would give tiny decimal numbers (0.005 kg, 0.000025 m3) that are awkward to write, read and calculate with, and invite mistakes. The smaller units gram and cubic centimetre give convenient, manageable numbers and are precise enough for laboratory work.

Q: 3(v) What difficulties we expect to encounter if we use different units of measurement in daily life.

If everyone used different units, measurements could not be compared or communicated: trade would be disputed, recipes, doses of medicines and engineering designs would go wrong during conversion, and scientific results could not be repeated. Conversion mistakes between systems have caused real accidents; a single standard system (SI) removes this confusion.

mcqs.q: The MKS system uses which three base units?
mcqs.why: MKS stands for metre-kilogram-second. The SI system grew out of MKS but is larger and fully coherent, with seven base units.

mcqs.q: The SI system has how many base units?
options: Seven: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela
mcqs.why: SI extends MKS by adding the ampere (electric current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance) and candela (luminous intensity) to the original metre, kilogram and second, and standardises symbols and prefixes in powers of ten.

mcqs.q: For length, mass and time, the SI units compared with the MKS units are:
options: Identical - SI simply extends MKS to more quantities
mcqs.why: SI grew out of MKS: for the quantities common to both (length, mass, time) the units are exactly the same. SI adds electricity, temperature, amount of substance and light, with a complete set of derived units.

mcqs.q: The five base SI units generally used in Chemistry are:
options: Metre, litre, second, degree Celsius and gram
Ampere, candela, metre, pound and second
Kelvin, mole, foot, gallon and hour
Metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K) and mole (mol)
mcqs.why: Chemistry mainly needs length, mass, time, temperature and amount of substance, so it uses m, kg, s, K and mol. The other two base units, ampere and candela, are rarely needed in chemistry.

mcqs.q: Which two SI base units are rarely needed in chemistry?
mcqs.why: The ampere (electric current) and candela (luminous intensity) belong mainly to physics and engineering; ordinary chemical work runs on m, kg, s, K and mol.

mcqs.q: The derived unit of volume is obtained from the base unit of length as:
options: Length cubed - the cubic metre (m3), in practice the cubic centimetre (cm3)
mcqs.why: Volume is a derived unit: (length)^3. The SI unit is the cubic metre, but laboratory work uses the cubic centimetre. Density (mass/volume) and pressure (force/area) are other derived units built the same way.

mcqs.q: The pascal, the derived SI unit of pressure, is built as:
options: One newton per square metre, from mass, length and time
mcqs.why: Pressure = force/area. The newton itself is built from kg, m and s, so the pascal (Pa = N/m2) is a derived unit constructed entirely from base units - an example of SI coherence.

mcqs.q: Density, a derived unit, is expressed in SI as:
options: Kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m3), practically gram per cubic centimetre
mcqs.why: Density = mass/volume, so its unit combines the base unit of mass with the derived unit of volume: kg/m3 in SI, and g/cm3 in everyday laboratory use.

mcqs.q: Smaller units of mass and volume (gram, cubic centimetre) are preferred in chemistry because:
options: Laboratory quantities are small, and kilograms/cubic metres would give tiny, awkward decimal numbers that invite mistakes
Grams are more accurate than kilograms by nature
mcqs.why: A few grams of solid or a few cm3 of liquid written as 0.005 kg or 0.000025 m3 are awkward to write, read and calculate with. The gram and cubic centimetre give convenient, manageable numbers that are precise enough for laboratory work.

mcqs.q: If different units of measurement were used by everyone, the expected difficulty is that:
options: Measurements could not be compared or communicated - trade, medicine doses and engineering designs would go wrong in conversion
Only scientists would be affected, never the public
mcqs.why: Without a single standard, recipes, doses of medicines and engineering designs fail when converted, trade is disputed and scientific results cannot be repeated. Conversion mistakes between systems have caused real accidents; SI removes this confusion.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) What are our indigenous units of measurement of mass, volume and length?

Our traditional (indigenous) units are: for mass: tola, chhatank, pao, seer and maund (1 maund = 40 seers). For volume/capacity, liquids and grains were measured by vessels such as the pao and seer measures (and the gallon in the British period). For length: ungal (finger), girah, hath (cubit) and gaz (about a yard). These units varied from place to place, which is why they have been replaced by SI units.

Q: 4(ii) Elaborate the difference between precision and accuracy.

Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; precision is how close repeated measurements are to one another. They are independent: readings of 17.3, 17.4 and 17.2 g for an object of true mass 20 g are precise (they agree with each other) but not accurate (they are all far from 20 g); readings of 19.8, 20.5 and 19.6 g are more accurate on average but less precise (they are scattered). Good experimental work must be both accurate and precise.

Q: 4(iii) How can you avoid systematic errors in your measurements?

Systematic errors are avoided or corrected by: calibrating the instruments against known standards before use; checking and setting the zero of balances and other instruments; using certified/standard apparatus (pipettes, burettes, standard weights); finding the constant error of an instrument and applying its correction to every reading; and maintaining instruments properly so their graduations remain true.

Q: 4(iv) How do taking measurements in SI units ensure safety and reliability?

When every laboratory and industry uses the same SI units, a stated quantity means exactly the same thing everywhere: a dose of medicine, a load on a structure or a volume of a chemical is unambiguous, and instruments are calibrated to the same standards. This removes conversion mistakes, which are a real cause of accidents and overdoses, and makes results reliable and repeatable from one place to another.

Q: 4(v) Can a student be both inaccurate and imprecise in his measurements?

Yes. If a student's readings are scattered widely (imprecise) and also centred far from the true value (inaccurate), he is both inaccurate and imprecise: for example, readings of 15.1, 18.9 and 16.4 g for a 20 g object. This happens when there is both a systematic error (faulty instrument or zero error) and poor, inconsistent technique causing random errors.

mcqs.q: Our indigenous (traditional) units of mass include:
options: Tola, chhatank, pao, seer and maund (1 maund = 40 seers)
mcqs.why: Before SI, mass in our region was measured in tola, chhatank, pao, seer and maund, with 1 maund = 40 seers. Liquids and grains were measured by pao and seer vessels (and the gallon in the British period).

mcqs.q: Traditional units of length in our region included:
options: Ungal (finger), girah, hath (cubit) and gaz (about a yard)
mcqs.why: Length was measured with body-based units: the ungal (finger breadth), girah, hath (cubit, elbow to fingertip) and gaz (about a yard). Being based on the body, they were always available but not exact.

mcqs.q: Indigenous units were replaced by SI units mainly because they:
options: Varied from place to place, so measurements were not uniform
mcqs.why: A seer or a gaz in one town was not exactly the same in another, causing disputes in trade and errors in work. A single worldwide standard (SI) removed this variation.

mcqs.q: Accuracy of a measurement means:
options: How close the measurement is to the true value
How close repeated measurements are to one another
How quickly the measurement is taken
How neatly the result is written
mcqs.why: Accuracy = closeness to the true value. Precision = closeness of repeated measurements to one another. The two are independent: good experimental work must be both accurate and precise.

mcqs.q: Readings of 17.3, 17.4 and 17.2 g for an object whose true mass is 20 g are:
mcqs.why: The readings agree closely with each other (within 0.2 g), so the work is precise; but all are about 2.7 g away from the true 20 g, so it is not accurate - probably a systematic error such as an unzeroed balance.

mcqs.q: Readings of 19.8, 20.5 and 19.6 g for a 20 g object are best described as:
options: More accurate on average but less precise, because they are scattered around the true value
mcqs.why: Their average is close to 20 g, so they are fairly accurate, but the spread (19.6 to 20.5 g) shows random errors, so the work is less precise. Compare the in-text example: three readings of 5.2 g for a 5.0 g mass are precise but not accurate.

mcqs.q: A student weighs a substance three times and gets 5.2 g each time, though the true weight is 5.0 g. The constant difference suggests:
options: That the true weight must be wrong
A systematic error, e.g. the balance was not zeroed
mcqs.why: Identical readings show precision, but the steady 0.2 g excess shows inaccuracy from a systematic error - most likely the balance was not set to zero before use. Zeroing or calibrating the balance removes it.

mcqs.q: Systematic errors can be avoided or corrected by:
options: Calibrating instruments against known standards, setting the zero, using certified apparatus and applying the known correction to every reading
Changing the units of the result
mcqs.why: Calibration against standards, zero checks on balances, certified pipettes, burettes and standard weights, and applying an instrument's known constant correction to every reading are the standard defences against systematic error.

mcqs.q: Using SI units in every laboratory and industry ensures safety because:
options: A stated quantity means exactly the same thing everywhere, removing conversion mistakes that cause accidents and overdoses
mcqs.why: A dose of medicine, a load on a structure or a volume of chemical is unambiguous in SI, and instruments are calibrated to the same standards everywhere. This makes results reliable and repeatable from place to place - and prevents real accidents caused by conversion errors.

mcqs.q: A student CAN be both inaccurate and imprecise when:
options: His readings are identical and correct
His readings are widely scattered AND centred far from the true value, e.g. 15.1, 18.9 and 16.4 g for a 20 g object
He repeats the measurement many times
mcqs.why: Scattered readings (15.1 to 18.9 g) show imprecision from random errors, while their centre (~16.8 g) lies far from 20 g, showing inaccuracy from a systematic error. Both faults together - a faulty instrument plus inconsistent technique - make work both inaccurate and imprecise.

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) Elaborate the importance of using SI units in space exploration.

Space missions are international projects in which components, fuel quantities, thrust, distances and timings are supplied by many countries and companies. If all of them use SI units, the data fit together exactly and no conversion mistakes can occur. A famous failure caused by mixing units (pound-force seconds instead of newton seconds) destroyed NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter in 1999. Uniform SI units are therefore essential for the safety, accuracy and success of space exploration.

mcqs.q: SI units are important in space exploration because space missions are:
options: Run by a single village team
International projects in which components, fuel, thrust, distances and timings from many countries must fit together exactly
mcqs.why: Many countries and companies supply parts and data for one mission. If all use SI units, the data fit together exactly and no conversion mistakes can occur - essential for safety, accuracy and success.

mcqs.q: NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was destroyed in 1999 because:
options: The spacecraft ran out of fuel by design
The crew made an arithmetic slip in addition
Units were mixed - pound-force seconds were used instead of newton seconds for thrust impulse
mcqs.why: One team reported the thruster impulse in pound-force seconds while the navigation software expected newton seconds. The wrong conversion sent the orbiter too low into the Martian atmosphere and it was destroyed - the most famous lesson on mixing units.

mcqs.q: The Mars Climate Orbiter failure teaches that mixing unit systems in a project can cause:
options: Conversion mistakes that destroy the whole mission
mcqs.why: A single unconverted quantity was enough to lose a spacecraft. Uniform SI units remove conversion steps, and with them the chance of such fatal mistakes - the core argument of this investigative answer.

mcqs.q: In SI, the impulse of a rocket thruster is expressed in:
mcqs.why: Thrust is a force (newtons) acting for a time (seconds), so impulse is measured in newton seconds in SI. The orbiter was lost precisely because pound-force seconds were supplied where newton seconds were expected.

mcqs.q: Fuel quantities, thrust values, distances and timings supplied by different countries for one mission must:
options: Each use a different local system
Be stated in the same (SI) units so that they fit together exactly
Be kept secret from other teams
mcqs.why: International cooperation works only when every number means the same to everyone. SI provides that common language for all mission data.

mcqs.q: Using one worldwide system (SI) in space projects removes the need for:
options: Risky conversions between different unit systems during the mission
mcqs.why: Every conversion is a chance to err. With SI used from design to flight, quantities pass from team to team unchanged, and the conversion-error risk disappears.

mcqs.q: The destruction of the Mars Climate Orbiter happened in the year:
mcqs.why: The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in September 1999 when it entered the Martian atmosphere too low because of the pound-force/newton unit mix-up.

mcqs.q: Quantities such as thrust and distance in a space mission are safety-critical because a wrong value can:
options: Only change the colour of reports
Send the spacecraft on a wrong path and destroy it
Have no effect once the craft is launched
Be corrected by the spacecraft itself in all cases
mcqs.why: Navigation depends entirely on measured and calculated quantities. The orbiter's wrong impulse value changed its trajectory fatally - which is why uniform, reliable SI measurement is a safety matter, not a formality.

mcqs.q: Uniform SI units in space exploration are essential for:
options: The safety, accuracy and success of the mission
mcqs.why: The investigative answer concludes: with components and data coming from many sources, only a single standard system guarantees that everything fits - keeping missions safe, accurate and successful.

mcqs.q: A team that supplies data in Imperial units to a project designed in SI creates the risk that:
options: Someone must convert the values, and a conversion mistake can occur
mcqs.why: This is exactly what happened with the Mars Climate Orbiter: data in pound-force seconds met software expecting newton seconds. Mixed systems force conversions, and conversions invite the mistakes that uniform SI avoids.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1(i) Safety in the chemistry laboratory is:
