(a) the responsibility of the students only (b) the responsibility of the professor only (c) the responsibility of the lab. incharge only (d) a shared responsibility
Correct answer: a shared responsibility

Q: 1(ii) Accidents often result from:

(a) making mistakes (b) failure to use common sense (c) failure to follow instructions (d) all of the above
Correct answer: all of the above

Q: 1(iii) The label "Warning" on a chemical bottle signifies:

(a) that the chemical can cause less serious injury (b) that the chemical can cause serious injury (c) that user should be careful when using chemical (d) that user should open it only in the presence of a teacher
Correct answer: that the chemical can cause less serious injury

Q: 1(iv) The label "Corrosive" on a chemical bottle indicates:

(a) that the material is an oxidizing agent (b) that the material can degrade rapidly upon exposure (c) that its contact destroys living tissue (d) that the chemical can explode
Correct answer: that its contact destroys living tissue

Q: 1(v) Example of highly toxic chemical:

(a) Ethanol (b) Acetic acid (c) Potassium cyanide (d) Potassium permanganate
Correct answer: Potassium cyanide

Q: 1(vi) Example of self-reactive chemical:

(a) Potassium (b) Phenol (c) Picric acid (d) n-Hexane
Correct answer: Picric acid

Q: 1(vii) When diluting an acid with water:

(a) do it quickly (b) do not stir the container (c) always add acid to water (d) always add water to acid
Correct answer: always add acid to water

Q: 1(viii) What should you do in case of a fire drill in the lab.?

(a) run to safety shower (b) climb into the fume cupboard (c) close gas valves and turn off all equipments (d) carry chemicals out of the lab.
Correct answer: close gas valves and turn off all equipments

mcqs.q: 1(i) Safety in the chemistry laboratory is:
options: the responsibility of the students only
the responsibility of the professor only
the responsibility of the lab. incharge only
mcqs.why: Safety in the chemistry laboratory is a shared responsibility: the teacher, the lab incharge and every student must all follow the safety rules. No single person can keep a laboratory safe alone.

mcqs.q: 1(ii) Accidents often result from:
options: Making mistakes, failing to use common sense and failing to follow instructions
Reading the label carefully before use
Working quietly under the teacher's supervision
mcqs.why: Laboratory accidents usually have human causes: making mistakes, failure to use common sense, and failure to follow instructions - all three together. (The book's own option 'all of the above' has been written out in full in this quiz, so that the correct option states the causes directly.)

mcqs.q: 1(iii) The label "Warning" on a chemical bottle signifies:
options: that the chemical can cause less serious injury
that the chemical can cause serious injury
that user should be careful when using chemical
that user should open it only in the presence of a teacher
mcqs.why: Hazard labels have grades: 'Warning' signals a chemical that can cause a LESS serious injury, while the stronger signal word 'Danger' is used for chemicals that can cause serious injury. Either way, the user should be careful.

mcqs.q: 1(iv) The label "Corrosive" on a chemical bottle indicates:
options: that the material is an oxidizing agent
that the material can degrade rapidly upon exposure
that its contact destroys living tissue
mcqs.why: 'Corrosive' means the material attacks and destroys living tissue (skin, eyes) on contact - as concentrated acids and caustic alkalis do. It does not mean the chemical explodes or is merely an oxidising agent.

mcqs.q: 1(v) Example of highly toxic chemical:
mcqs.why: Potassium cyanide is a classic highly toxic chemical: a very small quantity can kill by stopping the body's use of oxygen. Ethanol and acetic acid are far less dangerous, and potassium permanganate is mainly an oxidising agent.

mcqs.q: 1(vi) Example of self-reactive chemical:
mcqs.why: Picric acid is a self-reactive chemical: it can react and explode by itself, especially when dry or subjected to shock, so it is stored moist and handled with great care. Potassium is water-reactive, phenol is toxic/corrosive and n-hexane is flammable - different hazard classes.

mcqs.q: 1(vii) When diluting an acid with water:
mcqs.why: Always add acid to water, slowly and with stirring - never water to acid. Diluting a concentrated acid releases much heat; adding acid to a large volume of water lets the water absorb the heat safely, whereas adding water to acid can boil the first drops and splash concentrated acid out.

mcqs.q: 1(viii) What should you do in case of a fire drill in the lab.?
options: close gas valves and turn off all equipments
carry chemicals out of the lab.
mcqs.why: In a fire drill (and a real evacuation) the first duties are to close the gas valves and turn off all equipment, so that no new fire or explosion is fed while people leave. Chemicals are left behind; the safety shower and fume cupboard are for emergencies at the bench, not for drills.

mcqs.q: Sodium and potassium metals are stored under oil in the laboratory because they:
options: React violently with water and even with moist air
mcqs.why: Sodium and potassium are reactive chemicals: they react violently with water (and with the moisture in air), producing fires, bursts of gas and severe burns. Storing them under oil keeps air and water away from them.

mcqs.q: Reactions that produce toxic or corrosive gases, such as the preparation of chlorine, must be carried out:
options: On an open bench near the class
mcqs.why: The fume cupboard draws the harmful vapours away from the worker and exhausts them safely outside. Reactions giving off chlorine, bromine, acid fumes, H2S or SO2 must never be done on an open bench.

lessons.title: Questions for Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 2(i) Name some corrosive chemicals.

Concentrated sulphuric acid, concentrated nitric acid and concentrated hydrochloric acid; sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide (caustic alkalis); and bromine. All of these destroy living tissue on contact and must be handled with gloves and goggles, and corrosive vapours in a fume cupboard.

Q: 2(ii) What type of safety precautions are adopted to avoid damage due to explosive chemicals?

Explosive chemicals are stored in small quantities, in a cool place away from heat, flames and direct sunlight; they are never struck, ground or subjected to friction or shock; bottles are not dropped and are opened carefully; they are kept away from oxidising agents and flammable materials, and handled with protective equipment under the teacher's supervision.

Q: 2(iii) What type of damages can reactive chemicals cause?

Reactive chemicals can react violently with air, water or other common substances, producing fires, explosions, bursts of toxic gas and severe burns; they can damage eyes and skin, destroy apparatus and injure everyone nearby. Examples: sodium and potassium react violently with water, and concentrated acids react dangerously with many substances.

Q: 2(iv) Indicate two such safety instructions which are required to avoid radiation.

(1) Minimise the time of exposure: stay near radioactive sources for as short a time as possible and keep a maximum distance from them (shielding with lead screens where provided). (2) Never handle radioactive material with bare hands or bring it near the body or food; use tongs, wear protective clothing, and work only under supervision following the posted radiation warnings.

Q: 2(v) Which chemicals can cause suffocation?

Asphyxiant chemicals and gases cause suffocation by replacing or blocking oxygen: carbon monoxide (which also poisons the blood), carbon dioxide in excess, nitrogen and other inert gases in confined spaces, and vapours of volatile solvents. They must be used in well-ventilated places with protective dress, as the chapter directs.

Q: 2(vi) Why signs and symbols are posted on lab. and chemical bottles?

Signs and symbols warn everyone, at a glance and in any language, about the nature of the hazard of a chemical (flammable, corrosive, toxic, explosive, radioactive, etc.), so that the handler takes the right precautions before opening or using it. They prevent accidents by people who might otherwise not know that a bottle contains a dangerous substance.

Q: 2(vii) How fire caused by chemicals should be handled?

Stay calm and alert others; for a small fire use the correct fire extinguisher (never water on an oil, solvent or electrical fire: use CO2 or dry powder/sand), close doors to confine the fire, switch off gas and electricity, and evacuate if the fire spreads. If a person's clothing catches fire, use the safety shower or a fire blanket. Inform the teacher and call the emergency staff.

Q: 2(viii) Why emergency drills are important to face emergency situations?

Emergency drills train everyone to act quickly and correctly without panic: students learn the escape routes, the location and use of the fire extinguisher, safety shower and first-aid box, and their own duties (closing gas valves, switching off equipment). In a real emergency this practice saves time, prevents confusion and protects lives.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a corrosive chemical?
options: Concentrated sulphuric acid (and other concentrated acids, caustic alkalis and bromine)
mcqs.why: Corrosive chemicals destroy living tissue on contact: concentrated sulphuric, nitric and hydrochloric acids; sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide (caustic alkalis); and bromine. They are handled with gloves and goggles, and their vapours only in a fume cupboard.

mcqs.q: Explosive chemicals are stored safely by keeping them:
options: In large bottles near the burner
In small quantities, in a cool place away from heat, flames and direct sunlight
In sunlight to keep them dry
mcqs.why: Explosive chemicals are kept in small quantities in a cool place away from heat, flames and direct sunlight, away from oxidising agents and flammable materials, and are handled with protective equipment under the teacher's supervision.

mcqs.q: Explosive chemicals must never be struck, ground or dropped because:
options: Their bottles are made of thin glass only
Friction or shock can detonate them
mcqs.why: A sudden shock supplies the activation energy that starts the decomposition of an unstable explosive chemical; the heat released then triggers the rest almost instantaneously. Bottles are opened carefully and never subjected to friction or shock.

mcqs.q: Reactive chemicals can cause damage because they:
options: React violently with air, water or other common substances, producing fires, explosions, toxic gas and severe burns
mcqs.why: Sodium and potassium react violently with water, and concentrated acids react dangerously with many substances. Reactive chemicals can damage eyes and skin, destroy apparatus and injure everyone nearby.

mcqs.q: Two safety instructions for protection from radiation are:
options: Minimise the time of exposure and keep maximum distance from the source, using lead shielding where provided
Stay near the source for a long time
Hold the source close to the body
mcqs.why: Radiation protection rests on time, distance and shielding: stay near radioactive sources for as short a time as possible, keep as far away as possible, and use lead screens where provided.

mcqs.q: Radioactive material must never be handled with bare hands; instead you should:
options: Use tongs, wear protective clothing and work only under supervision, following the posted warnings
Bring it near food to test it
mcqs.why: Radioactive material is handled with tongs, never with bare hands, never brought near the body or food, and only under supervision following the posted radiation warnings - the trefoil symbol marks where it is present.

mcqs.q: Chemicals and gases that can cause suffocation include:
options: Carbon monoxide, excess carbon dioxide, nitrogen and other inert gases in confined spaces, and solvent vapours
Nitrogen from a fertiliser bag in the open air only
mcqs.why: Asphyxiants replace or block oxygen: CO (which also poisons the blood), CO2 in excess, inert gases accumulating in confined spaces and vapours of volatile solvents. They must be used in well-ventilated places with protective dress.

mcqs.q: Signs and symbols are posted on the lab and on chemical bottles so that:
options: Only the teacher can identify chemicals
Everyone can see the hazard at a glance, in any language, and take the right precautions before handling the chemical
mcqs.why: A pictogram warns instantly - flammable, corrosive, toxic, explosive, radioactive - whatever language the handler speaks. This forewarning prevents accidents by people who might not otherwise know that a bottle contains a dangerous substance.

mcqs.q: A fire caused by oil, a solvent or electricity must NOT be fought with water; instead use:
options: A CO2 or dry-powder extinguisher, or sand
An open flame to burn it off
mcqs.why: Water spreads burning oil, conducts electricity and can flash to steam. For chemical fires: stay calm, alert others, use the correct extinguisher (CO2 or dry powder/sand), close doors to confine the fire, switch off gas and electricity, and evacuate if it spreads.

mcqs.q: Emergency drills are important because they:
options: Give students a break from lessons
Train everyone to act quickly and correctly without panic - knowing escape routes, extinguishers, the safety shower, the first-aid box and their own duties
Are needed only once in a school career
mcqs.why: In a drill, students learn the escape routes, the location and use of the fire extinguisher, safety shower and first-aid box, and duties such as closing gas valves and switching off equipment. In a real emergency this practice saves time, prevents confusion and protects lives.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 3(i) How will you handle an emergency situation caused by fire due to short circuiting?

Stay calm and do not panic. Immediately switch off the main electrical supply to stop the short circuit; do not touch the burning equipment or use water while the current is on. Alert everyone to evacuate, close doors to confine the fire, and use a CO2 or dry-powder extinguisher (suitable for electrical fires). Call and assist the emergency staff/fire brigade, and give first aid to any injured person.

Q: 3(ii) What type of reactions should be carried out in fume cupboard?

Reactions that produce toxic, corrosive or suffocating gases and vapours must be carried out in a fume cupboard, e.g. preparing chlorine or bromine, reactions of concentrated acids, and reactions giving off acid fumes or poisonous gases like H2S and SO2. The fume cupboard draws the harmful vapours away and exhausts them safely outside.

Q: 3(iii) Put forward at least two suggestions to improve safety in the lab.

Suggestions: (1) Make personal protective equipment (lab coat, goggles, gloves) compulsory and check its use, with a safety briefing and a signed set of rules before the first practical. (2) Keep quantities of hazardous chemicals small, store them properly labelled in locked cupboards, and maintain and regularly inspect the safety equipment (extinguishers, showers, first-aid box) and conduct regular emergency drills. (Other good suggestions: better ventilation, no eating in the lab, immediate reporting of breakages and spills.)

Q: 3(iv) Can you identify warning symbols posted for radiation and asphyxiant chemicals?

Yes. The radiation warning symbol is the trefoil: three black (or magenta) blades radiating from a central disc on a yellow background, posted where radioactive material is present. For asphyxiant gases the relevant posted warnings are the 'toxic gas' skull-and-crossbones type hazard pictogram and the gas-cylinder symbol, together with the instruction to use the substance only in a well-ventilated place/fume cupboard; students should be able to recognise these before entering the lab. (Describe the symbols in the notes: yellow triangle/disc with the trefoil for radiation; skull and crossbones for lethal/toxic gases.)

Q: 3(v) Why sudden shock can cause some chemicals to explode?

Some chemicals (such as picric acid and certain peroxides and nitrates) are unstable: their molecules store a lot of energy and can decompose into gases almost instantaneously. A sudden shock supplies the activation energy locally and starts the decomposition at one point; the heat released triggers the neighbouring molecules, so the decomposition runs through the whole sample in a fraction of a second: an explosion. That is why such chemicals must never be struck, dropped or ground.

mcqs.q: In a fire caused by short circuiting, the FIRST thing to do is:
options: Pour water on the burning equipment
Switch off the main electrical supply to stop the short circuit
Touch the equipment to check it
Open all the windows and continue working
mcqs.why: Stay calm. Switching off the main supply stops the current feeding the fire. Never touch the burning equipment or use water while the current is on - water conducts electricity and would electrocute the rescuer.

mcqs.q: For an electrical fire, the suitable extinguisher is:
options: A bucket of sand mixed with water
No extinguisher - only blowing on it
mcqs.why: CO2 and dry powder do not conduct electricity, so they are safe on electrical fires. After switching off the supply and alerting everyone, evacuate, close doors to confine the fire, call the fire brigade and give first aid to any injured person.

mcqs.q: Reactions that must be carried out in a fume cupboard are those that produce:
options: Toxic, corrosive or suffocating gases and vapours - e.g. preparing chlorine or bromine, or reactions of concentrated acids
mcqs.why: Examples include preparing chlorine or bromine, reactions of concentrated acids, and reactions giving off acid fumes or poisonous gases like H2S and SO2. The fume cupboard draws the harmful vapours away and exhausts them safely outside.

mcqs.q: The fume cupboard protects the worker by:
options: Drawing harmful vapours away from the bench and exhausting them safely outside
mcqs.why: A continuous draught of air flows into the fume cupboard and up its duct, carrying toxic and corrosive vapours away from the student's face and out of the building.

mcqs.q: One suggestion to improve safety in the lab is to:
options: Make personal protective equipment (lab coat, goggles, gloves) compulsory, with a safety briefing and a signed set of rules before the first practical
Let students mix any chemicals freely
mcqs.why: Compulsory PPE, checked in use, plus a safety briefing and signed rules before the first practical, prevent most injuries before they can happen - the first of the book's suggestions for improving lab safety.

mcqs.q: Hazardous chemicals in the lab should be stored:
options: In unlabelled bottles on open shelves
In small quantities, properly labelled, in locked cupboards, with safety equipment regularly inspected and drills held regularly
mcqs.why: Small stocks, correct labels and locked storage limit any accident; maintained extinguishers, showers and first-aid boxes, and regular emergency drills, complete the system of lab safety.

mcqs.q: The radiation warning symbol (trefoil) consists of:
options: A skull and crossbones on white
A blue triangle with an exclamation mark
Three black (or magenta) blades radiating from a central disc on a yellow background
mcqs.why: The trefoil is posted wherever radioactive material is present. Recognising it - and the skull-and-crossbones for lethal/toxic gases, with the gas-cylinder symbol - is part of basic lab safety.

mcqs.q: The warning symbol for lethal/toxic gases is the:
options: Skull and crossbones pictogram (with the gas-cylinder symbol and a 'use in a ventilated place' instruction)
mcqs.why: Asphyxiant and toxic gases are marked with the skull-and-crossbones hazard pictogram and the gas-cylinder symbol, together with the instruction to use the substance only in a well-ventilated place or fume cupboard.

mcqs.q: A sudden shock can make some chemicals explode because:
options: Shock turns them into gases slowly over days
Their unstable molecules store much energy; the shock supplies activation energy at one point and the decomposition runs through the whole sample in a fraction of a second
mcqs.why: In chemicals such as picric acid, certain peroxides and nitrates, the molecules can decompose into gases almost instantaneously. Shock starts the decomposition locally; the heat released triggers neighbouring molecules, and the reaction races through the sample - an explosion. Such chemicals must never be struck, dropped or ground.

mcqs.q: Which of these chemicals is known to be shock-sensitive?
mcqs.why: Picric acid (also the book's example of a self-reactive chemical) and certain peroxides and nitrates can detonate from shock or friction, which is why picric acid is stored moist and handled with special care.

lessons.title: Descriptive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 4(i) Explain hazards due to explosive and toxic chemicals.

Explosive chemicals can detonate from shock, heat or friction, producing a sudden blast, flying debris and fire that can kill or seriously injure people and destroy the laboratory. Toxic chemicals poison the body through inhalation, skin contact or swallowing: they can damage the lungs, blood, liver and nervous system, cause unconsciousness and even death, sometimes from very small quantities (e.g. potassium cyanide). Both classes therefore need strict storage, labelling and handling rules.

Q: 4(ii) Write down five such common safety instructions which are used to avoid all types of hazards.

Five common safety instructions: (1) Wear personal protective equipment (lab coat, safety goggles, gloves) before entering the lab. (2) Never eat, drink or taste anything in the lab, and never smell a chemical directly. (3) Read the label and follow the teacher's instructions before using any chemical; never mix chemicals on your own. (4) Always add acid to water, never water to acid, and heat test tubes with the mouth pointed away from everyone. (5) Know the location and use of the fire extinguisher, safety shower and first-aid box, and report every accident, spill or breakage to the teacher at once.

Q: 4(iii) Explain the importance of warning signs and symbols to avoid any accident in the lab.

Warning signs and symbols communicate the hazard instantly to every person, whatever his language or experience: they tell whether a substance is flammable, corrosive, toxic, explosive or radioactive before the bottle is even opened. This forewarning makes the handler use the correct protective equipment and method, prevents the wrong use or mixing of chemicals, and so avoids accidents, injuries and damage in the laboratory.

Q: 4(iv) Name some toxic chemicals. Describe the effects of spreading toxic gas in the lab.

Toxic chemicals include potassium cyanide, mercury and its compounds, chlorine, carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulphide and benzene. If a toxic gas spreads in the lab it is inhaled by everyone present: it irritates and burns the eyes, nose, throat and lungs, causes coughing, suffocation and unconsciousness, and in higher concentration can kill within minutes. The correct response is to stop the source if safe, open ventilation/evacuate the lab at once, move the affected persons to fresh air and call emergency help.

Q: 4(v) A student has spilled over a corrosive and explosive chemical due to an accident. Which emergency measures you will take to tackle the situation.

Stay calm and do not panic. Alert everyone and evacuate the immediate area, keeping people away from the spilt (possibly explosive) chemical; do not touch it and avoid any shock, friction or spark near it. If the chemical has fallen on the student, remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin at once under the safety shower with plenty of water, and give first aid. Inform the teacher/lab incharge immediately and call the emergency staff; the spill of an explosive chemical should be cleaned only by trained staff following the safety procedure. Close doors to confine any fire and use the extinguisher only if a fire starts and it is safe to do so.

mcqs.q: Explosive chemicals are hazardous because they can:
options: Detonate from shock, heat or friction, producing a sudden blast, flying debris and fire that can kill or seriously injure
Damage only the bottle they are in
mcqs.why: An explosion in a laboratory can kill or seriously injure people and destroy the laboratory itself. Explosive chemicals therefore need strict storage, labelling and handling rules.

mcqs.q: Toxic chemicals poison the body through inhalation, skin contact or swallowing, and can:
options: Improve health in small doses by rule
Affect only the sense of smell
Damage the lungs, blood, liver and nervous system, cause unconsciousness and even death - sometimes from very small quantities, e.g. potassium cyanide
mcqs.why: Because even tiny amounts of a chemical like potassium cyanide can kill, toxic chemicals are stored, labelled and handled under strict rules, and their gases are used only in a fume cupboard.

mcqs.q: A common safety instruction before starting any practical is to:
options: Wear personal protective equipment - lab coat, safety goggles and gloves
Taste a small amount of each chemical
Work without a lab coat in summer
mcqs.why: PPE is the first of the five common safety instructions: (1) wear lab coat, goggles and gloves; (2) never eat, drink, taste or smell chemicals directly; (3) read the label and follow the teacher, never mixing chemicals on your own; (4) add acid to water and point heated test tubes away; (5) know the safety equipment and report every accident at once.

mcqs.q: In the laboratory you must never:
options: Read the label of a bottle
Eat, drink or taste anything, or smell a chemical directly
mcqs.why: Food and drink pick up poisonous contamination, tasting can poison directly, and sniffing a bottle can burn the nose and lungs with corrosive vapour. Chemicals are smelt, if at all, only by wafting the vapour gently - never directly.

mcqs.q: Before using any chemical, a student should:
options: Mix it with another chemical to test it
Read its label and follow the teacher's instructions, and never mix chemicals on his own
mcqs.why: The label tells the hazard and the method; the teacher's instructions give the safe procedure. Mixing chemicals on your own can produce toxic gases, fires or explosions.

mcqs.q: Every student must know, before an emergency happens:
options: Only the location of the exit
The home address of the lab incharge
The location and use of the fire extinguisher, safety shower and first-aid box, and must report every accident, spill or breakage to the teacher at once
mcqs.why: Quick, correct first action limits every accident: extinguish a small fire, wash chemicals off under the safety shower, give first aid - and always inform the teacher immediately, even for a minor spill or breakage.

mcqs.q: Warning signs and symbols prevent accidents because they:
options: Communicate the hazard instantly to every person, whatever his language or experience, before the bottle is even opened
Replace the need for protective equipment
mcqs.why: A symbol tells at a glance whether a substance is flammable, corrosive, toxic, explosive or radioactive. Forewarned, the handler uses the correct protective equipment and method, and avoids wrong use or mixing - so accidents, injuries and damage are prevented.

mcqs.q: If a toxic gas spreads in the laboratory, it harms everyone present by:
options: Irritating and burning the eyes, nose, throat and lungs, causing coughing, suffocation and unconsciousness - and death within minutes at high concentration
Only affecting the person who made it
mcqs.why: Toxic gases such as chlorine, carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulphide (and vapours of benzene) spread through the whole room and are inhaled by all. The correct response is to stop the source if safe, ventilate and evacuate at once, move affected persons to fresh air and call emergency help.

mcqs.q: The correct response when a toxic gas spreads in the lab is to:
options: Close all windows and stay inside
Stop the source if safe, open ventilation and evacuate the lab at once, move affected persons to fresh air and call emergency help
Spray water in the air and remain seated
mcqs.why: Fresh air is the first treatment for gas inhalation, and no one should remain in the contaminated room. Evacuation, ventilation and emergency help - in that order - are the safe response.

mcqs.q: A student spills a corrosive and explosive chemical. The correct emergency measures are to:
options: Wipe it up quickly with bare hands
Stamp on it to neutralise it

Evacuate the immediate area, keep everyone away without touching the chemical or causing shock or sparks, wash any skin contact under the safety shower, inform the teacher at once and let trained staff clean the spill
mcqs.why: Stay calm: alert everyone and clear the area (an explosive spill must not be touched, shocked or sparked); if the chemical is on the student, remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin at once under the safety shower with plenty of water and give first aid; inform the teacher/lab incharge and call emergency staff - only trained staff clean up an explosive spill.

lessons.title: Investigative Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 5(i) A few decades ago, a tanker carrying poisonous chlorine gas leaked and the gas spread over a large area in Lahore. The accident killed a few persons as well as animals. Give some concrete proposals to avoid such an accident in future.

Concrete proposals: (1) Use specially designed, double-walled and pressure-tested tankers for chlorine and other toxic gases, with regular inspection and certification, and valves fitted with leak detectors and emergency shut-off systems. (2) Transport such chemicals on fixed, less populated routes, in daylight, with trained drivers and an escort, and with the hazard symbols clearly displayed. (3) Set up a quick emergency response system: the tanker crew and the local administration should have gas masks, neutralising material (e.g. lime/alkali for chlorine) and a plan to evacuate and warn the public immediately. (4) Enforce strict laws and penalties for negligence, maintain the vehicles regularly, and train drivers in first response. (5) Store and fill such gases away from populated areas.

mcqs.q: To transport chlorine and other toxic gases safely, tankers should be:
options: Specially designed, double-walled and pressure-tested, with regular inspection and certification
mcqs.why: After the Lahore chlorine tanker accident, the first proposal is about the vehicle itself: double-walled, pressure-tested tankers, regularly inspected and certified, so the gas cannot escape in the first place.

mcqs.q: The valves of a toxic-gas tanker should be fitted with:
options: Leak detectors and emergency shut-off systems
mcqs.why: Leak detectors warn of an escape at once, and emergency shut-off systems let the crew stop the leak before the gas spreads over a populated area.

mcqs.q: Toxic gases should be transported:
options: On fixed, less populated routes, in daylight, with trained drivers and an escort, and hazard symbols clearly displayed
By untrained drivers without any markings
Along any route the driver chooses
mcqs.why: Choosing quiet routes and daylight hours, trained and escorted drivers, and clear hazard symbols all reduce both the chance of an accident and the number of people exposed if one occurs.

mcqs.q: The tanker crew and local administration should be ready with an emergency response system that includes:
options: Extra fuel for a quick escape
Gas masks, neutralising material (e.g. lime/alkali for chlorine) and a plan to evacuate and warn the public immediately
mcqs.why: Chlorine can be neutralised by alkalis such as lime. Crews with gas masks and neutralising material, plus a ready plan to warn and evacuate the public, can limit an accident's harm within minutes.

mcqs.q: Chlorine gas leaking from a tanker can be neutralised with:
options: Sand only, which neutralises it chemically
mcqs.why: Chlorine is an acidic gas and reacts with alkalis; lime/alkali spread at the leak absorbs and neutralises it. This is why neutralising material is part of the emergency kit for chlorine transport.

mcqs.q: Accidents like the Lahore chlorine leak can be discouraged by:
options: Strict laws and penalties for negligence, regular vehicle maintenance and training drivers in first response
Allowing any vehicle to carry gas
mcqs.why: Enforced laws and penalties make owners maintain vehicles and follow the rules; regular maintenance prevents failures, and drivers trained in first response act correctly in the first critical minutes.

mcqs.q: Toxic gases should be stored and filled:
options: In the middle of a city
mcqs.why: Even with the best tankers, storage and filling stations are fixed risk points; keeping them away from homes and schools means a leak there exposes far fewer people.

mcqs.q: If a toxic-gas leak occurs despite precautions, the public around the area should be:
options: Told nothing until the gas clears
Asked to gather near the tanker
Warned and evacuated immediately by the crew and the local administration
mcqs.why: Chlorine spread over a large area in the Lahore accident and killed people and animals. Immediate warning and evacuation upwind are what save lives when prevention fails.

mcqs.q: Drivers of toxic-gas tankers should be trained in:
options: First response - what to do immediately when a leak or accident happens
mcqs.why: The driver is the first person at the scene: shutting off the leak, using the gas mask and neutraliser, and raising the alarm are first-response skills that every such driver must be trained in.

mcqs.q: Displaying hazard symbols clearly on a toxic-gas tanker helps because:
options: Other road users and emergency staff can see the danger at a glance and keep away or respond correctly
It makes the tanker look official
It replaces the need for inspections
mcqs.why: Just as in the laboratory, symbols communicate the hazard instantly to everyone - warning the public to keep away and telling the fire and rescue staff exactly what they are dealing with.
